abstract: Typical methods for gradient descent in neural network learning involve calculation of derivatives based on a detailed knowledge of the network model. This requires extensive, time consuming calculations for each pat(cid:173) tern presentation and high precision that makes it difficult to implement in VLSI. We present here a perturbation technique that measures, not calculates, the gradient. Since the technique uses the actual network as a measuring device, errors in modeling neuron activation and synaptic weights do not cause errors in gradient descent. The method is parallel in nature and easy to implement in VLSI. We describe the theory of such an algorithm, an analysis of its domain of applicability, some simulations using it and an outline of a hardware implementation.

We present here a perturbation technique that measures, not calculates, the gradient. Since the technique uses the actual network as a measuring device, errors in modeling neuron activation and synaptic weights do not cause errors in gradient descent. paragraphs: Training a neural network by gradient descent usually requires calculating how changes in its parameters affect error. The paper identifies a hardware difficulty with this approach: those calculations can be extensive and depend on a detailed, sufficiently precise model of the network. Such requirements complicate implementation in analog VLSI circuits.

The proposed method uses perturbations to measure the gradient through the actual network. Instead of relying entirely on calculated derivatives of an idealized model, it observes the system's response to changes. Consequently, mismatches in models of neuron activation or synaptic weights do not themselves introduce the corresponding errors into gradient descent.

The method is parallel and is described as straightforward to implement in VLSI. The paper develops its theory, examines where it applies, presents simulations, and outlines a hardware implementation. Its practical importance is the connection between learning and direct physical measurement: the circuit being trained also supplies information needed to guide its own parameter updates.
summary.tldr: A parallel perturbation method measures learning gradients directly from analog neural hardware, avoiding errors caused by inaccurate network models.

title: A Parallel Gradient Descent Method for Learning in Analog VLSI Neural Networks

abstract: We present a new algorithm, Prioritized Sweeping, for efficient prediction and control of stochastic Markov systems. Incremental learning methods such as Temporal Differencing and Q-Iearning have fast real time perfor(cid:173) mance. Classical methods are slower, but more accurate, because they make full use of the observations. Prioritized Sweeping aims for the best of both worlds. It uses all previous experiences both to prioritize impor(cid:173) tant dynamic programming sweeps and to guide the exploration of state(cid:173) space. We compare Prioritized Sweeping with other reinforcement learning schemes for a number of different stochastic optimal control problems. It successfully solves large state-space real time problems with which other methods have difficulty. 1 STOCHASTIC PREDICTION The paper introduces a memory-based technique, prioritized 6weeping, which is used both for stochastic prediction and reinforcement learning. A fuller version of this paper is in preparation [Moore and Atkeson, 1992]. Consider the 500 state Markov system depicted in Figure 1. The system has sixteen absorbing states, depicted by white and black circles. The prediction problem is to estimate, for every state, the long-term probability that it will terminate in a white, rather than black, circle. The data available to the learner is a sequence of observed state transitions. Let us consider two existing methods along with prioritized sweeping.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Prioritized Sweeping for prediction and control in stochastic Markov systems. It addresses a tradeoff between fast incremental learning and more computationally demanding methods that make fuller use of observations. The aim is to preserve responsiveness while gaining more value from accumulated experience.

Prioritized Sweeping uses previous experiences to decide which dynamic programming sweeps deserve attention and to guide exploration of the state space. A sweep revisits estimates using available information; prioritizing these computations concentrates effort on important updates. Memory therefore supports both internal computation and decisions about what parts of the environment to explore.

The paper compares the method with other reinforcement learning approaches on several stochastic optimal control problems and reports success on large-state-space real-time problems that challenge other methods. The supplied example also illustrates prediction: estimating the probability of eventually reaching one kind of terminal state from observed transitions. The central contribution is coordinating experience reuse, computational priorities, and exploration within one learning method.
summary.tldr: Prioritized Sweeping uses stored experience to focus planning updates and exploration, enabling efficient prediction and control in large stochastic systems.

title: Memory-Based Reinforcement Learning: Efficient Computation with Prioritized Sweeping

abstract: Casting neural network weights in symbolic terms is crucial for interpreting and explaining the behavior of a network. Additionally, in some domains, a symbolic description may lead to more robust generalization. We present a principled approach to symbolic rule extraction based on the notion of weight templates, parameterized regions of weight space corresponding to specific symbolic expressions. With an appropriate choice of representation, we show how template parameters may be efficiently identified and instantiated to yield the optimal match to a unit's actual weights. Depending on the requirements of the application domain, our method can accommodate arbitrary disjunctions and conjunctions with O(k) complexity, simple n-of-m expressions with O( k!) complexity, or a more general class of recursive n-of-m expressions with O(k!) complexity, where k is the number of inputs to a unit. Our method of rule extraction offers several benefits over alternative approaches in the literature, and simulation results on a variety of problems demonstrate its effectiveness.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to translate neural network weights into symbolic rules. Such rules can help explain network behavior, and the authors note that symbolic descriptions may also improve generalization in some domains. The central problem is to connect a unit's numerical parameters with a meaningful logical expression in a principled way.

The method uses weight templates: parameterized regions of weight space associated with particular symbolic expressions. With an appropriate representation, template parameters can be identified and instantiated to find the optimal match to a unit's actual weights. This makes rule extraction a structured matching problem between learned numerical behavior and available symbolic forms.

The supported rule families have different computational costs. Arbitrary conjunctions and disjunctions can be handled in O(k), where k is the number of inputs. Simple and recursive n-of-m expressions require O(k!) under the stated method. These expressions describe threshold-like combinations of conditions. Simulations across several problems demonstrate effectiveness, while the complexity results make the cost of choosing richer rule forms explicit.
summary.tldr: Parameterized weight templates extract symbolic rules from neural units, with explicit computational costs for different rule families.

title: Template-Based Algorithms for Connectionist Rule Extraction

abstract: We report on our development of a high-performance system for neural network and other signal processing applications. We have designed and implemented a vector microprocessor and pack(cid:173) aged it as an attached processor for a conventional workstation. We present performance comparisons with commercial worksta(cid:173) tions on neural network backpropagation training. The SPERT-II system demonstrates significant speedups over extensively hand(cid:173) optimization code running on the workstations.

We have designed and implemented a vector microprocessor and pack(cid:173) aged it as an attached processor for a conventional workstation. We present performance comparisons with commercial worksta(cid:173) tions on neural network backpropagation training. The SPERT-II system demonstrates significant speedups over extensively hand(cid:173) optimization code running on the workstations.

paragraphs: The paper presents SPERT-II, a hardware system developed for neural network computation and other signal processing applications. The authors design and implement a vector microprocessor, then package it as an attached processor for a conventional workstation. The workstation can thus use an additional processor built for these computational workloads.

The evaluation focuses on neural network training with backpropagation. Performance is compared with commercial workstations running code that has received extensive manual optimization. This comparison matters because the reported advantage is measured against implementations whose software performance has already been carefully improved, giving the hardware result a demanding reference point.

SPERT-II delivers significant speedups in those training comparisons. The abstract presents the contribution as a completed processor and system implementation with demonstrated performance benefits. Its significance is the connection between processor design and the computational demands of neural training: an attached vector processor can substantially accelerate the evaluated backpropagation work while remaining part of a conventional workstation-based computing setup.
summary.tldr: SPERT-II is an attached vector processor that significantly accelerates backpropagation training relative to heavily optimized workstation implementations.

title: SPERT-II: A Vector Microprocessor System and its Application to Large Problems in Backpropagation Training

abstract: A unique architecture of winner search hardware has been de(cid:173) veloped using a novel neuron-like high functionality device called Neuron MOS transistor (or vMOS in short) [1,2] as a key circuit element. The circuits developed in this work can find the location of the maximum (or minimum) signal among a number of input data on the continuous-time basis, thus enabling real-time winner tracking as well as fully-parallel sorting of multiple input data. We have developed two circuit schemes. One is an ensemble of self(cid:173) loop-selecting v M OS ring oscillators finding the winner as an oscil(cid:173) lating node. The other is an ensemble of vMOS variable threshold inverters receiving a common ramp-voltage for competitive excita(cid:173) tion where data sorting is conducted through consecutive winner search actions. Test circuits were fabricated by a double-polysilicon CMOS process and their operation has been experimentally veri(cid:173) fied.

paragraphs: This paper presents hardware for locating the largest or smallest signal among multiple inputs. Its key component is a neuron-like transistor called Neuron MOS. The circuits operate continuously in time, allowing the winning input to be tracked as signals change and supporting parallel processing for sorting multiple values.

The authors develop two circuit schemes. One uses an ensemble of ring oscillators with self-loop selection, where the winning location becomes an oscillating node. The other uses variable-threshold inverters driven by a shared ramp voltage. In that design, competitive excitation identifies winners, and a sequence of winner searches performs sorting.

The two schemes express selection through circuit dynamics: oscillation marks a winner in one, while responses to the common voltage ramp organize competition in the other. Test circuits were fabricated using a double-polysilicon CMOS process, and their operation was experimentally verified. The contribution therefore includes physical implementations of the proposed architectures, connecting continuous-time winner selection with demonstrated electronic behavior.
summary.tldr: Two experimentally verified Neuron MOS circuit designs perform continuous-time winner selection and support parallel sorting.

title: Neuron-MOS Temporal Winner Search Hardware for Fully-Parallel Data Processing

abstract: We have calculated analytical expressions for how the bias and variance of the estimators provided by various temporal difference value estimation algorithms change with offline updates over trials in absorbing Markov chains using lookup table representations. We illustrate classes of learning curve behavior in various chains, and show the manner in which TD is sensitive to the choice of its step(cid:173) size and eligibility trace parameters.
originalAbstract: We have calculated analytical expressions for how the bias and variance of the estimators provided by various temporal difference value estimation algorithms change with offline updates over trials in absorbing Markov chains using lookup table representations. We illustrate classes of learning curve behavior in various chains, and show the manner in which TD is sensitive to the choice of its step(cid:173) size and eligibility trace parameters.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning estimates values from sequences of state transitions. This paper studies how the errors in those estimates change over learning, separating systematic error, or bias, from variability across estimates, or variance. The goal is an analytical account of learning curves that explains how repeated updates affect both components.

The analysis covers several temporal-difference value-estimation algorithms with offline updates over trials. It assumes absorbing Markov chains, whose trajectories can reach terminal states, and lookup-table representations, which store separate estimates for states. Within that setting, the authors calculate expressions for the evolution of bias and variance, making the relationship between updates and mean squared error explicit.

Examples across different chains illustrate distinct classes of learning-curve behavior. The analysis also shows how strongly those curves depend on step size and eligibility trace parameters. Step size controls the scale of updates, while eligibility traces govern how updates reach earlier states. The contribution is a way to understand parameter sensitivity through the changing structure of estimation error.
summary.tldr: The paper derives bias and variance learning curves for tabular temporal-difference methods, revealing sensitivity to step size and eligibility traces.

title: Analytical Mean Squared Error Curves in Temporal Difference Learning

abstract: The mortality related to cervical cancer can be substantially re(cid:173) duced through early detection and treatment. However, cur(cid:173) rent detection techniques, such as Pap smear and colposcopy, fail to achieve a concurrently high sensitivity and specificity. In vivo fluorescence spectroscopy is a technique which quickly, non(cid:173) invasively and quantitatively probes the biochemical and morpho(cid:173) logical changes that occur in pre-cancerous tissue. RBF ensemble algorithms based on such spectra provide automated, and near real(cid:173) time implementation of pre-cancer detection in the hands of non(cid:173) experts. The results are more reliable, direct and accurate than those achieved by either human experts or multivariate statistical algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper explores automated detection of cervical precancer from fluorescence spectra measured in living tissue. The motivation is early detection: the abstract identifies difficulty achieving both high sensitivity and high specificity with existing detection techniques. A useful detector must recognize affected tissue while also distinguishing it from tissue that should not be classified as precancerous.

Fluorescence spectroscopy provides a rapid, noninvasive, quantitative way to probe biochemical and morphological changes in tissue. The proposed system applies ensembles of radial basis function networks to those measurements. The networks turn spectral information into a detection result, linking a physical measurement of tissue properties with an automated classification procedure.

The authors describe near-real-time operation suitable for use by nonexperts and report more reliable, direct, and accurate results than those obtained by human experts or multivariate statistical algorithms in their comparison. The contribution is the combination of spectroscopy and neural-network ensembles for accessible automated detection, with the reported advantage arising from how the spectral evidence is interpreted.
summary.tldr: Radial basis function ensembles interpret fluorescence spectra for rapid automated cervical precancer detection with reported comparative accuracy gains.

title: Spectroscopic Detection of Cervical Pre-Cancer through Radial Basis Function Networks

abstract: Signal processing and pattern recognition algorithms make exten(cid:173) sive use of convolution. In many cases, computational accuracy is not as important as computational speed. In feature extraction, for instance, the features of interest in a signal are usually quite distorted. This form of noise justifies some level of quantization in order to achieve faster feature extraction . Our approach consists of approximating regions of the signal with low degree polynomi(cid:173) als, and then differentiating the resulting signals in order to obtain impulse functions (or derivatives of impulse functions). With this representation, convolution becomes extremely simple and can be implemented quite effectively. The true convolution can be recov(cid:173) ered by integrating the result of the convolution. This method yields substantial speed up in feature extraction and is applicable to convolutional neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a faster way to compute convolution, an operation widely used in signal processing and pattern recognition. Its motivation is that feature extraction often deals with signals whose relevant features are already distorted. In such settings, accepting some approximation can be worthwhile when it substantially reduces the computation needed to extract those features.

The method first approximates regions of a signal with low-degree polynomials. It then differentiates this representation until the resulting signal consists of impulses or their derivatives. Convolution becomes particularly simple in that form. Integrating the convolution result reverses the differentiation step, recovering the corresponding convolution while retaining the initial signal approximation.

The authors report substantial acceleration in feature extraction and identify convolutional neural networks as an application. The key idea is to change the representation in which convolution is performed so that the expensive operation becomes simpler. Its practical justification is the stated tradeoff between computational accuracy and speed in applications where precise reproduction of an already distorted signal is less important.
summary.tldr: Boxlets accelerate convolution by approximating signals with polynomials, differentiating them into impulses, and integrating the simplified convolution result.

title: Boxlets: A Fast Convolution Algorithm for Signal Processing and Neural Networks

abstract: We present a variational Bayesian method for model selection over families of kernels classifiers like Support Vector machines or Gaus(cid:173) sian processes. The algorithm needs no user interaction and is able to adapt a large number of kernel parameters to given data without having to sacrifice training cases for validation. This opens the pos(cid:173) sibility to use sophisticated families of kernels in situations where the small "standard kernel" classes are clearly inappropriate. We relate the method to other work done on Gaussian processes and clarify the relation between Support Vector machines and certain Gaussian process models.

paragraphs: This paper presents a variational Bayesian approach to choosing models within families of kernel classifiers, including support vector machines and Gaussian processes. Kernel parameters determine aspects of the model's representation of the data. Selecting those parameters is therefore part of deciding which classifier is appropriate for a particular learning problem.

The proposed algorithm adapts many kernel parameters without user interaction and without setting aside training examples for validation. This matters especially when choosing among more elaborate kernel families: the method provides a way to fit their parameters while keeping the available cases in the training process. Variational Bayesian inference supplies the framework for that selection.

The authors argue that this capability opens the possibility of using sophisticated kernels when small, standard kernel families are inappropriate. This is a statement about the opportunities the method creates, rather than a universal performance guarantee. The paper also relates the approach to Gaussian-process research and clarifies connections between support vector machines and certain Gaussian-process models.
summary.tldr: Variational Bayesian model selection adapts many kernel parameters automatically without holding out training cases for validation.

title: Bayesian Model Selection for Support Vector Machines, Gaussian Processes and Other Kernel Classifiers

abstract: Many control problems take place in continuous state-action spaces, e.g., as in manipulator robotics, where the control objective is of- ten deﬂned as ﬂnding a desired trajectory that reaches a particular goal state. While reinforcement learning oﬁers a theoretical frame- work to learn such control policies from scratch, its applicability to higher dimensional continuous state-action spaces remains rather limited to date. Instead of learning from scratch, in this paper we suggest to learn a desired complex control policy by transforming an existing simple canonical control policy. For this purpose, we represent canonical policies in terms of diﬁerential equations with well-deﬂned attractor properties. By nonlinearly transforming the canonical attractor dynamics using techniques from nonparametric regression, almost arbitrary new nonlinear policies can be gener- ated without losing the stability properties of the canonical sys- tem. We demonstrate our techniques in the context of learning a set of movement skills for a humanoid robot from demonstrations of a human teacher. Policies are acquired rapidly, and, due to the properties of well formulated diﬁerential equations, can be re-used and modiﬂed on-line under dynamic changes of the environment. The linear parameterization of nonparametric regression moreover lends itself to recognize and classify previously learned movement skills. Evaluations in simulations and on an actual 30 degree-of- freedom humanoid robot exemplify the feasibility and robustness of our approach.

paragraphs: Learning control policies from scratch can be difficult in high-dimensional spaces with continuous states and actions. This paper instead starts from a simple existing policy and learns how to transform it into a more complex movement. The starting policy is represented by differential equations with well-defined attractor and stability properties.

Nonparametric regression supplies a nonlinear transformation of these canonical dynamics. The authors describe how this can generate almost arbitrary nonlinear policies while retaining the original system's stability properties. This makes the starting dynamics a useful foundation: the learned transformation changes the movement while preserving the stated stability behavior.

The method learns movement skills for a humanoid robot from human demonstrations. Policies are acquired rapidly and can be reused or modified online as the environment changes. The regression model's linear parameterization also supports recognizing and classifying previously learned movements. Evaluations in simulation and on a physical humanoid robot with 30 degrees of freedom demonstrate the approach's feasibility and robustness.
summary.tldr: Transforming stable canonical dynamics lets a humanoid robot learn flexible movement skills from demonstrations while retaining stability properties.

title: Learning Attractor Landscapes for Learning Motor Primitives

abstract: Low rank approximation techniques are widespread in pattern recogni- tion research — they include Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), Proba- bilistic LSA, Principal Components Analysus (PCA), the Generative As- pect Model, and many forms of bibliometric analysis. All make use of a low-dimensional manifold onto which data are projected. Such techniques are generally “unsupervised,” which allows them to model data in the absence of labels or categories. With many practi- cal problems, however, some prior knowledge is available in the form of context. In this paper, I describe a principled approach to incorpo- rating such information, and demonstrate its application to PCA-based approximations of several data sets.

paragraphs: The paper considers low-rank approximation methods that represent data through a lower-dimensional space. Examples include principal components analysis and latent semantic analysis. Such techniques generally operate without labels or categories, which makes them useful when those annotations are unavailable but leaves open how to use other knowledge that may already exist.

The author focuses on prior information supplied by context. The proposed approach provides a principled way to incorporate that information into a projection. The key idea is that constructing a compact representation need not depend only on the observed data considered without context; relevant knowledge can also inform how the approximation is formed.

The paper demonstrates the approach through PCA-based approximations of several datasets. These applications show how the general idea can be used within an established projection method. The contribution is a way to connect contextual knowledge with low-dimensional representation learning, illustrated through those approximations. It addresses the practical middle ground in which a problem lacks explicit labels but still comes with useful information about the setting.
summary.tldr: Informed projections incorporate contextual prior knowledge into low-dimensional approximations, with demonstrations using PCA on several datasets.

title: Informed Projections

abstract: We have constructed a system that uses an array of 9,600 spiking sili- con neurons, a fast microcontroller, and digital memory, to implement a reconﬁgurable network of integrate-and-ﬁre neurons. The system is designed for rapid prototyping of spiking neural networks that require high-throughput communication with external address-event hardware. Arbitrary network topologies can be implemented by selectively rout- ing address-events to speciﬁc internal or external targets according to a memory-based projective ﬁeld mapping. The utility and versatility of the system is demonstrated by conﬁguring it as a three-stage network that accepts input from an address-event imager, detects salient regions of the image, and performs spatial acuity modulation around a high-resolution fovea that is centered on the location of highest salience.

The system is designed for rapid prototyping of spiking neural networks that require high-throughput communication with external address-event hardware. paragraphs: The authors build a configurable neural hardware system containing 9,600 spiking silicon neurons, a fast microcontroller, and digital memory. It implements networks of integrate-and-fire neurons and is intended for rapid experimentation with spiking architectures. A key design goal is high-throughput communication with external hardware that represents activity as addressed events.

Network connections are implemented by selectively routing those events to internal or external destinations. A mapping stored in memory determines where activity is sent, allowing arbitrary network topologies to be configured. This makes the routing mechanism central to the system's flexibility: changing the mapping changes how the available hardware participates in a network.

The demonstration configures a three-stage visual network. It receives events from an imager, identifies salient image regions, and adjusts spatial acuity around a high-resolution fovea positioned at the most salient location. This shows the platform coordinating sensing, saliency detection, and selective image resolution, providing a concrete illustration of its usefulness for prototyping interconnected spiking systems.
summary.tldr: A reconfigurable system of 9,600 spiking silicon neurons demonstrates saliency-guided control of image resolution.

title: Saliency-Driven Image Acuity Modulation on a Reconfigurable Array of Spiking Silicon Neurons

abstract: We propose a new technique for sampling the solutions of combinatorial problems in a near-uniform manner. We focus on problems specified as a Boolean formula, i.e., on SAT instances. Sampling for SAT problems has been shown to have interesting connections with probabilistic reasoning, making practical sampling algorithms for SAT highly desirable. The best current approaches are based on Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, which have some practical limitations. Our approach exploits combinatorial properties of random parity (X O R) constraints to prune away solutions near-uniformly. The final sample is identified amongst the remaining ones using a state-of-the-art SAT solver. The resulting sampling distribution is provably arbitrarily close to uniform. Our experiments show that our technique achieves a significantly better sampling quality than the best alternative.

We focus on problems specified as a Boolean formula, i.e., on SAT instances. Sampling for SAT problems has been shown to have interesting connections with probabilistic reasoning, making practical sampling algorithms for SAT highly desirable. The best current approaches are based on Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, which have some practical limitations. Our approach exploits combinatorial properties of random parity (X O R) constraints to prune away solutions near-uniformly. paragraphs: Finding a satisfying assignment to a Boolean formula and sampling satisfying assignments nearly uniformly are different tasks. This paper addresses the sampling task for SAT problems, where the aim is to avoid strongly favoring particular solutions. Such sampling has connections to probabilistic reasoning, motivating methods that are practical as well as statistically well behaved.

The proposed method adds random parity, or XOR, constraints. Their combinatorial properties allow the algorithm to remove solutions in a near-uniform manner. A state-of-the-art SAT solver then identifies the final sample among the surviving solutions. This combines randomized pruning of the solution space with an existing solver's ability to find a satisfying assignment.

The authors prove that the resulting sampling distribution can be made arbitrarily close to uniform. Their experiments also show significantly better sampling quality than the best alternative considered. The contribution is therefore both theoretical and empirical: it gives a closeness-to-uniformity guarantee and demonstrates a practical alternative to the Markov chain Monte Carlo approaches discussed in the paper.
summary.tldr: Random XOR constraints prune SAT solutions nearly uniformly, enabling solver-based sampling with a distribution provably arbitrarily close to uniform.

title: Near-Uniform Sampling of Combinatorial Spaces Using XOR Constraints

abstract: Many computer aided diagnosis (CAD) problems can be best modelled as a multiple-instance learning (MIL) problem with unbalanced data: i.e. , the training data typically consists of a few positive bags, and a very large number of negative instances. Existing MIL algorithms are much too computationally expensive for these datasets. We describe CH, a framework for learning a Convex Hull representation of multiple instances that is significantly faster than existing MIL algorithms. Our CH framework applies to any standard hyperplane-based learning algorithm, and for some algorithms, is guaranteed to find the global optimal solution. Experimental studies on two different CAD applications further demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly improves diagnostic accuracy when compared to both MIL and traditional classifiers. Although not designed for standard MIL problems (which have both positive and negative bags and relatively balanced datasets), comparisons against other MIL methods on benchmark problems also indicate that the proposed method is competitive with the state-of-the-art.

It introduces CH, a framework based on learning a convex-hull representation of multiple instances.

The results support a formulation designed around diagnostic data imbalance while showing usefulness beyond that original setting.
summary.tldr: A convex-hull learning framework speeds up imbalanced multiple-instance diagnosis problems and improves accuracy in two applications.

title: Multiple Instance Learning for Computer Aided Diagnosis

abstract: We extend position and phase-shift tuning, concepts already well established in the disparity energy neuron literature, to motion energy neurons. We show that Reichardt-like detectors can be considered examples of position tuning, and that motion energy filters whose complex valued spatio-temporal receptive fields are space-time separable can be considered examples of phase tuning. By combining these two types of detectors, we obtain an architecture for constructing motion energy neurons whose center frequencies can be adjusted by both phase and posi- tion shifts. Similar to recently described neurons in the primary visual cortex, these new motion energy neurons exhibit tuning that is between purely space- time separable and purely speed tuned. We propose a functional role for this intermediate level of tuning by demonstrating that comparisons between pairs of these motion energy neurons can reliably discriminate between inputs whose velocities lie above or below a given reference velocity.

It transfers two ideas from disparity-energy models—position tuning and phase-shift tuning—to motion-energy neurons. The aim is to construct detectors whose response properties provide a useful intermediate form of motion tuning.

The authors identify Reichardt-like detectors as examples of position tuning. They identify motion-energy filters with complex receptive fields that separate into spatial and temporal components as examples of phase tuning. summary.tldr: Combining position and phase tuning produces motion-energy neurons whose paired responses can distinguish velocities above or below a reference.

title: Extending position/phase-shift tuning to motion energy neurons improves velocity discrimination

abstract: Given an $n$-vertex weighted tree with structural diameter $S$ and a subset of $m$ vertices, we present a technique to compute a corresponding $m \times m$ Gram matrix of the pseudoinverse of the graph Laplacian in $O(n+ m^2 + m S)$ time. We discuss the application of this technique to fast label prediction on a generic graph. We approximate the graph with a spanning tree and then we predict with the kernel perceptron. We address the approximation of the graph with either a minimum spanning tree or a shortest path tree. The fast computation of the pseudoinverse enables us to address prediction problems on large graphs. To this end we present experiments on two web-spam classification tasks, one of which includes a graph with 400,000 nodes and more than 10,000,000 edges. The results indicate that the accuracy of our technique is competitive with previous methods using the full graph information.

For a weighted tree with n vertices and structural diameter S, it computes a kernel matrix for a selected set of m vertices. The matrix comes from the pseudoinverse of the graph Laplacian.

They consider both minimum spanning trees and shortest path trees as ways to construct that approximation.

Experiments address two web-spam classification tasks, including a graph with 400,000 nodes and more than 10 million edges. Accuracy is reported as competitive with earlier methods that use the full graph. The result suggests that, in these tasks, a tree approximation can retain useful predictive information while enabling efficient computation at a substantial graph scale.
summary.tldr: Fast tree-based kernel computation enables large-graph prediction with competitive accuracy in web-spam experiments.

title: Fast Prediction on a Tree

abstract: In multi-task learning several related tasks are considered simultaneously, with the hope that by an appropriate sharing of information across tasks, each task may benefit from the others. In the context of learning linear functions for supervised classification or regression, this can be achieved by including a priori information about the weight vectors associated with the tasks, and how they are expected to be related to each other. In this paper, we assume that tasks are clustered into groups, which are unknown beforehand, and that tasks within a group have similar weight vectors. We design a new spectral norm that encodes this a priori assumption, without the prior knowledge of the partition of tasks into groups, resulting in a new convex optimization formulation for multi-task learning. We show in simulations on synthetic examples and on the iedb MHC-I binding dataset, that our approach outperforms well-known convex methods for multi-task learning, as well as related non convex methods dedicated to the same problem.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning trains related prediction tasks together so that information from one can help another. This paper considers linear classification and regression models, where each task has a vector of weights. Its central assumption is that tasks form groups, with similar weight vectors within each group, even though the group assignments are unknown beforehand.

The authors design a spectral norm that expresses this assumed grouping structure without requiring a supplied partition of the tasks. Incorporating that norm produces a convex optimization formulation. The contribution is therefore a way to represent a particular kind of task relatedness while retaining a convex learning problem.

Experiments use synthetic examples and the iedb MHC-I binding dataset. In these evaluations, the approach outperforms established convex multi-task methods and related nonconvex methods aimed at the same problem. The findings support this formulation as a useful way to share information when tasks have clustered similarities, rather than requiring their relationships to be specified in advance.
summary.tldr: A convex multi-task learning formulation captures similarities within unknown groups of tasks.

title: Clustered Multi-Task Learning: A Convex Formulation

abstract: Extracting good representations from images is essential for many computer vision tasks. In this paper, we propose hierarchical matching pursuit (HMP), which builds a feature hierarchy layer-by-layer using an efficient matching pursuit encoder. It includes three modules: batch (tree) orthogonal matching pursuit, spatial pyramid max pooling, and contrast normalization. We investigate the architecture of HMP, and show that all three components are critical for good performance. To speed up the orthogonal matching pursuit, we propose a batch tree orthogonal matching pursuit that is particularly suitable to encode a large number of observations that share the same large dictionary. HMP is scalable and can efficiently handle full-size images. In addition, HMP enables linear support vector machines (SVM) to match the performance of nonlinear SVM while being scalable to large datasets. We compare HMP with many state-of-the-art algorithms including convolutional deep belief networks, SIFT based single layer sparse coding, and kernel based feature learning. HMP consistently yields superior accuracy on three types of image classification problems: object recognition (Caltech-101), scene recognition (MIT-Scene), and static event recognition (UIUC-Sports).

Its architecture combines an efficient matching pursuit encoder, spatial pyramid max pooling, and contrast normalization. The authors investigate these components and find that all three are important for good performance, making the overall representation more than a choice of encoding algorithm.

These results connect the architecture’s representation quality with its computational design: the hierarchy supports strong classification performance while the encoder makes processing larger collections practical.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical matching pursuit combines layered image features with fast encoding to achieve superior reported classification accuracy and scalable linear classification.

title: Hierarchical Matching Pursuit for Image Classification: Architecture and Fast Algorithms

abstract: Topic modeling is a widely used approach to analyzing large text collections. A small number of multilingual topic models have recently been explored to discover latent topics among parallel or comparable documents, such as in Wikipedia. Other topic models that were originally proposed for structured data are also applicable to multilingual documents. Correspondence Latent Dirichlet Allocation (CorrLDA) is one such model; however, it requires a pivot language to be specified in advance. We propose a new topic model, Symmetric Correspondence LDA (SymCorrLDA), that incorporates a hidden variable to control a pivot language, in an extension of CorrLDA. We experimented with two multilingual comparable datasets extracted from Wikipedia and demonstrate that SymCorrLDA is more effective than some other existing multilingual topic models.

We propose a new topic model, Symmetric Correspondence LDA (SymCorrLDA), that incorporates a hidden variable to control a pivot language, in an extension of CorrLDA. paragraphs: Multilingual topic models seek shared latent themes in collections of documents written in different languages. The paper considers parallel or comparable documents, including collections drawn from Wikipedia. Correspondence Latent Dirichlet Allocation can be applied to this setting, but it requires choosing a pivot language before learning, making that choice a fixed part of the model.

The authors propose Symmetric Correspondence LDA, an extension that introduces a hidden variable to control the pivot language. This moves the pivot into the probabilistic model rather than requiring it to be specified in advance. The change addresses how languages are related within topic discovery while retaining the correspondence-model approach.

Experiments use two multilingual comparable datasets extracted from Wikipedia. On these datasets, SymCorrLDA is more effective than some existing multilingual topic models. The stated result supports modeling the pivot through a latent variable in this setting. Its significance is that the organization of cross-language correspondence itself can be represented within the model, alongside the hidden topics being discovered.
summary.tldr: SymCorrLDA models the pivot language as a hidden variable and outperforms some multilingual topic models on two Wikipedia datasets.

title: Symmetric Correspondence Topic Models for Multilingual Text Analysis

abstract: We address the problem of deciding whether there exists a consistent estimator of a given relation Q, when data are missing not at random. We employ a formal representation called `Missingness Graphs' to explicitly portray the causal mechanisms responsible for missingness and to encode dependencies between these mechanisms and the variables being measured. Using this representation, we define the notion of \textit{recoverability} which ensures that, for a given missingness-graph $G$ and a given query $Q$ an algorithm exists such that in the limit of large samples, it produces an estimate of $Q$ \textit{as if} no data were missing. We further present conditions that the graph should satisfy in order for recoverability to hold and devise algorithms to detect the presence of these conditions.

We employ a formal representation called `Missingness Graphs' to explicitly portray the causal mechanisms responsible for missingness and to encode dependencies between these mechanisms and the variables being measured. Using this representation, we define the notion of \textit{recoverability} which ensures that, for a given missingness-graph $G$ and a given query $Q$ an algorithm exists such that in the limit of large samples, it produces an estimate of $Q$ \textit{as if} no data were missing. paragraphs: When data are missing not at random, the pattern of missingness is tied to the variables being studied. The central question in this paper is whether a particular target relation can still be estimated consistently. Rather than treating missing entries as a uniform obstacle, the authors make the mechanism causing missingness an explicit part of the problem.

They introduce missingness graphs to represent causal mechanisms behind missing data and their dependencies on measured variables. Within this representation, recoverability is defined for a particular graph and query. A recoverable query has an estimation algorithm that, as the sample size grows, estimates the target as though the data had been fully observed.

The paper gives graphical conditions under which recoverability holds and algorithms that detect those conditions. This turns a question about what missing data permit into a structural analysis of the assumed mechanism. The guarantee is query-specific and asymptotic: it concerns consistent estimation under the given graph, rather than promising that every missing value or every relation can be reconstructed.
summary.tldr: Missingness graphs provide conditions and detection algorithms for determining when a target relation remains consistently estimable despite nonrandom missing data.

title: Graphical Models for Inference with Missing Data

abstract: Dropout is a relatively new algorithm for training neural networks which relies on stochastically dropping out'' neurons during training in order to avoid the co-adaptation of feature detectors. We introduce a general formalism for studying dropout on either units or connections, with arbitrary probability values, and use it to analyze the averaging and regularizing properties of dropout in both linear and non-linear networks. For deep neural networks, the averaging properties of dropout are characterized by three recursive equations, including the approximation of expectations by normalized weighted geometric means. We provide estimates and bounds for these approximations and corroborate the results with simulations. We also show in simple cases how dropout performs stochastic gradient descent on a regularized error function."
originalAbstract: Dropout is a relatively new algorithm for training neural networks which relies on stochastically dropping out'' neurons during training in order to avoid the co-adaptation of feature detectors. We introduce a general formalism for studying dropout on either units or connections, with arbitrary probability values, and use it to analyze the averaging and regularizing properties of dropout in both linear and non-linear networks. For deep neural networks, the averaging properties of dropout are characterized by three recursive equations, including the approximation of expectations by normalized weighted geometric means. We provide estimates and bounds for these approximations and corroborate the results with simulations. We also show in simple cases how dropout performs stochastic gradient descent on a regularized error function."

paragraphs: Dropout trains a neural network while randomly removing units, discouraging feature detectors from relying too closely on one another. This paper develops a general mathematical framework for analyzing that procedure. The framework covers dropout on either units or connections and allows arbitrary dropout probabilities, rather than restricting attention to one standard configuration.

The analysis examines both averaging and regularization in linear and nonlinear networks. For deep networks, three recursive equations characterize the averaging behavior, including an approximation that replaces expectations with normalized weighted geometric means. The authors provide estimates and bounds for these approximations and use simulations to corroborate the theoretical results.

The paper also shows, in simple cases, that dropout performs stochastic gradient descent on an error function with regularization. This gives a concrete connection between random removal during training and a modified optimization objective. Its scope matters: the regularized-objective interpretation is established for those simple cases, while the deeper-network averaging analysis explicitly involves approximations. Together, the results explain distinct mathematical effects of dropout without treating every effect as exact in every network.
summary.tldr: A general dropout framework analyzes its averaging approximations and establishes a regularized-optimization interpretation in simple cases.

title: Understanding Dropout

abstract: Many large-scale machine learning problems (such as clustering, non-parametric learning, kernel machines, etc.) require selecting, out of a massive data set, a manageable, representative subset. Such problems can often be reduced to maximizing a submodular set function subject to cardinality constraints. Classical approaches require centralized access to the full data set; but for truly large-scale problems, rendering the data centrally is often impractical. In this paper, we consider the problem of submodular function maximization in a distributed fashion. We develop a simple, two-stage protocol GreeDI, that is easily implemented using MapReduce style computations. We theoretically analyze our approach, and show, that under certain natural conditions, performance close to the (impractical) centralized approach can be achieved. In our extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several applications, including sparse Gaussian process inference on tens of millions of examples using Hadoop.

paragraphs: Many learning methods need a manageable subset that represents a much larger dataset. The selection problem can often be expressed as maximizing a submodular set function while limiting the number of chosen elements. Classical approaches assume access to all the data in one place, which can be impractical at very large scales.

The paper introduces GreeDI, a simple two-stage distributed protocol that fits MapReduce-style computation. It addresses representative selection while the data are distributed, allowing the computation to be organized without relying on the centralized access required by classical approaches. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis of the protocol's performance.

That analysis shows that performance close to the centralized approach can be achieved under certain natural conditions; it is not an unconditional equivalence. Extensive experiments demonstrate effectiveness across several applications. These include sparse Gaussian process inference using Hadoop on tens of millions of examples, showing the method's relevance to representative selection at substantial data scales.
summary.tldr: GreeDI distributes representative-subset selection and can approach centralized performance under stated conditions.

title: Distributed Submodular Maximization: Identifying Representative Elements in Massive Data

abstract: We propose a general formalism of iterated random functions with semigroup property, under which exact and approximate Bayesian posterior updates can be viewed as specific instances. A convergence theory for iterated random functions is presented. As an application of the general theory we analyze convergence behaviors of exact and approximate message-passing algorithms that arise in a sequential change point detection problem formulated via a latent variable directed graphical model. The sequential inference algorithm and its supporting theory are illustrated by simulated examples.

A convergence theory for iterated random functions is presented. As an application of the general theory we analyze convergence behaviors of exact and approximate message-passing algorithms that arise in a sequential change point detection problem formulated via a latent variable directed graphical model. The sequential inference algorithm and its supporting theory are illustrated by simulated examples.

paragraphs: The paper develops a mathematical framework for understanding repeated Bayesian updates. As observations arrive, an inference procedure repeatedly transforms its current posterior distribution into a new one. The authors describe these transformations as iterated random functions, allowing exact updates and approximate updates to be studied within the same formal language.

The framework includes a semigroup property, which organizes how successive transformations compose. The authors establish a convergence theory for these iterated functions. This supplies a common basis for analyzing the behavior of repeated inference steps, rather than treating each particular posterior-update algorithm as an entirely separate mathematical problem.

They apply the theory to sequential change point detection in a directed graphical model with latent variables. Within that application, they analyze the convergence behavior of both exact and approximate message-passing algorithms. Simulated examples illustrate the inference procedure and its supporting theory. The contribution connects a general account of repeated probabilistic transformations to a concrete setting where inference must continually respond to incoming data.
summary.tldr: A shared framework for repeated random transformations provides convergence theory for exact and approximate Bayesian updates.

title: Bayesian inference as iterated random functions with applications to sequential inference in graphical models

abstract: We study a multitask learning problem in which each task is parametrized by a weight vector and indexed by a pair of indices, which can be e.g, (consumer, time). The weight vectors can be collected into a tensor and the (multilinear-)rank of the tensor controls the amount of sharing of information among tasks. Two types of convex relaxations have recently been proposed for the tensor multilinear rank. However, we argue that both of them are not optimal in the context of multitask learning in which the dimensions or multilinear rank are typically heterogeneous. We propose a new norm, which we call the scaled latent trace norm and analyze the excess risk of all the three norms. The results apply to various settings including matrix and tensor completion, multitask learning, and multilinear multitask learning. Both the theory and experiments support the advantage of the new norm when the tensor is not equal-sized and we do not a priori know which mode is low rank.

paragraphs: The paper studies related prediction tasks indexed by pairs such as consumer and time. Each task has a weight vector, and these vectors form a tensor. The tensor's multilinear rank controls how much information tasks share, connecting multitask learning with the problem of finding low-rank multidimensional structure.

The authors argue that two existing convex relaxations of multilinear rank are not optimal for multitask settings with unequal dimensions or differing ranks across tensor directions. They introduce the scaled latent trace norm to address this heterogeneity. They then analyze excess risk for the new norm and the two existing alternatives.

The analysis covers settings including matrix completion, tensor completion, multitask learning, and multilinear multitask learning. Both theoretical results and experiments support the new norm's advantage when tensor dimensions are unequal and the low-rank direction is not known beforehand. This qualification is central to the contribution: the proposed regularizer is motivated by uncertainty about where useful shared structure lies in an unevenly shaped collection of tasks.
summary.tldr: The scaled latent trace norm improves supported multitask and completion settings with unequal tensor dimensions and an unknown low-rank direction.

title: Multitask learning meets tensor factorization: task imputation via convex optimization

abstract: We study the residual bootstrap (RB) method in the context of high-dimensional linear regression. Specifically, we analyze the distributional approximation of linear contrasts $c^{\top}(\hat{\beta}_{\rho}-\beta)$, where $\hat{\beta}_{\rho}$ is a ridge-regression estimator. When regression coefficients are estimated via least squares, classical results show that RB consistently approximates the laws of contrasts, provided that $p\ll n$, where the design matrix is of size $n\times p$. Up to now, relatively little work has considered how additional structure in the linear model may extend the validity of RB to the setting where $p/n\asymp 1$. In this setting, we propose a version of RB that resamples residuals obtained from ridge regression. Our main structural assumption on the design matrix is that it is nearly low rank --- in the sense that its singular values decay according to a power-law profile. Under a few extra technical assumptions, we derive a simple criterion for ensuring that RB consistently approximates the law of a given contrast. We then specialize this result to study confidence intervals for mean response values $X_i^{\top} \beta$, where $X_i^{\top}$ is the $i$th row of the design. More precisely, we show that conditionally on a Gaussian design with near low-rank structure, RB \emph{simultaneously} approximates all of the laws $X_i^{\top}(\hat{\beta}_{\rho}-\beta)$, $i=1,\dots,n$. This result is also notable as it imposes no sparsity assumptions on $\beta$. Furthermore, since our consistency results are formulated in terms of the Mallows (Kantorovich) metric, the existence of a limiting distribution is not required.

paragraphs: The residual bootstrap estimates uncertainty by resampling errors left after fitting a regression model. Classical guarantees for least-squares regression apply when the number of predictors is much smaller than the number of observations. This paper studies whether useful guarantees remain possible when those two quantities are comparable, using residuals from ridge regression.

The key assumption concerns the design matrix: its singular values must decay according to a power law, giving it a nearly low-rank structure. Under additional technical assumptions, the authors derive a criterion for consistently approximating the distribution of a specified linear contrast of the coefficient estimation error. The guarantee therefore depends on both structural conditions and the contrast being studied.

For Gaussian designs with the required structure, the authors further show that the bootstrap simultaneously approximates the error distributions for all observed-design mean responses. This supports studying confidence intervals for those responses without assuming sparse regression coefficients. The results use the Mallows, or Kantorovich, metric, so consistency does not require the estimation error to converge to a limiting distribution.
summary.tldr: A ridge-residual bootstrap consistently approximates certain regression error distributions under near-low-rank design assumptions, without requiring sparse coefficients.

title: A Residual Bootstrap for High-Dimensional Regression with Near Low-Rank Designs

abstract: Lifted inference rules exploit symmetries for fast reasoning in statistical rela-tional models. Computational complexity of these rules is highly dependent onthe choice of the constraint language they operate on and therefore coming upwith the right kind of representation is critical to the success of lifted inference.In this paper, we propose a new constraint language, called setineq, which allowssubset, equality and inequality constraints, to represent substitutions over the vari-ables in the theory. Our constraint formulation is strictly more expressive thanexisting representations, yet easy to operate on. We reformulate the three mainlifting rules: decomposer, generalized binomial and the recently proposed singleoccurrence for MAP inference, to work with our constraint representation. Exper-iments on benchmark MLNs for exact and sampling based inference demonstratethe effectiveness of our approach over several other existing techniques.

paragraphs: Lifted inference speeds up reasoning in statistical relational models by exploiting repeated structure and symmetries. Whether an inference rule is computationally useful depends strongly on how constraints over logical variables are represented. A restrictive representation can prevent the algorithm from expressing useful groups of equivalent substitutions.

The paper introduces setineq, a constraint language with subset, equality, and inequality constraints. It represents substitutions over variables and is claimed to be strictly more expressive than existing representations while remaining easy to manipulate. The authors reformulate the decomposer, generalized binomial, and single-occurrence lifting rules for this language, including the latter rule’s use in MAP inference.

Experiments on benchmark Markov logic networks evaluate exact and sampling-based inference and demonstrate advantages over several existing techniques. No numerical gains are given in the abstract. The contribution centers on representation and inference rules, with empirical support that additional expressiveness can translate into practical reasoning improvements.
summary.tldr: A more expressive constraint language lets lifted inference exploit relational symmetries.

title: Lifted Inference Rules With Constraints

abstract: We consider a generalization of the submodular cover problem based on the concept of diminishing return property on the integer lattice. We are motivated by real scenarios in machine learning that cannot be captured by (traditional) submodular set functions. We show that the generalized submodular cover problem can be applied to various problems and devise a bicriteria approximation algorithm. Our algorithm is guaranteed to output a log-factor approximate solution that satisfies the constraints with the desired accuracy. The running time of our algorithm is roughly $O(n\log (nr) \log{r})$, where $n$ is the size of the ground set and $r$ is the maximum value of a coordinate. The dependency on $r$ is exponentially better than the naive reduction algorithms. Several experiments on real and artificial datasets demonstrate that the solution quality of our algorithm is comparable to naive algorithms, while the running time is several orders of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Traditional submodular cover uses sets, where an element is either selected or absent. This paper extends the problem to integer-valued decisions, allowing each coordinate to represent an amount. It retains a diminishing-returns property: additional increments provide less benefit as the existing allocation grows. This formulation captures machine learning scenarios that ordinary set functions cannot express.

The authors develop a bicriteria approximation algorithm, giving guarantees on both solution quality and constraint satisfaction. It returns a solution within a logarithmic approximation factor while meeting the constraints to the requested accuracy. These are approximation guarantees, so the result does not require finding an exact optimum.

The running time is roughly O(n log(nr) log r), with n coordinates and maximum coordinate value r. Its dependence on r is exponentially better than that of naive reductions. Experiments on real and artificial datasets report comparable solution quality to naive algorithms, with runtime improvements of several orders of magnitude. The contribution therefore joins a broader decision model with a substantially more efficient way to solve it approximately.
summary.tldr: The paper extends submodular cover to integer allocations and gives an approximation algorithm with much better dependence on allocation size.

title: A Generalization of Submodular Cover via the Diminishing Return Property on the Integer Lattice

abstract: We study how well one can recover sparse principal componentsof a data matrix using a sketch formed from a few of its elements. We show that for a wide class of optimization problems,if the sketch is close (in the spectral norm) to the original datamatrix, then one can recover a near optimal solution to the optimizationproblem by using the sketch. In particular, we use this approach toobtain sparse principal components and show that for \math{m} data pointsin \math{n} dimensions,\math{O(\epsilon^{-2}\tilde k\max{m,n})} elements gives an\math{\epsilon}-additive approximation to the sparse PCA problem(\math{\tilde k} is the stable rank of the data matrix).We demonstrate our algorithms extensivelyon image, text, biological and financial data.The results show that not only are we able to recover the sparse PCAs from the incomplete data, but by using our sparse sketch, the running timedrops by a factor of five or more.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether sparse principal components can be recovered from a sketch containing only a small selection of a data matrix's entries. Its approach connects incomplete data to optimization accuracy: instead of requiring the full matrix, it studies when a smaller representation preserves enough information to obtain a nearly optimal answer.

The central result applies to a broad class of optimization problems. If the sketch approximates the original matrix closely in spectral norm, optimizing with the sketch can yield a near-optimal solution. For sparse PCA on m observations with n dimensions, the authors obtain an ε-additive approximation using O(ε^(-2) k̃ max{m,n}) entries, where k̃ is the matrix's stable rank.

The experiments cover image, text, biological, and financial data. They demonstrate recovery of sparse principal components from incomplete data and report runtime reductions of at least a factor of five using the sparse sketch. The findings connect a conditional approximation guarantee with a practical computational benefit: fewer retained entries can support useful sparse PCA solutions while reducing processing time.
summary.tldr: Spectrally accurate sketches support provably approximate sparse PCA from relatively few matrix entries and substantially reduce runtime in the reported experiments.

title: Approximating Sparse PCA from Incomplete Data

abstract: Online optimization covers problems such as online resource allocation, online bipartite matching, adwords (a central problem in e-commerce and advertising), and adwords with separable concave returns. We analyze the worst case competitive ratio of two primal-dual algorithms for a class of online convex (conic) optimization problems that contains the previous examples as special cases defined on the positive orthant. We derive a sufficient condition on the objective function that guarantees a constant worst case competitive ratio (greater than or equal to $\frac{1}{2}$) for monotone objective functions. We provide new examples of online problems on the positive orthant % and the positive semidefinite cone that satisfy the sufficient condition. We show how smoothing can improve the competitive ratio of these algorithms, and in particular for separable functions, we show that the optimal smoothing can be derived by solving a convex optimization problem. This result allows us to directly optimize the competitive ratio bound over a class of smoothing functions, and hence design effective smoothing customized for a given cost function.

paragraphs: Online optimization makes decisions as information arrives, so an algorithm must perform without knowing the full future problem. This paper studies two primal-dual algorithms through their worst-case competitive ratios. Its framework includes resource allocation, online bipartite matching, and advertising allocation, including settings with separable concave returns.

The authors derive a sufficient condition on the objective that guarantees a constant competitive ratio of at least one half for monotone objectives. They also give additional examples satisfying that condition. The qualification matters: the result supplies a condition under which the guarantee holds, rather than asserting that every monotone online objective automatically enjoys the same protection.

The paper then shows how smoothing the objective can improve these algorithms’ competitive-ratio bounds. For separable functions, finding optimal smoothing within the considered class becomes a convex optimization problem. This turns smoothing into something that can be designed for a particular cost function by directly optimizing the bound. The contribution connects an algorithmic design choice to a formal guarantee about performance under unfavorable input sequences.
summary.tldr: The paper derives conditional performance guarantees for online optimization and optimizes smoothing functions to improve those guarantees.

title: Designing smoothing functions for improved worst-case competitive ratio in online optimization

abstract: The algorithmic advancement of synchronizing maps is important in order to solve a wide range of practice problems with possible large-scale dataset. In this paper, we provide theoretical justifications for spectral techniques for the map synchronization problem, i.e., it takes as input a collection of objects and noisy maps estimated between pairs of objects, and outputs clean maps between all pairs of objects. We show that a simple normalized spectral method that projects the blocks of the top eigenvectors of a data matrix to the map space leads to surprisingly good results. As the noise is modelled naturally as random permutation matrix, this algorithm NormSpecSync leads to competing theoretical guarantees as state-of-the-art convex optimization techniques, yet it is much more efficient. We demonstrate the usefulness of our algorithm in a couple of applications, where it is optimal in both complexity and exactness among existing methods.

paragraphs: Map synchronization starts with a collection of objects and noisy maps estimated between pairs. Its goal is to produce clean maps between all pairs, using the collection jointly rather than considering each estimated relationship in isolation. This paper gives theoretical support for a computationally efficient spectral approach to that problem.

The proposed algorithm, NormSpecSync, uses the top eigenvectors of a data matrix. It normalizes the spectral construction and projects blocks of those eigenvectors into the space of valid maps. This turns information from the overall collection into admissible pairwise relationships through a relatively simple spectral procedure.

With noise modeled as random permutation matrices, the authors establish theoretical guarantees competitive with state-of-the-art convex optimization methods, while reporting substantially greater efficiency. They also demonstrate the algorithm in a couple of applications, where they report optimal complexity and exactness among existing methods. The significance is that this simpler spectral construction can achieve strong recovery guarantees; those theoretical comparisons are supported under the stated permutation-noise model.
summary.tldr: A normalized spectral algorithm cleans noisy pairwise maps with guarantees competitive with convex methods under a random-permutation noise model.

title: Normalized Spectral Map Synchronization

abstract: Given only information in the form of similarity triplets "Object A is more similar to object B than to object C" about a data set, we propose two ways of defining a kernel function on the data set. While previous approaches construct a low-dimensional Euclidean embedding of the data set that reflects the given similarity triplets, we aim at defining kernel functions that correspond to high-dimensional embeddings. These kernel functions can subsequently be used to apply any kernel method to the data set.
originalAbstract: Given only information in the form of similarity triplets "Object A is more similar to object B than to object C" about a data set, we propose two ways of defining a kernel function on the data set. While previous approaches construct a low-dimensional Euclidean embedding of the data set that reflects the given similarity triplets, we aim at defining kernel functions that correspond to high-dimensional embeddings. These kernel functions can subsequently be used to apply any kernel method to the data set.

paragraphs: Some datasets describe objects only through relative similarity judgments: one object resembles a second more than a third. These triplets give comparative information without supplying ordinary feature vectors or exact numerical distances. The paper asks how such evidence can support the use of kernel methods on the objects.

The authors propose two constructions of kernel functions from similarity triplets. Earlier approaches described in the abstract first seek a low-dimensional Euclidean embedding that reflects the comparisons. Here, the goal is to define kernels corresponding to high-dimensional embeddings, making a different representation of the same type of evidence available for learning.

The practical contribution is the connection to the broader kernel-method framework. Once a kernel is defined on the dataset, it can be used by any kernel method. Thus, the triplet information becomes an input to an existing family of learning techniques rather than serving only to arrange objects in a low-dimensional space. The stated contribution concerns these constructions and their downstream applicability, without asserting a particular empirical accuracy gain.
summary.tldr: Two kernel constructions turn relative similarity triplets into representations usable by kernel methods.

title: Kernel functions based on triplet comparisons

abstract: We describe an approach to learning from long-tailed, imbalanced datasets that are prevalent in real-world settings. Here, the challenge is to learn accurate "few-shot'' models for classes in the tail of the class distribution, for which little data is available. We cast this problem as transfer learning, where knowledge from the data-rich classes in the head of the distribution is transferred to the data-poor classes in the tail. Our key insights are as follows. First, we propose to transfer meta-knowledge about learning-to-learn from the head classes. This knowledge is encoded with a meta-network that operates on the space of model parameters, that is trained to predict many-shot model parameters from few-shot model parameters. Second, we transfer this meta-knowledge in a progressive manner, from classes in the head to the "body'', and from the "body'' to the tail. That is, we transfer knowledge in a gradual fashion, regularizing meta-networks for few-shot regression with those trained with more training data. This allows our final network to capture a notion of model dynamics, that predicts how model parameters are likely to change as more training data is gradually added. We demonstrate results on image classification datasets (SUN, Places, and ImageNet) tuned for the long-tailed setting, that significantly outperform common heuristics, such as data resampling or reweighting.

paragraphs: Long-tailed datasets contain a few well-represented classes and many classes with little training data. This paper treats learning the rare classes as a transfer problem: use the data-rich classes to learn how a model changes when more examples become available, then apply that knowledge to models trained on scarce data.

The method trains a meta-network in the space of model parameters. Its input is a model learned from few examples, and its target is the parameters of a model learned from many examples. Transfer proceeds gradually from the head of the class distribution through its body to its tail. Meta-networks trained with more data regularize those handling fewer examples.

This progressive construction captures a notion of model dynamics, predicting how parameters are likely to evolve as training data increase. On SUN, Places, and ImageNet datasets adjusted for long-tailed classification, the approach significantly outperforms common resampling and reweighting heuristics. The stated results support transferring knowledge about the learning process itself to improve data-poor classes.
summary.tldr: Progressive meta-networks transfer how model parameters change with more data from common classes to rare classes, improving long-tailed image classification.

title: Learning to Model the Tail

abstract: The Zap Q-learning algorithm introduced in this paper is an improvement of Watkins' original algorithm and recent competitors in several respects. It is a matrix-gain algorithm designed so that its asymptotic variance is optimal. Moreover, an ODE analysis suggests that the transient behavior is a close match to a deterministic Newton-Raphson implementation. This is made possible by a two time-scale update equation for the matrix gain sequence. The analysis suggests that the approach will lead to stable and efficient computation even for non-ideal parameterized settings. Numerical experiments confirm the quick convergence, even in such non-ideal cases.
