It is a matrix-gain algorithm designed so that its asymptotic variance is optimal. Moreover, an ODE analysis suggests that the transient behavior is a close match to a deterministic Newton-Raphson implementation. This is made possible by a two time-scale update equation for the matrix gain sequence. The analysis suggests that the approach will lead to stable and efficient computation even for non-ideal parameterized settings. Numerical experiments confirm the quick convergence, even in such non-ideal cases.

paragraphs: Zap Q-learning modifies Q-learning using a matrix gain, with the aim of improving both long-run statistical behavior and the speed of learning. The algorithm is designed to have optimal asymptotic variance. This criterion concerns variability in its asymptotic behavior, giving the update design an explicit statistical target.

The matrix gain is adjusted through an update equation operating on two time scales. An ordinary differential equation analysis suggests that the algorithm's transient behavior closely resembles a deterministic Newton-Raphson implementation. This connects the proposed learning dynamics to an established root-finding approach and provides a reason to expect efficient progress before reaching the asymptotic regime.

The analysis also suggests stable, efficient computation in non-ideal parameterized settings, and numerical experiments show rapid convergence even in those cases. The paper thus combines an optimal asymptotic-variance design with analytical indications and empirical evidence about convergence speed. The claims about transient behavior and stability remain suggestions from the analysis, supported by the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Zap Q-learning uses a two-time-scale matrix gain designed for optimal asymptotic variance and demonstrates fast numerical convergence.

title: Zap Q-Learning

abstract: In the context of advertising auctions, finding good reserve prices is a notoriously challenging learning problem. This is due to the heterogeneity of ad opportunity types, and the non-convexity of the objective function. In this work, we show how to reduce reserve price optimization to the standard setting of prediction under squared loss, a well understood problem in the learning community. We further bound the gap between the expected bid and revenue in terms of the average loss of the predictor. This is the first result that formally relates the revenue gained to the quality of a standard machine learned model.

In this work, we show how to reduce reserve price optimization to the standard setting of prediction under squared loss, a well understood problem in the learning community. We further bound the gap between the expected bid and revenue in terms of the average loss of the predictor. This is the first result that formally relates the revenue gained to the quality of a standard machine learned model.

paragraphs: Choosing reserve prices in advertising auctions is difficult because advertising opportunities differ and the revenue objective is nonconvex. This paper connects that difficult optimization task to a more familiar learning problem: predicting bids under squared loss. The connection provides a way to approach reserve-price selection through a standard prediction objective.

The main methodological result is a reduction from reserve-price optimization to squared-loss prediction. This matters because it relates the auction decision to a well-understood form of machine learning. The contribution is not merely to suggest that accurate predictions might help; it establishes a formal relationship between predictive quality and revenue.

Specifically, the authors bound the difference between the expected bid and revenue using the predictor's average loss. That bound explains how prediction error enters a revenue guarantee. It connects a quantity used to assess a learned predictor with a quantity relevant to auction performance. The abstract presents this as the first formal link between revenue gained and the quality of a standard machine-learned model.
summary.tldr: The paper reduces auction reserve-price optimization to squared-loss prediction and bounds the expected-bid–revenue gap using prediction error.

title: Revenue Optimization with Approximate Bid Predictions

abstract: Adaptive stimulus selection methods in neuroscience have primarily focused on maximizing the firing rate of a single recorded neuron. When recording from a population of neurons, it is usually not possible to find a single stimulus that maximizes the firing rates of all neurons. This motivates optimizing an objective function that takes into account the responses of all recorded neurons together. We propose “Adept,” an adaptive stimulus selection method that can optimize population objective functions. In simulations, we first confirmed that population objective functions elicited more diverse stimulus responses than single-neuron objective functions. Then, we tested Adept in a closed-loop electrophysiological experiment in which population activity was recorded from macaque V4, a cortical area known for mid-level visual processing. To predict neural responses, we used the outputs of a deep convolutional neural network model as feature embeddings. Images chosen by Adept elicited mean neural responses that were 20% larger than those for randomly-chosen natural images, and also evoked a larger diversity of neural responses. Such adaptive stimulus selection methods can facilitate experiments that involve neurons far from the sensory periphery, for which it is often unclear which stimuli to present.

paragraphs: A stimulus that strongly activates one neuron may not be useful for an entire recorded population. This paper develops Adept, an adaptive selection method that optimizes objectives involving responses across multiple neurons. The goal is to support experiments where useful stimuli are difficult to identify in advance.

Simulations first show that population objectives elicit more diverse responses than single-neuron objectives. The authors then test Adept in closed-loop electrophysiology in macaque V4, using deep-convolutional-network outputs as feature embeddings for predicting neural responses and selecting images.

Images chosen by Adept produce mean neural responses 20% larger than randomly selected natural images and evoke greater response diversity. These findings support the approach in the tested population and stimulus setting. They do not imply that one image maximizes every neuron simultaneously; the method explicitly targets an objective that evaluates the recorded population together.
summary.tldr: Adept selects images adaptively to elicit stronger and more varied population neural responses.

title: Adaptive stimulus selection for optimizing neural population responses

abstract: We compare the robustness of humans and current convolutional deep neural networks (DNNs) on object recognition under twelve different types of image degradations. First, using three well known DNNs (ResNet-152, VGG-19, GoogLeNet) we find the human visual system to be more robust to nearly all of the tested image manipulations, and we observe progressively diverging classification error-patterns between humans and DNNs when the signal gets weaker. Secondly, we show that DNNs trained directly on distorted images consistently surpass human performance on the exact distortion types they were trained on, yet they display extremely poor generalisation abilities when tested on other distortion types. For example, training on salt-and-pepper noise does not imply robustness on uniform white noise and vice versa. Thus, changes in the noise distribution between training and testing constitutes a crucial challenge to deep learning vision systems that can be systematically addressed in a lifelong machine learning approach. Our new dataset consisting of 83K carefully measured human psychophysical trials provide a useful reference for lifelong robustness against image degradations set by the human visual system.

paragraphs: This paper compares human object recognition with three convolutional networks under twelve kinds of image degradation. The networks are ResNet-152, VGG-19, and GoogLeNet. Humans are more robust to nearly all tested manipulations, and the patterns of classification errors increasingly differ between humans and networks as the visual signal becomes weaker.

Training networks directly on distorted images changes the comparison. They consistently exceed human performance on the exact distortion types included in training, but generalize extremely poorly to other types. The paper gives a concrete example: learning robustness to salt-and-pepper noise does not provide robustness to uniform white noise, and the reverse transfer also fails.

The findings separate success on familiar degradation from robustness when the noise distribution changes. That distinction makes variation between training and testing a central challenge for the evaluated vision systems. The authors point to lifelong machine learning as an approach for systematically addressing it. They also provide a dataset of 83,000 measured human psychophysical trials, offering a human reference for studying robustness to degraded images.
summary.tldr: Networks can surpass humans on trained image distortions yet transfer that robustness poorly to different distortion types.

title: Generalisation in humans and deep neural networks

abstract: The recent success in human action recognition with deep learning methods mostly adopt the supervised learning paradigm, which requires significant amount of manually labeled data to achieve good performance. However, label collection is an expensive and time-consuming process. In this work, we propose an unsupervised learning framework, which exploits unlabeled data to learn video representations. Different from previous works in video representation learning, our unsupervised learning task is to predict 3D motion in multiple target views using video representation from a source view. By learning to extrapolate cross-view motions, the representation can capture view-invariant motion dynamics which is discriminative for the action. In addition, we propose a view-adversarial training method to enhance learning of view-invariant features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the learned representations for action recognition on multiple datasets.

However, label collection is an expensive and time-consuming process. In this work, we propose an unsupervised learning framework, which exploits unlabeled data to learn video representations. Different from previous works in video representation learning, our unsupervised learning task is to predict 3D motion in multiple target views using video representation from a source view. By learning to extrapolate cross-view motions, the representation can capture view-invariant motion dynamics which is discriminative for the action. In addition, we propose a view-adversarial training method to enhance learning of view-invariant features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the learned representations for action recognition on multiple datasets.

paragraphs: Recognizing human actions from video often relies on large amounts of manually labeled data. This paper develops an unsupervised framework to learn video representations from unlabeled data, reducing reliance on expensive annotation for representation learning. Its central objective is to capture motion in a form that remains useful when the viewing direction changes.

The learning task asks a representation extracted from one source view to predict three-dimensional motion in multiple target views. Successful cross-view motion prediction encourages the representation to capture underlying motion dynamics that distinguish actions across viewpoints. The authors additionally introduce view-adversarial training to strengthen the learning of features that are invariant to the view.

The learned representations are evaluated for action recognition on multiple datasets, where the authors demonstrate their effectiveness. The contribution lies in using cross-view motion prediction as the training signal, together with an adversarial mechanism for reducing view dependence. This connects an unlabeled prediction task to the desired downstream behavior: recognizing an action through motion information that remains meaningful across different views.
summary.tldr: Predicting motion across views and using view-adversarial training yields useful action representations from unlabeled video.

title: Unsupervised Learning of View-invariant Action Representations

abstract: This paper introduces versatile filters to construct efficient convolutional neural network. Considering the demands of efficient deep learning techniques running on cost-effective hardware, a number of methods have been developed to learn compact neural networks. Most of these works aim to slim down filters in different ways, e.g., investigating small, sparse or binarized filters. In contrast, we treat filters from an additive perspective. A series of secondary filters can be derived from a primary filter. These secondary filters all inherit in the primary filter without occupying more storage, but once been unfolded in computation they could significantly enhance the capability of the filter by integrating information extracted from different receptive fields. Besides spatial versatile filters, we additionally investigate versatile filters from the channel perspective. The new techniques are general to upgrade filters in existing CNNs. Experimental results on benchmark datasets and neural networks demonstrate that CNNs constructed with our versatile filters are able to achieve comparable accuracy as that of original filters, but require less memory and FLOPs.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces versatile filters to construct efficient convolutional neural network. Considering the demands of efficient deep learning techniques running on cost-effective hardware, a number of methods have been developed to learn compact neural networks. Most of these works aim to slim down filters in different ways, e.g., investigating small, sparse or binarized filters. In contrast, we treat filters from an additive perspective. A series of secondary filters can be derived from a primary filter. These secondary filters all inherit in the primary filter without occupying more storage, but once been unfolded in computation they could significantly enhance the capability of the filter by integrating information extracted from different receptive fields. Besides spatial versatile filters, we additionally investigate versatile filters from the channel perspective. The new techniques are general to upgrade filters in existing CNNs. Experimental results on benchmark datasets and neural networks demonstrate that CNNs constructed with our versatile filters are able to achieve comparable accuracy as that of original filters, but require less memory and FLOPs.

paragraphs: Efficient convolutional networks need to make good use of limited memory and computation. Many compact-network methods reduce filters through smaller, sparse, or binary representations. This paper introduces versatile filters, which take an additive approach: a primary filter contains the basis for a series of secondary filters that can be derived from it.

Those secondary filters do not require additional filter storage. When unfolded during computation, they can combine information extracted from different receptive fields, increasing the capability of the stored filter. The authors investigate this idea in both spatial and channel dimensions and describe the techniques as applicable to filters in existing convolutional networks.

Experiments across benchmark datasets and networks show comparable accuracy to the original filters with lower memory requirements and fewer floating-point operations. The result matters because it connects a richer use of stored filter information with overall resource savings. The secondary filters provide multiple computational uses of the underlying representation, while the reported network-level comparisons assess whether that design preserves accuracy efficiently.
summary.tldr: Versatile filters derive multiple secondary filters from shared stored weights, preserving reported accuracy while reducing memory and computation.

title: Learning Versatile Filters for Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: In distributed machine learning (DML), the network performance between machines significantly impacts the speed of iterative training. In this paper we propose BML, a new gradient synchronization algorithm with higher network performance and lower network cost than the current practice. BML runs on BCube network, instead of using the traditional Fat-Tree topology. BML algorithm is designed in such a way that, compared to the parameter server (PS) algorithm on a Fat-Tree network connecting the same number of server machines, BML achieves theoretically 1/k of the gradient synchronization time, with k/5 of switches (the typical number of k is 2∼4). Experiments of LeNet-5 and VGG-19 benchmarks on a testbed with 9 dual-GPU servers show that, BML reduces the job completion time of DML training by up to 56.4%.

BML addresses this communication step with a gradient synchronization algorithm designed for a BCube network. The proposal joins an algorithmic choice with a network topology choice, making the communication infrastructure part of the training-speed solution.

In that comparison, BML achieves one divided by k times the synchronization time while using k divided by five times as many switches. The abstract gives two to four as typical values of k.

The authors also test LeNet-5 and VGG-19 training on nine servers, each equipped with two GPUs. They report reductions in total training job completion time of up to 56.4%. This complements the synchronization analysis with an end-to-end measurement, while the phrase 'up to' identifies the largest reported improvement rather than a uniform reduction across every experiment.
summary.tldr: BML combines gradient synchronization with BCube networking to reduce communication cost and accelerate distributed training.

title: BML: A High-performance, Low-cost Gradient Synchronization Algorithm for DML Training

abstract: Scaling up deep neural network capacity has been known as an effective approach to improving model quality for several different machine learning tasks. In many cases, increasing model capacity beyond the memory limit of a single accelerator has required developing special algorithms or infrastructure. These solutions are often architecture-specific and do not transfer to other machine learning tasks. To address the need for efficient and task-independent model parallelism, we introduce TensorPipe, a pipeline parallelism library that allows scaling any network that can be expressed as a sequence of layers. By pipelining different sub-sequences of layers on separate accelerators, TensorPipe provides the flexibility of scaling a variety of different networks to gigantic sizes efficiently. Moreover, TensorPipe utilizes a novel batch-splitting pipelining algorithm, resulting in almost linear speedup when a model is partitioned across multiple accelerators. We demonstrate the advantages of TensorPipe by training large-scale neural networks on two different tasks with distinct network architectures: (i)Image Classification: We train a 557-million-parameter AmoebaNet model and attain a top-1 accuracy of 84.4% on ImageNet-2012, (ii)Multilingual Neural Machine Translation: We train a single 6-billion-parameter, 128-layer Transformer model on a corpus spanning over 100 languages and achieve better quality than all bilingual models.

This paper presents a pipeline-parallel library, called TensorPipe in the supplied abstract, for networks expressible as sequences of layers. Its purpose is to make large-model training transferable across tasks and architectures.

The method assigns successive groups of layers to separate accelerators. A batch-splitting pipeline algorithm then organizes work across those groups, allowing different parts of the network to run on different devices. A single six-billion-parameter, 128-layer Transformer trained on over 100 languages achieves better quality than all bilingual models in the reported comparison. These examples show the approach supporting large networks with distinct architectures under the common requirement of a layered sequence.
summary.tldr: Pipeline parallelism and batch splitting enable efficient training of very large layered networks across multiple accelerators.

title: GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism

abstract: We study the design of computationally efficient algorithms with provable guarantees, that are robust to adversarial (test time) perturbations. While there has been an explosion of recent work on this topic due to its connections to test time robustness of deep networks, there is limited theoretical understanding of several basic questions like (i) when and how can one design provably robust learning algorithms? (ii) what is the price of achieving robustness to adversarial examples in a computationally efficient manner? The main contribution of this work is to exhibit a strong connection between achieving robustness to adversarial examples, and a rich class of polynomial optimization problems, thereby making progress on the above questions. In particular, we leverage this connection to (a) design computationally efficient robust algorithms with provable guarantees for a large class of hypothesis, namely linear classifiers and degree-2 polynomial threshold functions~(PTFs), (b) give a precise characterization of the price of achieving robustness in a computationally efficient manner for these classes, (c) design efficient algorithms to certify robustness and generate adversarial attacks in a principled manner for 2-layer neural networks. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of these attacks on real data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to make learning algorithms provably robust to adversarial changes in their test-time inputs without making computation impractical. It asks both when efficient robust learning is possible and what price must be paid for that efficiency. Its main contribution is a connection between these questions and polynomial optimization.

Using that connection, the authors design computationally efficient robust algorithms with guarantees for linear classifiers and degree-two polynomial threshold functions. They also characterize the price of obtaining robustness efficiently for those hypothesis classes. The scope matters: these are guarantees for the specified model families, rather than a general solution for every deep network.

The same perspective yields efficient procedures for certifying robustness and constructing adversarial attacks on two-layer neural networks. Certification and attack generation address complementary questions: whether robustness can be established and how vulnerable inputs can be found. Experiments on real data demonstrate the effectiveness of the attacks. The paper thus combines theoretical learning guarantees with concrete methods for examining the robustness of another class of models.
summary.tldr: Connecting adversarial robustness to polynomial optimization yields provable learning algorithms and principled certification and attack methods for specified model classes.

title: On Robustness to Adversarial Examples and Polynomial Optimization

abstract: This paper considers submodular function minimization with \textit{noisy evaluation oracles} that return the function value of a submodular objective with zero-mean additive noise. For this problem, we provide an algorithm that returns an $O(n^{3/2}/\sqrt{T})$-additive approximate solution in expectation, where $n$ and $T$ stand for the size of the problem and the number of oracle calls, respectively. There is no room for reducing this error bound by a factor smaller than $O(1/\sqrt{n})$. Indeed, we show that any algorithm will suffer additive errors of $\Omega(n/\sqrt{T})$ in the worst case. Further, we consider an extended problem setting with \textit{multiple-point feedback} in which we can get the feedback of $k$ function values with each oracle call. Under the additional assumption that each noisy oracle is submodular and that $2 \leq k = O(1)$, we provide an algorithm with an $O(n/\sqrt{T})$-additive error bound as well as a worst-case analysis including a lower bound of $\Omega(n/\sqrt{T})$, which together imply that the algorithm achieves an optimal error bound up to a constant.

paragraphs: The paper studies minimizing a submodular function when evaluations contain zero-mean additive noise. Instead of assuming exact access to the objective, it asks how solution quality improves with the number of oracle calls T and the problem size n.

For ordinary feedback, the proposed algorithm achieves expected additive error O(n^(3/2)/sqrt(T)). A worst-case lower bound of Omega(n/sqrt(T)) limits how much that dependence can improve. These bounds describe optimization error from noisy information rather than exact recovery of the minimum.

If every noisy oracle is itself submodular and 2 <= k = O(1), an algorithm achieves O(n/sqrt(T)) error with a matching lower bound up to constants. The optimality claim therefore belongs to this stronger feedback model and its additional assumptions, not automatically to the original single-value setting.
summary.tldr: Noisy submodular minimization has explicit error bounds, with optimal rates under multipoint feedback.

title: Submodular Function Minimization with Noisy Evaluation Oracle

abstract: Sparse representation with respect to an overcomplete dictionary is often used when regularizing inverse problems in signal and image processing. In recent years, the Convolutional Sparse Coding (CSC) model, in which the dictionary consists of shift invariant filters, has gained renewed interest. While this model has been successfully used in some image processing problems, it still falls behind traditional patch-based methods on simple tasks such as denoising. In this work we provide new insights regarding the CSC model and its capability to represent natural images, and suggest a Bayesian connection between this model and its patch-based ancestor. Armed with these observations, we suggest a novel feed-forward network that follows an MMSE approximation process to the CSC model, using strided convolutions. The performance of this supervised architecture is shown to be on par with state of the art methods while using much fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Sparse image representations describe an image using a relatively small selection from a larger dictionary of components. Convolutional Sparse Coding uses filters that can appear at different image locations. Although this model has been useful in image processing, the paper notes that it has lagged behind traditional patch-based methods on tasks such as denoising.

The authors revisit how well the convolutional model represents natural images and suggest a Bayesian connection to its patch-based predecessor. Those observations motivate a supervised feed-forward network built around an approximation to minimum mean squared error estimation under the convolutional model. The architecture uses strided convolutions, linking its network design to the underlying estimation process.

The resulting architecture performs on par with state-of-the-art methods while using substantially fewer parameters, according to the reported results. The contribution therefore combines an examination of an image model with a practical network derived from that examination. It shows how reconsidering the relationship between convolutional and patch-based representations can lead to a competitive, parameter-efficient supervised architecture.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian reconsideration of convolutional sparse coding motivates a supervised network that matches state-of-the-art performance with far fewer parameters.

title: Rethinking the CSC Model for Natural Images

abstract: Landing probabilities (LP) of random walks (RW) over graphs encode rich information regarding graph topology. Generalized PageRanks (GPR), which represent weighted sums of LPs of RWs, utilize the discriminative power of LP features to enable many graph-based learning studies. Previous work in the area has mostly focused on evaluating suitable weights for GPRs, and only a few studies so far have attempted to derive the optimal weights of GPRs for a given application. We take a fundamental step forward in this direction by using random graph models to better our understanding of the behavior of GPRs. In this context, we provide a rigorous non-asymptotic analysis for the convergence of LPs and GPRs to their mean-field values on edge-independent random graphs. Although our theoretical results apply to many problem settings, we focus on the task of seed-expansion community detection over stochastic block models. There, we find that the predictive power of LPs decreases significantly slower than previously reported based on asymptotic findings. Given this result, we propose a new GPR, termed Inverse PR (IPR), with LP weights that increase for the initial few steps of the walks. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real, large-scale networks illustrate the superiority of IPR compared to other GPRs for seeded community detection.

paragraphs: Random-walk landing probabilities describe where a walk is likely to arrive after different numbers of steps. Generalized PageRank combines these probabilities with weights, making the weighting scheme important for extracting useful graph information. This paper studies how those weights should be chosen for expanding a seed into a detected community.

The authors provide a non-asymptotic analysis of landing probabilities and generalized PageRank on random graphs with independent edges. It describes convergence toward mean-field values without relying only on limiting behavior. For community detection under stochastic block models, they find that the predictive usefulness of landing probabilities declines substantially more slowly than earlier asymptotic findings had suggested.

That result motivates Inverse PageRank, which increases the weights assigned to the first few walk lengths. The weighting preserves more influence for steps that the analysis indicates still carry useful information. Experiments on synthetic graphs and large real networks show superior seeded community detection compared with the other generalized PageRank methods considered. The paper thus connects finite-size theoretical analysis to a concrete change in graph-based prediction.
summary.tldr: Finite-size analysis motivates Inverse PageRank's increasing early-step weights, improving seeded community detection in the reported experiments.

title: Optimizing Generalized PageRank Methods for Seed-Expansion Community Detection

abstract: Self-supervision provides effective representations for downstream tasks without requiring labels. However, existing approaches lag behind fully supervised training and are often not thought beneficial beyond obviating or reducing the need for annotations. We find that self-supervision can benefit robustness in a variety of ways, including robustness to adversarial examples, label corruption, and common input corruptions. Additionally, self-supervision greatly benefits out-of-distribution detection on difficult, near-distribution outliers, so much so that it exceeds the performance of fully supervised methods. These results demonstrate the promise of self-supervision for improving robustness and uncertainty estimation and establish these tasks as new axes of evaluation for future self-supervised learning research.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning obtains useful representations without requiring labels. It is often evaluated mainly through downstream task performance or reduced annotation needs. This paper asks whether it also helps models behave more reliably when inputs or labels are problematic, broadening the criteria used to judge the usefulness of self-supervision.

The authors find benefits for robustness to adversarial examples, corrupted labels, and common input corruptions. These cover different ways that learning or prediction can be disrupted. The results show that self-supervision can contribute to robustness across several settings, even though the abstract notes that existing self-supervised approaches lag behind fully supervised training on conventional performance comparisons.

The paper also reports strong improvements in detecting out-of-distribution inputs that closely resemble the training distribution. On these difficult outliers, self-supervision surpasses fully supervised methods. Together, the findings support robustness and uncertainty estimation as additional evaluation dimensions for self-supervised learning. The claim is that these benefits can occur, rather than that every self-supervised method will outperform supervised learning everywhere.
summary.tldr: Self-supervision can improve robustness to several kinds of corruption and outperform fully supervised methods on difficult out-of-distribution detection.

title: Using Self-Supervised Learning Can Improve Model Robustness and Uncertainty

abstract: Given a linear regression setting, Iterative Least Trimmed Squares (ILTS) involves alternating between (a) selecting the subset of samples with lowest current loss, and (b) re-fitting the linear model only on that subset. Both steps are very fast and simple. In this paper, we analyze ILTS in the setting of mixed linear regression with corruptions (MLR-C). We first establish deterministic conditions (on the features etc.) under which the ILTS iterate converges linearly to the closest mixture component. We also provide a global algorithm that uses ILTS as a subroutine, to fully solve mixed linear regressions with corruptions. We then evaluate it for the widely studied setting of isotropic Gaussian features, and establish that we match or better existing results in terms of sample complexity. Finally, we provide an ODE analysis for a gradient-descent variant of ILTS that has optimal time complexity. Our results provide initial theoretical evidence that iteratively fitting to the best subset of samples -- a potentially widely applicable idea -- can provably provide state of the art performance in bad training data settings.

paragraphs: Iterative Least Trimmed Squares alternates two simple operations: select the samples that the current linear model fits best, then refit using only that subset. This paper analyzes the method when observations come from multiple linear regression components and some data are corrupted. The challenge is to recover the underlying components despite that mixture and corruption.

The authors establish deterministic conditions on the features and related quantities under which the iterations converge linearly to the nearest mixture component. They then build a global algorithm that uses this local procedure as a subroutine to solve the full corrupted mixed regression problem. The local convergence statement is explicitly conditional on the established requirements.

For isotropic Gaussian features, the sample complexity matches or improves existing results. An ordinary differential equation analysis also supports a gradient-descent variant with optimal time complexity. Together, these results provide initial theoretical evidence for repeatedly fitting the best-fitting subset as a strategy for difficult training data. The guarantees are grounded in the analyzed regression settings and conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper proves conditional convergence and strong efficiency guarantees for repeatedly fitting low-loss subsets in corrupted mixed linear regression.

title: Iterative Least Trimmed Squares for Mixed Linear Regression

abstract: Current algorithms for deep learning probably cannot run in the brain because they rely on weight transport, where forward-path neurons transmit their synaptic weights to a feedback path, in a way that is likely impossible biologically. An algorithm called feedback alignment achieves deep learning without weight transport by using random feedback weights, but it performs poorly on hard visual-recognition tasks. Here we describe two mechanisms — a neural circuit called a weight mirror and a modification of an algorithm proposed by Kolen and Pollack in 1994 — both of which let the feedback path learn appropriate synaptic weights quickly and accurately even in large networks, without weight transport or complex wiring. Tested on the ImageNet visual-recognition task, these mechanisms outperform both feedback alignment and the newer sign-symmetry method, and nearly match backprop, the standard algorithm of deep learning, which uses weight transport.

paragraphs: Standard deep learning relies on weight transport: weights used in the forward computation must also be available to a feedback pathway. The paper argues that this requirement is probably incompatible with biological learning. Random feedback weights avoid transporting weights, but the existing feedback alignment approach performs poorly on difficult visual recognition tasks.

The authors introduce two mechanisms that allow the feedback pathway to learn suitable weights. One is a neural circuit called a weight mirror; the other modifies an earlier algorithm by Kolen and Pollack. Both are described as learning feedback weights quickly and accurately in large networks without weight transport or complicated wiring.

On ImageNet, the mechanisms outperform feedback alignment and the newer sign-symmetry method, while nearly matching standard backpropagation. The result narrows the performance gap between backpropagation and approaches that avoid its weight-transport requirement. It provides evidence for effective alternative learning mechanisms on a challenging recognition task, while the motivation about biological feasibility remains a qualified argument.
summary.tldr: Two mechanisms learn effective feedback weights without weight transport and nearly match backpropagation on ImageNet.

title: Deep Learning without Weight Transport

abstract: Tractable models of human perception have proved to be challenging to build. Hand-designed models such as MS-SSIM remain popular predictors of human image quality judgements due to their simplicity and speed. Recent modern deep learning approaches can perform better, but they rely on supervised data which can be costly to gather: large sets of class labels such as ImageNet, image quality ratings, or both. We combine recent advances in information-theoretic objective functions with a computational architecture informed by the physiology of the human visual system and unsupervised training on pairs of video frames, yielding our Perceptual Information Metric (PIM). We show that PIM is competitive with supervised metrics on the recent and challenging BAPPS image quality assessment dataset and outperforms them in predicting the ranking of image compression methods in CLIC 2020. We also perform qualitative experiments using the ImageNet-C dataset, and establish that PIM is robust with respect to architectural details.

paragraphs: Predicting human judgments of image quality is difficult. Hand-designed measures remain attractive for their speed and simplicity, while stronger learned measures can depend on costly class labels or quality ratings. This paper develops a learned perceptual quality measure using unsupervised training on pairs of video frames.

The proposed Perceptual Information Metric, or PIM, combines information-theoretic training objectives with an architecture informed by human visual physiology. The approach brings together a learning objective and a perceptually motivated computational design, while avoiding the supervised labels used by the compared modern approaches. Video frame pairs supply the material from which the metric is learned.

PIM is competitive with supervised metrics on the BAPPS image quality assessment dataset and performs better at predicting the ranking of image compression methods in CLIC 2020. The authors also conduct qualitative experiments on ImageNet-C and report robustness to architectural details. The findings show that an unsupervised training approach can yield a useful perceptual metric, with the strength of the reported comparison varying by evaluation task.
summary.tldr: PIM learns perceptual image quality from unlabeled video frame pairs and competes with supervised metrics on the reported evaluations.

title: An Unsupervised Information-Theoretic Perceptual Quality Metric

abstract: Two major challenges in distributed learning and estimation are 1) preserving the privacy of the local samples; and 2) communicating them efficiently to a central server, while achieving high accuracy for the end-to-end task. While there has been significant interest in addressing each of these challenges separately in the recent literature, treatments that simultaneously address both challenges are still largely missing. In this paper, we develop novel encoding and decoding mechanisms that simultaneously achieve optimal privacy and communication efficiency in various canonical settings. In particular, we consider the problems of mean estimation and frequency estimation under epsilon-local differential privacy and b-bit communication constraints. For mean estimation, we propose a scheme based on Kashin’s representation and random sampling, with order-optimal estimation error under both constraints. For frequency estimation, we present a mechanism that leverages the recursive structure of Walsh-Hadamard matrices and achieves order-optimal estimation error for all privacy levels and communication budgets. As a by-product, we also construct a distribution estimation mechanism that is rate-optimal for all privacy regimes and communication constraints, extending recent work that is limited to b = 1 and epsilon = O(1). Our results demonstrate that intelligent encoding under joint privacy and communication constraints can yield a performance that matches the optimal accuracy achievable under either constraint alone.

For mean estimation, we propose a scheme based on Kashin’s representation and random sampling, with order-optimal estimation error under both constraints. For frequency estimation, we present a mechanism that leverages the recursive structure of Walsh-Hadamard matrices and achieves order-optimal estimation error for all privacy levels and communication budgets. As a by-product, we also construct a distribution estimation mechanism that is rate-optimal for all privacy regimes and communication constraints, extending recent work that is limited to b = 1 and epsilon = O(1). Our results demonstrate that intelligent encoding under joint privacy and communication constraints can yield a performance that matches the optimal accuracy achievable under either constraint alone.

paragraphs: Distributed estimation often needs to protect each participant's data while limiting how much information they send to a server. Both restrictions can affect accuracy. This paper studies them together, imposing epsilon-local differential privacy and a communication budget of b bits. It develops coordinated encoding and decoding mechanisms for mean, frequency, and distribution estimation.

For mean estimation, the proposed method combines Kashin's representation with random sampling and achieves order-optimal error under both constraints. For frequency estimation, it uses the recursive structure of Walsh-Hadamard matrices to achieve order-optimal error across privacy levels and communication budgets. The authors also obtain a rate-optimal distribution estimator that extends earlier results restricted to one-bit communication and a bounded privacy parameter.

The central finding is that carefully designed encoding can avoid an additional loss in the accuracy rate simply from having both restrictions present. In the settings studied, jointly constrained mechanisms can match the optimal accuracy available under either constraint alone. These are optimality statements about estimation rates, connecting privacy and communication within a single design.
summary.tldr: Jointly designed encoding mechanisms achieve optimal estimation rates while satisfying both local privacy and limited communication requirements.

title: Breaking the Communication-Privacy-Accuracy Trilemma

abstract: Machine learning transparency calls for interpretable explanations of how inputs relate to predictions. Feature attribution is a way to analyze the impact of features on predictions. Feature interactions are the contextual dependence between features that jointly impact predictions. There are a number of methods that extract feature interactions in prediction models; however, the methods that assign attributions to interactions are either uninterpretable, model-specific, or non-axiomatic. We propose an interaction attribution and detection framework called Archipelago which addresses these problems and is also scalable in real-world settings. Our experiments on standard annotation labels indicate our approach provides significantly more interpretable explanations than comparable methods, which is important for analyzing the impact of interactions on predictions. We also provide accompanying visualizations of our approach that give new insights into deep neural networks.

paragraphs: Explaining a prediction requires more than identifying influential individual inputs when their effects depend on one another. Feature interactions capture this contextual dependence: a group of features can jointly affect a prediction in a way that deserves its own explanation. This paper addresses both finding those interactions and assigning interpretable attributions to them.

The authors introduce Archipelago, a framework designed to address shortcomings of existing interaction attribution methods. Those methods may be difficult to interpret, restricted to particular models, or lack an axiomatic foundation. Archipelago brings interaction detection and attribution together while also aiming to scale to real-world settings. Its purpose is to explain how joint effects contribute to predictions, beyond merely reporting that an interaction exists.

Experiments using standard annotation labels indicate significantly more interpretable explanations than comparable approaches. The paper also provides visualizations that offer insights into deep neural networks. These results concern the usefulness of interaction-level explanations: identifying related inputs becomes more informative when the explanation also communicates their combined impact on the model’s prediction.
summary.tldr: Archipelago detects feature interactions and attributes their joint effects to make model predictions more interpretable.

title: How does This Interaction Affect Me? Interpretable Attribution for Feature Interactions

abstract: Differentiation lies at the core of many machine-learning algorithms, and is well-supported by popular autodiff systems, such as TensorFlow and PyTorch. Originally, these systems have been developed to compute derivatives of differentiable functions, but in practice, they are commonly applied to functions with non-differentiabilities. For instance, neural networks using ReLU define non-differentiable functions in general, but the gradients of losses involving those functions are computed using autodiff systems in practice. This status quo raises a natural question: are autodiff systems correct in any formal sense when they are applied to such non-differentiable functions? In this paper, we provide a positive answer to this question. Using counterexamples, we first point out flaws in often-used informal arguments, such as: non-differentiabilities arising in deep learning do not cause any issues because they form a measure-zero set. We then investigate a class of functions, called PAP functions, that includes nearly all (possibly non-differentiable) functions in deep learning nowadays. For these PAP functions, we propose a new type of derivatives, called intensional derivatives, and prove that these derivatives always exist and coincide with standard derivatives for almost all inputs. We also show that these intensional derivatives are what most autodiff systems compute or try to compute essentially. In this way, we formally establish the correctness of autodiff systems applied to non-differentiable functions.

The result explains correctness through a suitable derivative concept and a specified function class, while preserving the distinction between agreement almost everywhere and ordinary differentiability at every input.
summary.tldr: Intensional derivatives provide a formal correctness framework for automatic differentiation on a broad class of nondifferentiable functions.

title: On Correctness of Automatic Differentiation for Non-Differentiable Functions

abstract: The randomized midpoint method, proposed by (Shen and Lee, 2019), has emerged as an optimal discretization procedure for simulating the continuous time underdamped Langevin diffusion. In this paper, we analyze several probabilistic properties of the randomized midpoint discretization method, considering both overdamped and underdamped Langevin dynamics. We first characterize the stationary distribution of the discrete chain obtained with constant step-size discretization and show that it is biased away from the target distribution. Notably, the step-size needs to go to zero to obtain asymptotic unbiasedness. Next, we establish the asymptotic normality of numerical integration using the randomized midpoint method and highlight the relative advantages and disadvantages over other discretizations. Our results collectively provide several insights into the behavior of the randomized midpoint discretization method, including obtaining confidence intervals for numerical integrations.

paragraphs: The randomized midpoint method approximates continuous-time Langevin dynamics with discrete simulation steps. This paper studies its probabilistic behavior for both overdamped and underdamped dynamics. The questions concern what distribution the discrete process settles into and how numerical integration estimates behave as the method runs for longer.

For a constant step size, the authors characterize the stationary distribution of the discrete chain and show that it differs from the intended target distribution. Consequently, running a fixed-step simulation longer does not remove this discretization bias. The step size must tend to zero to obtain asymptotic unbiasedness, separating the effects of simulation duration from those of discretization.

The paper also establishes asymptotic normality for numerical integration using the method. This describes the limiting statistical behavior needed to construct confidence intervals for integral estimates. By examining relative advantages and disadvantages against other discretizations, the analysis gives a fuller account of the method than its discretization efficiency alone, connecting long-run distributional bias with uncertainty in numerical estimates.
summary.tldr: The analysis identifies fixed-step bias in randomized midpoint sampling and establishes asymptotic normality for numerical integration and confidence intervals.

title: On the Ergodicity, Bias and Asymptotic Normality of Randomized Midpoint Sampling Method

abstract: Training generative adversarial networks (GAN) using too little data typically leads to discriminator overfitting, causing training to diverge. We propose an adaptive discriminator augmentation mechanism that significantly stabilizes training in limited data regimes. The approach does not require changes to loss functions or network architectures, and is applicable both when training from scratch and when fine-tuning an existing GAN on another dataset. We demonstrate, on several datasets, that good results are now possible using only a few thousand training images, often matching StyleGAN2 results with an order of magnitude fewer images. We expect this to open up new application domains for GANs. We also find that the widely used CIFAR-10 is, in fact, a limited data benchmark, and improve the record FID from 5.59 to 2.42.

paragraphs: Training a generative adversarial network on too few images can cause its discriminator to overfit, destabilizing the training process. This paper introduces adaptive discriminator augmentation to address that problem. Its purpose is to make GAN training work reliably in settings where the available image collection is small.

The mechanism can be used without changing network architectures or loss functions. It applies both to training a new GAN from scratch and to adapting an existing GAN to another dataset. This makes the contribution a training mechanism that fits multiple workflows, including cases where a model is already available and cases where learning must begin anew.

They also identify CIFAR-10 as a limited-data benchmark in this context and improve the reported record FID from 5.59 to 2.42. These findings support adaptive augmentation as a practical response to discriminator overfitting and suggest opportunities for GAN use with smaller datasets.
summary.tldr: Adaptive discriminator augmentation stabilizes GAN training with limited data, often matching StyleGAN2 results with roughly ten times fewer images.

title: Training Generative Adversarial Networks with Limited Data

abstract: Many processes, such as discrete event systems in engineering or population dynamics in biology, evolve in discrete space and continuous time. We consider the problem of optimal decision making in such discrete state and action space systems under partial observability. This places our work at the intersection of optimal filtering and optimal control. At the current state of research, a mathematical description for simultaneous decision making and filtering in continuous time with finite state and action spaces is still missing. In this paper, we give a mathematical description of a continuous-time partial observable Markov decision process (POMDP). By leveraging optimal filtering theory we derive a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) type equation that characterizes the optimal solution. Using techniques from deep learning we approximately solve the resulting partial integro-differential equation. We present (i) an approach solving the decision problem offline by learning an approximation of the value function and (ii) an online algorithm which provides a solution in belief space using deep reinforcement learning. We show the applicability on a set of toy examples which pave the way for future methods providing solutions for high dimensional problems.

paragraphs: Some systems change among discrete states while time runs continuously, and their true state is only partly observable. A decision maker must then estimate what is happening while choosing actions. This paper develops a mathematical description that brings those estimation and control problems together for finite state and action spaces.

Using optimal filtering theory, the authors formulate a continuous-time partially observable Markov decision process and derive a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-type equation characterizing its optimal solution. The mathematical formulation supplies the target that the learned approximations seek to satisfy.

Two computational approaches are presented. One learns a value-function approximation offline; the other uses deep reinforcement learning online in belief space, where decisions depend on uncertainty about the hidden state. Demonstrations on toy examples establish applicability in those settings. The paper positions these results as groundwork for future methods addressing high-dimensional problems, rather than claiming that such problems have already been solved.
summary.tldr: The paper formulates continuous-time POMDPs with finite states and actions and develops two deep-learning approaches to approximate their solutions.

title: POMDPs in Continuous Time and Discrete Spaces

abstract: Video frame interpolation, which aims to synthesize non-exist intermediate frames in a video sequence, is an important research topic in computer vision. Existing video frame interpolation methods have achieved remarkable results under specific assumptions, such as instant or known exposure time. However, in complicated real-world situations, the temporal priors of videos, i.e. frames per second (FPS) and frame exposure time, may vary from different camera sensors. When test videos are taken under different exposure settings from training ones, the interpolated frames will suffer significant misalignment problems. In this work, we solve the video frame interpolation problem in a general situation, where input frames can be acquired under uncertain exposure (and interval) time. Unlike previous methods that can only be applied to a specific temporal prior, we derive a general curvilinear motion trajectory formula from four consecutive sharp frames or two consecutive blurry frames without temporal priors. Moreover, utilizing constraints within adjacent motion trajectories, we devise a novel optical flow refinement strategy for better interpolation results. Finally, experiments demonstrate that one well-trained model is enough for synthesizing high-quality slow-motion videos under complicated real-world situations. Codes are available on https://github.com/yjzhang96/UTI-VFI.

paragraphs: Video interpolation creates frames between recorded images, but the appearance of those images depends on exposure duration and the interval between frames. A method trained for one timing setup can misalign its predictions when a different camera uses different settings. This paper addresses interpolation when those temporal quantities are uncertain.

The authors derive a general curved-motion trajectory formula using either four consecutive sharp frames or two consecutive blurry frames, without requiring temporal priors. This provides a way to describe movement without fixing the input video's timing assumptions in advance. They also refine optical flow using constraints between neighboring motion trajectories to improve the interpolated results.

Experiments show that a single trained model can generate high-quality slow-motion video under the varied real-world conditions considered. The contribution connects a motion formulation that accommodates uncertain exposure and intervals with a refinement method that exploits relationships among trajectories. Its practical significance is that the reported model need not be restricted to one particular temporal prior when producing intermediate frames.
summary.tldr: A general motion formulation and optical-flow refinement enable frame interpolation without known exposure times or frame intervals.

title: Video Frame Interpolation without Temporal Priors

abstract: Recent theoretical and experimental results suggest that the dopamine system implements distributional temporal difference backups, allowing learning of the entire distributions of the long-run values of states rather than just their expected values. However, the distributional codes explored so far rely on a complex imputation step which crucially relies on spatial non-locality: in order to compute reward prediction errors, units must know not only their own state but also the states of the other units. It is far from clear how these steps could be implemented in realistic neural circuits. Here, we introduce the Laplace code: a local temporal difference code for distributional reinforcement learning that is representationally powerful and computationally straightforward. The code decomposes value distributions and prediction errors across three separated dimensions: reward magnitude (related to distributional quantiles), temporal discounting (related to the Laplace transform of future rewards) and time horizon (related to eligibility traces). Besides lending itself to a local learning rule, the decomposition recovers the temporal evolution of the immediate reward distribution, indicating all possible rewards at all future times. This increases representational capacity and allows for temporally-flexible computations that immediately adjust to changing horizons or discount factors.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning represents the range of possible long-term outcomes instead of only their average. The paper starts from evidence suggesting that dopamine systems may perform this kind of learning. A difficulty with previously explored representations is that computing a unit's prediction error requires information about other units, making the required computation difficult to explain in realistic neural circuits.

The authors introduce the Laplace code, which separates reward information along three dimensions: reward magnitude, temporal discounting, and time horizon. These connect respectively to distributional quantiles, the Laplace transform of future rewards, and eligibility traces. The separation supports a local temporal-difference learning rule while retaining a rich representation of possible outcomes.

The representation also recovers how the immediate reward distribution evolves over future time, rather than only summarizing long-run value. This gives it the capacity to represent which rewards may occur at different future moments. The resulting computations can immediately adjust to changed horizons or discount factors. The contribution is a computationally straightforward candidate code with these capabilities, rather than a demonstration that biological circuits necessarily use it.
summary.tldr: The Laplace code supports local distributional reinforcement learning while representing possible rewards across future times and adapting to changed horizons or discounting.

title: A Local Temporal Difference Code for Distributional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) refers to the problem of learning policies entirely from a batch of previously collected data. This problem setting is compelling, because it offers the promise of utilizing large, diverse, previously collected datasets to acquire policies without any costly or dangerous active exploration, but it is also exceptionally difficult, due to the distributional shift between the offline training data and the learned policy. While there has been significant progress in model-free offline RL, the most successful prior methods constrain the policy to the support of the data, precluding generalization to new states. In this paper, we observe that an existing model-based RL algorithm on its own already produces significant gains in the offline setting, as compared to model-free approaches, despite not being designed for this setting. However, although many standard model-based RL methods already estimate the uncertainty of their model, they do not by themselves provide a mechanism to avoid the issues associated with distributional shift in the offline setting. We therefore propose to modify existing model-based RL methods to address these issues by casting offline model-based RL into a penalized MDP framework. We theoretically show that, by using this penalized MDP, we are maximizing a lower bound of the return in the true MDP. Based on our theoretical results, we propose a new model-based offline RL algorithm that applies the variance of a Lipschitz-regularized model as a penalty to the reward function. We find that this algorithm outperforms both standard model-based RL methods and existing state-of-the-art model-free offline RL approaches on existing offline RL benchmarks, as well as two challenging continuous control tasks that require generalizing from data collected for a different task.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains a policy entirely from previously collected data. Its central difficulty is distributional shift: the learned policy may visit situations poorly represented in that data. A learned dynamics model can support planning beyond recorded experiences, but its predictions may be unreliable where evidence is sparse.

MOPO addresses this problem by reducing rewards according to model uncertainty. The paper formulates offline model-based learning as optimization in a penalized Markov decision process and theoretically connects its objective to a lower bound on return in the true environment. The proposed algorithm uses the variance of a Lipschitz-regularized dynamics model as the reward penalty, making uncertain predictions less attractive during policy optimization.

The authors first observe that an existing model-based method already performs strongly offline, then report further gains from their uncertainty penalty. MOPO outperforms standard model-based methods and the compared leading model-free offline methods on the evaluated benchmarks. It also performs better on two continuous-control tasks requiring generalization from data gathered for a different task, supporting the usefulness of uncertainty-aware model-based learning beyond the original data-collection objective.
summary.tldr: MOPO penalizes uncertain model predictions during offline reinforcement learning, improving tested policy performance and supporting generalization across tasks.

title: MOPO: Model-based Offline Policy Optimization

abstract: In order to deal with the curse of dimensionality in reinforcement learning (RL), it is common practice to make parametric assumptions where values or policies are functions of some low dimensional feature space. This work focuses on the representation learning question: how can we learn such features? Under the assumption that the underlying (unknown) dynamics correspond to a low rank transition matrix, we show how the representation learning question is related to a particular non-linear matrix decomposition problem. Structurally, we make precise connections between these low rank MDPs and latent variable models, showing how they significantly generalize prior formulations, such as block MDPs, for representation learning in RL. Algorithmically, we develop FLAMBE, which engages in exploration and representation learning for provably efficient RL in low rank transition models. On a technical level, our analysis eliminates reachability assumptions that appear in prior results on the simpler block MDP model and may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often becomes more manageable when values or policies can be expressed through a small set of features. But assuming those features are already available leaves a major question unanswered: how should an agent learn them? This paper addresses that question under the assumption that the environment’s unknown transition matrix has low rank.

The authors connect learning a representation to a particular nonlinear matrix decomposition problem. They also clarify the relationship between low-rank Markov decision processes and latent-variable models. This structural analysis shows that low-rank models substantially extend earlier representation-learning formulations, including block MDPs, giving the learning problem a broader mathematical foundation.

Their algorithm, FLAMBE, combines exploration with representation learning and provides provably efficient reinforcement learning for low-rank transition models. Its analysis also removes reachability assumptions used in earlier results for the simpler block-MDP setting. The contribution therefore concerns both what kinds of environments can be represented and how an agent can learn within them. The efficiency claim remains tied to the low-rank model assumption.
summary.tldr: FLAMBE jointly explores and learns representations for provably efficient reinforcement learning under a low-rank transition assumption.

title: FLAMBE: Structural Complexity and Representation Learning of Low Rank MDPs

abstract: We introduce a generic template for developing regret minimization algorithms in the Stochastic Shortest Path (SSP) model, which achieves minimax optimal regret as long as certain properties are ensured. The key of our analysis is a new technique called implicit finite-horizon approximation, which approximates the SSP model by a finite-horizon counterpart only in the analysis without explicit implementation. Using this template, we develop two new algorithms: the first one is model-free (the first in the literature to our knowledge) and minimax optimal under strictly positive costs; the second one is model-based and minimax optimal even with zero-cost state-action pairs, matching the best existing result from [Tarbouriech et al., 2021b]. Importantly, both algorithms admit highly sparse updates, making them computationally more efficient than all existing algorithms. Moreover, both can be made completely parameter-free.

paragraphs: Stochastic shortest path learning concerns decisions that accumulate costs while progressing toward a destination under uncertainty. This paper introduces a general template for algorithms that minimize regret in this setting. The template achieves minimax optimal regret when specified properties hold, giving a route to optimal guarantees rather than a guarantee for every possible implementation.

Its central analytical technique is implicit finite-horizon approximation. The analysis relates the shortest path problem to a counterpart with a finite horizon, without requiring the implemented algorithm to perform that conversion explicitly. This separation allows the proof to benefit from a finite-horizon formulation while keeping the actual learning procedure computationally efficient.

The template yields two algorithms with different cost conditions. The model-free algorithm is minimax optimal when costs are strictly positive; the model-based algorithm retains optimality when some state-action pairs have zero cost. Both permit highly sparse updates, which the authors identify as more computationally efficient than existing algorithms. Both can also be made completely parameter-free, combining regret guarantees with reduced implementation overhead.
summary.tldr: An implicit finite-horizon analysis yields efficient stochastic shortest path algorithms with optimal regret under their respective cost conditions.

title: Implicit Finite-Horizon Approximation and Efficient Optimal Algorithms for Stochastic Shortest Path

abstract: We consider online sequential decision problems where an agent must balance exploration and exploitation. We derive a set of Bayesian `optimistic' policies which, in the stochastic multi-armed bandit case, includes the Thompson sampling policy. We provide a new analysis showing that any algorithm producing policies in the optimistic set enjoys $\tilde O(\sqrt{AT})$ Bayesian regret for a problem with $A$ actions after $T$ rounds. We extend the regret analysis for optimistic policies to bilinear saddle-point problems which include zero-sum matrix games and constrained bandits as special cases. In this case we show that Thompson sampling can produce policies outside of the optimistic set and suffer linear regret in some instances. Finding a policy inside the optimistic set amounts to solving a convex optimization problem and we call the resulting algorithm `variational Bayesian optimistic sampling' (VBOS). The procedure works for any posteriors, \ie, it does not require the posterior to have any special properties, such as log-concavity, unimodality, or smoothness. The variational view of the problem has many useful properties, including the ability to tune the exploration-exploitation tradeoff, add regularization, incorporate constraints, and linearly parameterize the policy.

title: Variational Bayesian Optimistic Sampling

abstract: First-order methods for quadratic optimization such as OSQP are widely used for large-scale machine learning and embedded optimal control, where many related problems must be rapidly solved. These methods face two persistent challenges: manual hyperparameter tuning and convergence time to high-accuracy solutions. To address these, we explore how Reinforcement Learning (RL) can learn a policy to tune parameters to accelerate convergence. In experiments with well-known QP benchmarks we find that our RL policy, RLQP, significantly outperforms state-of-the-art QP solvers by up to 3x. RLQP generalizes surprisingly well to previously unseen problems with varying dimension and structure from different applications, including the QPLIB, Netlib LP and Maros-M{\'e}sz{\'a}ros problems. Code, models, and videos are available at https://berkeleyautomation.github.io/rlqp/.

paragraphs: Quadratic optimization problems appear in large-scale machine learning and embedded control, where many related problems may need solutions quickly. First-order solvers such as OSQP are widely used, but their settings often require manual tuning, and reaching a highly accurate solution can take time. This paper treats parameter selection as something a reinforcement-learning policy can learn.

The resulting policy, RLQP, tunes solver parameters to accelerate convergence. The learned component therefore helps guide an optimization method toward its solution. This connects the two challenges identified by the authors: parameter choices are no longer purely a manual task, and those choices are directed toward reducing the work needed for convergence.

On established quadratic-programming benchmarks, the authors report performance improvements of up to threefold over leading solvers. They also find that RLQP transfers well to previously unseen problems with different dimensions, structures, and application origins, including QPLIB, Netlib LP, and Maros-Mészáros problems. These are empirical findings supporting learned parameter tuning across varied optimization instances; the largest reported improvement is not a uniform guarantee.
summary.tldr: RLQP learns to tune quadratic-optimization solver parameters and reports benchmark improvements of up to threefold, with transfer to unseen problem types.

title: Accelerating Quadratic Optimization with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Self-supervised speech representation learning (speech SSL) has demonstrated the benefit of scale in learning rich representations for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) with limited paired data, such as wav2vec 2.0. We investigate the existence of sparse subnetworks in pre-trained speech SSL models that achieve even better low-resource ASR results. However, directly applying widely adopted pruning methods such as the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) is suboptimal in the computational cost needed. Moreover, we show that the discovered subnetworks yield minimal performance gain compared to the original dense network.We present Prune-Adjust-Re-Prune (PARP), which discovers and finetunes subnetworks for much better performance, while only requiring a single downstream ASR finetuning run. PARP is inspired by our surprising observation that subnetworks pruned for pre-training tasks need merely a slight adjustment to achieve a sizeable performance boost in downstream ASR tasks. Extensive experiments on low-resource ASR verify (1) sparse subnetworks exist in mono-lingual/multi-lingual pre-trained speech SSL, and (2) the computational advantage and performance gain of PARP over baseline pruning methods.In particular, on the 10min Librispeech split without LM decoding, PARP discovers subnetworks from wav2vec 2.0 with an absolute 10.9%/12.6% WER decrease compared to the full model. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of PARP via: cross-lingual pruning without any phone recognition degradation, the discovery of a multi-lingual subnetwork for 10 spoken languages in 1 finetuning run, and its applicability to pre-trained BERT/XLNet for natural language tasks1.

title: PARP: Prune, Adjust and Re-Prune for Self-Supervised Speech Recognition

abstract: Multilingual models are parameter-efficient and especially effective in improving low-resource languages by leveraging crosslingual transfer. Despite recent advance in massive multilingual translation with ever-growing model and data, how to effectively train multilingual models has not been well understood. In this paper, we show that a common situation in multilingual training, data imbalance among languages, poses optimization tension between high resource and low resource languages where the found multilingual solution is often sub-optimal for low resources. We show that common training method which upsamples low resources can not robustly optimize population loss with risks of either underfitting high resource languages or overfitting low resource ones. Drawing on recent findings on the geometry of loss landscape and its effect on generalization, we propose a principled optimization algorithm, Curvature Aware Task Scaling (CATS), which adaptively rescales gradients from different tasks with a meta objective of guiding multilingual training to low-curvature neighborhoods with uniformly low loss for all languages. We ran experiments on common benchmarks (TED, WMT and OPUS-100) with varying degrees of data imbalance. CATS effectively improved multilingual optimization and as a result demonstrated consistent gains on low resources ($+0.8$ to $+2.2$ BLEU) without hurting high resources. In addition, CATS is robust to overparameterization and large batch size training, making it a promising training method for massive multilingual models that truly improve low resource languages.

This paper shows that common upsampling of low-resource languages can lead to either underfitting high-resource languages or overfitting low-resource ones, leaving population-level performance poorly optimized.

summary.tldr: CATS uses loss curvature to adapt language-task gradients, improving low-resource translation without hurting high-resource results in reported experiments.

title: Robust Optimization for Multilingual Translation with Imbalanced Data

abstract: We present a novel approach to unsupervised learning for video object segmentation (VOS). Unlike previous work, our formulation allows to learn dense feature representations directly in a fully convolutional regime. We rely on uniform grid sampling to extract a set of anchors and train our model to disambiguate between them on both inter- and intra-video levels. However, a naive scheme to train such a model results in a degenerate solution. We propose to prevent this with a simple regularisation scheme, accommodating the equivariance property of the segmentation task to similarity transformations. Our training objective admits efficient implementation and exhibits fast training convergence. On established VOS benchmarks, our approach exceeds the segmentation accuracy of previous work despite using significantly less training data and compute power.

However, a naive scheme to train such a model results in a degenerate solution.
