paragraphs: Video object segmentation requires representations that distinguish regions throughout a video. This paper develops an unsupervised way to learn dense features directly through a fully convolutional model. The formulation makes spatially detailed representation learning part of the training process, connecting the learned features to the dense nature of the segmentation task.

The method samples anchors on a uniform grid and trains the model to distinguish them both within individual videos and across different videos. A straightforward version of this objective produces a degenerate solution. The authors address that failure with a regularization scheme based on equivariance to similarity transformations: segmentation behavior should transform consistently when the input undergoes those transformations.

The resulting objective supports an efficient implementation and fast training convergence. On established video object segmentation benchmarks, the method achieves higher segmentation accuracy than previous work while using substantially less training data and computation. These reported results connect the design choices to both output quality and training efficiency. The regularizer is especially consequential because it makes the otherwise degenerate anchor-based training scheme usable.
summary.tldr: Dense anchor-based learning with an equivariance regularizer improves unsupervised video segmentation accuracy while reducing training data and computation in reported benchmarks.

title: Dense Unsupervised Learning for Video Segmentation

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed learning framework, in which the local data never leaves clients’ devices to preserve privacy, and the server trains models on the data via accessing only the gradients of those local data. Without further privacy mechanisms such as differential privacy, this leaves the system vulnerable against an attacker who inverts those gradients to reveal clients’ sensitive data. However, a gradient is often insufficient to reconstruct the user data without any prior knowledge. By exploiting a generative model pretrained on the data distribution, we demonstrate that data privacy can be easily breached. Further, when such prior knowledge is unavailable, we investigate the possibility of learning the prior from a sequence of gradients seen in the process of FL training. We experimentally show that the prior in a form of generative model is learnable from iterative interactions in FL. Our findings demonstrate that additional mechanisms are necessary to prevent privacy leakage in FL.

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps local training data on client devices while allowing a server to learn from gradients computed on those data. This arrangement can still leak private information. The paper studies gradient inversion, where an attacker attempts to reconstruct sensitive inputs from the gradients that clients reveal.

A gradient alone is often insufficient for reconstruction without prior knowledge. The authors show that a generative model pretrained on the relevant data distribution supplies useful prior information and can enable a privacy breach. The contribution highlights how knowledge of the kinds of images users hold can make an otherwise difficult reconstruction problem substantially more revealing.

The paper also investigates the case where such a pretrained prior is unavailable. Experiments show that a generative prior can itself be learned from gradients observed over repeated federated-learning interactions. Consequently, privacy exposure can depend on a sequence of shared updates, not just one isolated gradient. The findings demonstrate why retaining raw data locally does not by itself prevent leakage and motivate additional privacy mechanisms, such as differential privacy.
summary.tldr: Generative image priors enable gradient-based data reconstruction, and experiments show that such priors can also be learned from federated updates.

title: Gradient Inversion with Generative Image Prior

abstract: This paper presents a new efficient black-box attribution method built on Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC). Based on Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHS), HSIC measures the dependence between regions of an input image and the output of a model using the kernel embedding of their distributions. It thus provides explanations enriched by RKHS representation capabilities. HSIC can be estimated very efficiently, significantly reducing the computational cost compared to other black-box attribution methods.Our experiments show that HSIC is up to 8 times faster than the previous best black-box attribution methods while being as faithful.Indeed, we improve or match the state-of-the-art of both black-box and white-box attribution methods for several fidelity metrics on Imagenet with various recent model architectures.Importantly, we show that these advances can be transposed to efficiently and faithfully explain object detection models such as YOLOv4. Finally, we extend the traditional attribution methods by proposing a new kernel enabling an ANOVA-like orthogonal decomposition of importance scores based on HSIC, allowing us to evaluate not only the importance of each image patch but also the importance of their pairwise interactions. Our implementation is available at \url{https://github.com/paulnovello/HSIC-Attribution-Method}.

paragraphs: This paper explains image-model predictions by measuring statistical dependence between input regions and model outputs. Its attribution method uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, or HSIC, with kernel representations of distributions. This provides a way to assign importance to image regions while treating the prediction model as a black box.

The authors emphasize that HSIC can be estimated efficiently. In their experiments, the method is up to eight times faster than previous leading black-box attribution methods while retaining comparable faithfulness. Across several fidelity metrics on ImageNet and multiple recent architectures, it matches or improves on leading black-box and white-box attribution approaches. The method also extends to explaining object detectors such as YOLOv4.

A further contribution is a kernel that separates importance scores into components in an ANOVA-like decomposition. This allows the method to assess both individual image patches and pairwise interactions between patches. The explanation can therefore describe contributions associated with combinations of regions, expanding the information available beyond a collection of separate patch importance scores.
summary.tldr: HSIC-based attribution efficiently explains image predictions and can separate individual patch importance from pairwise interactions.

title: Making Sense of Dependence: Efficient Black-box Explanations Using Dependence Measure

abstract: The ability to detect anomaly has long been recognized as an inherent human ability, yet to date, practical AI solutions to mimic such capability have been lacking. This lack of progress can be attributed to several factors. To begin with, the distribution of ``abnormalities'' is intractable. Anything outside of a given normal population is by definition an anomaly. This explains why a large volume of work in this area has been dedicated to modeling the normal distribution of a given task followed by detecting deviations from it. This direction is however unsatisfying as it would require modeling the normal distribution of every task that comes along, which includes tedious data collection. In this paper, we report our work aiming to handle these issues. To deal with the intractability of abnormal distribution, we leverage Energy Based Model (EBM). EBMs learn to associates low energies to correct values and higher energies to incorrect values. At its core, the EBM employs Langevin Dynamics (LD) in generating these incorrect samples based on an iterative optimization procedure, alleviating the intractable problem of modeling the world of anomalies. Then, in order to avoid training an anomaly detector for every task, we utilize an adaptive sparse coding layer. Our intention is to design a plug and play feature that can be used to quickly update what is normal during inference time. Lastly, to avoid tedious data collection, this mentioned update of the sparse coding layer needs to be achievable with just a few shots. Here, we employ a meta learning scheme that simulates such a few shot setting during training. We support our findings with strong empirical evidence.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection faces two linked problems: abnormalities are difficult to enumerate, and what counts as normal changes between tasks. Learning a separate normal-data distribution for every new task can require substantial data collection and training. This paper develops an approach intended to adapt quickly from only a few examples.

Its energy-based model assigns lower energy to correct values and higher energy to incorrect ones. Langevin dynamics generates incorrect samples through an iterative optimization procedure. This provides a way to train around unfavorable examples without attempting to explicitly model the entire space of possible anomalies.

An adaptive sparse coding layer supplies the mechanism for updating what is normal during inference. The authors train with a meta-learning scheme that simulates adaptation from a few examples, aligning training with the intended deployment behavior. The combination addresses sample generation, rapid adaptation, and limited task-specific data within one approach. The abstract reports strong empirical support for the findings, while framing fast adaptation as the central design objective.
summary.tldr: The method combines energy-based learning, adaptive sparse coding, and meta-learning to support anomaly detection that adapts from a few examples.

title: Few-Shot Fast-Adaptive Anomaly Detection

abstract: The spatial acoustic information of a scene, i.e., how sounds emitted from a particular location in the scene are perceived in another location, is key for immersive scene modeling. Robust representation of scene's acoustics can be formulated through a continuous field formulation along with impulse responses varied by emitter-listener locations. The impulse responses are then used to render sounds perceived by the listener. While such representation is advantageous, parameterization of impulse responses for generic scenes presents itself as a challenge. Indeed, traditional pre-computation methods have only implemented parameterization at discrete probe points and require large storage, while other existing methods such as geometry-based sound simulations still suffer from inability to simulate all wave-based sound effects. In this work, we introduce a novel neural network for light-weight Implicit Neural Representation for Audio Scenes (INRAS), which can render a high fidelity time-domain impulse responses at any arbitrary emitter-listener positions by learning a continuous implicit function. INRAS disentangles scene’s geometry features with three modules to generate independent features for the emitter, the geometry of the scene, and the listener respectively. These lead to an efficient reuse of scene-dependent features and support effective multi-condition training for multiple scenes. Our experimental results show that INRAS outperforms existing approaches for representation and rendering of sounds for varying emitter-listener locations in all aspects, including the impulse response quality, inference speed, and storage requirements.

paragraphs: A scene’s acoustics determine how sound changes between its source and a listener. This relationship can be represented by an impulse response for each pair of positions, which is then used to render the heard sound. Storing responses at discrete probe points can require substantial space, while geometry-based simulation can miss some wave effects.

INRAS represents these responses with a continuous neural function. Given emitter and listener positions, it produces a time-domain impulse response, allowing evaluation at arbitrary positions. The network separates its representation into features for the emitter, scene geometry, and listener. This organization allows scene-dependent features to be reused and supports training across multiple scenes and conditions.

The experiments compare representation and sound rendering as emitter and listener locations vary. The authors report improvements over existing approaches in impulse-response quality, inference speed, and storage requirements. The method’s significance is that a compact learned representation can connect continuous spatial queries to usable acoustic responses, with the reported results supporting both rendering quality and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: INRAS learns a compact continuous acoustic field that renders impulse responses for arbitrary emitter and listener positions.

title: INRAS: Implicit Neural Representation for Audio Scenes

abstract: Due to the widespread use of complex machine learning models in real-world applications, it is becoming critical to explain model predictions. However, these models are typically black-box deep neural networks, explained post-hoc via methods with known faithfulness limitations. Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) are an inherently interpretable class of models that address this limitation by learning a non-linear shape function for each feature separately, followed by a linear model on top. However, these models are typically difficult to train, require numerous parameters, and are difficult to scale. We propose an entirely new subfamily of GAMs that utilizes basis decomposition of shape functions. A small number of basis functions are shared among all features, and are learned jointly for a given task, thus making our model scale much better to large-scale data with high-dimensional features, especially when features are sparse. We propose an architecture denoted as the Neural Basis Model (NBM) which uses a single neural network to learn these bases. On a variety of tabular and image datasets, we demonstrate that for interpretable machine learning, NBMs are the state-of-the-art in accuracy, model size, and, throughput and can easily model all higher-order feature interactions. Source code is available at \href{https://github.com/facebookresearch/nbm-spam}{\ttfamily github.com/facebookresearch/nbm-spam}.

This structure supports interpretation directly through the model, avoiding reliance on post-hoc explanations of a black box. However, learning many separate feature functions can require numerous parameters and become difficult to scale.

Neural Basis Models represent these feature functions using a small collection of shared basis functions. A single neural network learns the bases jointly for the task, and the feature-specific functions are built from that common collection. Sharing these components reduces the need to learn each function independently and improves scaling to high-dimensional data, especially when features are sparse.

The authors evaluate the approach on tabular and image datasets and report leading accuracy, model size, and throughput among interpretable methods. They also state that the model can represent higher-order feature interactions. The main contribution is a reusable functional representation within an interpretable modeling family: common learned components provide flexibility while addressing the parameter and computation costs of separate feature functions.
summary.tldr: Neural Basis Models share learned basis functions across features to make interpretable models more accurate and scalable.

title: Neural Basis Models for Interpretability

abstract: Zero-sum stochastic games have found important applications in a variety of fields, from machine learning to economics. Work on this model has primarily focused on the computation of Nash equilibrium due to its effectiveness in solving adversarial board and video games. Unfortunately, a Nash equilibrium is not guaranteed to exist in zero-sum stochastic games when the payoffs at each state are not convex-concave in the players' actions. A Stackelberg equilibrium, however, is guaranteed to exist. Consequently, in this paper, we study zero-sum stochastic Stackelberg games. Going beyond known existence results for (non-stationary) Stackelberg equilibria, we prove the existence of recursive (i.e., Markov perfect) Stackelberg equilibria (recSE) in these games, provide necessary and sufficient conditions for a policy profile to be a recSE, and show that recSE can be computed in (weakly) polynomial time via value iteration. Finally, we show that zero-sum stochastic Stackelberg games can model the problem of pricing and allocating goods across agents and time. More specifically, we propose a zero-sum stochastic Stackelberg game whose recSE correspond to the recursive competitive equilibria of a large class of stochastic Fisher markets. We close with a series of experiments that showcase how our methodology can be used to solve the consumption-savings problem in stochastic Fisher markets.

abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/chenyd7/PEFD.

paragraphs: Feature distillation trains a student network using internal representations from a teacher. This paper investigates the projector that connects their features, a component whose role extends beyond matching feature dimensions. The authors observe that a projector can benefit the student even when teacher and student representations already have the same size.

Their explanation treats direct feature distillation as two simultaneous tasks: learning features useful for classification and matching the teacher's feature distribution. They hypothesize, and provide empirical support, that direct matching can make the student overfit the teacher's representations despite differences in architecture and initialization. That can degrade the features the student ultimately uses for classification.

A projector separates these demands, allowing the student's backbone to focus more on discriminative feature extraction while receiving teacher guidance through the projection. Motivated by that effect, the authors propose using an ensemble of projectors to further improve student features. Experiments across multiple datasets and teacher-student pairs support the method's effectiveness, alongside the proposed explanation for why projectors help.
summary.tldr: An ensemble of feature projectors improves distillation by helping separate teacher-feature matching from the student's classification feature learning.

title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble

abstract: Animal pose estimation and tracking (APT) is a fundamental task for detecting and tracking animal keypoints from a sequence of video frames. Previous animal-related datasets focus either on animal tracking or single-frame animal pose estimation, and never on both aspects. The lack of APT datasets hinders the development and evaluation of video-based animal pose estimation and tracking methods, limiting the applications in real world, e.g., understanding animal behavior in wildlife conservation. To fill this gap, we make the first step and propose APT-36K, i.e., the first large-scale benchmark for animal pose estimation and tracking. Specifically, APT-36K consists of 2,400 video clips collected and filtered from 30 animal species with 15 frames for each video, resulting in 36,000 frames in total. After manual annotation and careful double-check, high-quality keypoint and tracking annotations are provided for all the animal instances. Based on APT-36K, we benchmark several representative models on the following three tracks: (1) supervised animal pose estimation on a single frame under intra- and inter-domain transfer learning settings, (2) inter-species domain generalization test for unseen animals, and (3) animal pose estimation with animal tracking. Based on the experimental results, we gain some empirical insights and show that APT-36K provides a useful animal pose estimation and tracking benchmark, offering new challenges and opportunities for future research. The code and dataset will be made publicly available at https://github.com/pandorgan/APT-36K.

paragraphs: Understanding animal movement in video requires both locating body keypoints and tracking animals across frames. The paper identifies a dataset gap: earlier animal datasets focused on tracking or pose estimation in individual images, without supporting both together. APT-36K supplies a benchmark designed to evaluate these connected parts of video-based animal analysis.

The dataset contains 2,400 video clips covering 30 animal species. Each clip contributes 15 frames, producing 36,000 frames overall. All animal instances receive manually created keypoint and tracking annotations, which are double-checked. This provides linked information about body configuration and animal identity across the selected video frames.

The authors benchmark representative models in three settings: single-frame pose estimation with transfer learning, generalization to unseen animal species, and pose estimation combined with tracking. These settings distinguish learning within familiar conditions from transferring knowledge to different domains or animals. The experiments support the dataset’s usefulness as a research benchmark and expose challenges for future methods. Its contribution is shared evaluation infrastructure for capabilities relevant to applications such as understanding animal behavior in wildlife conservation.
summary.tldr: APT-36K provides 36,000 annotated video frames for jointly studying animal pose estimation, tracking, and transfer across species.

title: APT-36K: A Large-scale Benchmark for Animal Pose Estimation and Tracking

abstract: Software packages like TensorFlow and PyTorch are designed to support linear algebra operations, and their speed and usability determine their success. However, by prioritising speed, they often neglect memory requirements. As a consequence, the implementations of memory-intensive algorithms that are convenient in terms of software design can often not be run for large problems due to memory overflows. Memory-efficient solutions require complex programming approaches with significant logic outside the computational framework. This impairs the adoption and use of such algorithms. To address this, we developed an XLA compiler extension that adjusts the computational data-flow representation of an algorithm according to a user-specified memory limit. We show that k-nearest neighbour, sparse Gaussian process regression methods and Transformers can be run on a single device at a much larger scale, where standard implementations would have failed. Our approach leads to better use of hardware resources. We believe that further focus on removing memory constraints at a compiler level will widen the range of machine learning methods that can be developed in the future.

paragraphs: Convenient implementations of machine-learning algorithms can consume too much memory to run on large problems. Making them fit often requires complicated programming outside the main computational framework. This paper addresses that burden at the compiler level, aiming to make memory-intensive methods usable without requiring developers to manage all memory-saving logic themselves.

The authors extend the XLA compiler so that it adjusts an algorithm's computational data-flow representation according to a memory limit supplied by the user. This places the memory constraint inside the process that transforms the computation for execution. The approach connects an explicit resource budget to how the algorithm's computation is organized.

The paper demonstrates larger single-device computations for k-nearest neighbors, sparse Gaussian process regression, and Transformers in cases where standard implementations fail. These examples support improved use of available hardware resources across several kinds of methods. The authors further suggest that compiler-level work on memory constraints could expand the range of machine-learning algorithms that researchers can develop and use.
summary.tldr: An XLA compiler extension reorganizes computations around a user-specified memory limit, enabling larger single-device workloads.

title: Memory safe computations with XLA compiler

abstract: Test-time training adapts to a new test distribution on the fly by optimizing a model for each test input using self-supervision.In this paper, we use masked autoencoders for this one-sample learning problem.Empirically, our simple method improves generalization on many visual benchmarks for distribution shifts.Theoretically, we characterize this improvement in terms of the bias-variance trade-off.
originalAbstract: Test-time training adapts to a new test distribution on the fly by optimizing a model for each test input using self-supervision.In this paper, we use masked autoencoders for this one-sample learning problem.Empirically, our simple method improves generalization on many visual benchmarks for distribution shifts.Theoretically, we characterize this improvement in terms of the bias-variance trade-off.

paragraphs: A model can encounter test images from a distribution different from the one it learned during training. This paper studies test-time training, which adapts the model as each new input arrives. The adaptation uses self-supervision on that input, making the problem one of learning from a single test example.

The authors use masked autoencoders as the mechanism for this one-sample learning. The central choice is to make the incoming image itself provide a learning signal during prediction-time adaptation. This connects the model's adjustment to the particular example it must handle, rather than relying entirely on what was learned before encountering the changed distribution.

Experiments show improved generalization across many visual benchmarks involving distribution shifts. The paper also characterizes the improvement theoretically through the bias-variance trade-off, linking the observed benefit to a statistical account of adaptation. Together, the contributions present a simple self-supervised method and an explanation of its gains; the empirical claim concerns the evaluated visual shift benchmarks.
summary.tldr: Masked autoencoders enable self-supervised adaptation to individual test images, improving reported robustness to visual distribution shifts.

title: Test-Time Training with Masked Autoencoders

abstract: We propose \textbf{JAWS}, a series of wrapper methods for distribution-free uncertainty quantification tasks under covariate shift, centered on the core method \textbf{JAW}, the \textbf{JA}ckknife+ \textbf{W}eighted with data-dependent likelihood-ratio weights. JAWS also includes computationally efficient \textbf{A}pproximations of JAW using higher-order influence functions: \textbf{JAWA}. Theoretically, we show that JAW relaxes the jackknife+'s assumption of data exchangeability to achieve the same finite-sample coverage guarantee even under covariate shift. JAWA further approaches the JAW guarantee in the limit of the sample size or the influence function order under common regularity assumptions. Moreover, we propose a general approach to repurposing predictive interval-generating methods and their guarantees to the reverse task: estimating the probability that a prediction is erroneous, based on user-specified error criteria such as a safe or acceptable tolerance threshold around the true label. We then propose \textbf{JAW-E} and \textbf{JAWA-E} as the repurposed proposed methods for this \textbf{E}rror assessment task. Practically, JAWS outperform state-of-the-art predictive inference baselines in a variety of biased real world data sets for interval-generation and error-assessment predictive uncertainty auditing tasks.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals are useful only if their reliability survives the conditions under which predictions are made. JAWS addresses uncertainty quantification under covariate shift, where the input distribution changes. Its core method, JAW, modifies jackknife+ using data-dependent likelihood-ratio weights to account for that shift.

The authors prove that JAW retains the same finite-sample coverage guarantee while relaxing jackknife+'s exchangeability assumption to accommodate covariate shift. They also introduce JAWA, computationally efficient approximations based on higher-order influence functions. Under common regularity assumptions, these approximations approach JAW's guarantee as sample size or influence-function order increases. The finite-sample result for JAW and the limiting result for JAWA are distinct guarantees.

The paper additionally reverses the usual interval-generation task: given a user-defined error tolerance, it estimates the probability that a prediction is erroneous. JAW-E and JAWA-E apply the proposed methods to this assessment. Experiments on biased real-world datasets show improvements over predictive-inference baselines for both interval generation and error assessment, connecting uncertainty guarantees to practical auditing questions.
summary.tldr: JAWS adapts jackknife-based uncertainty auditing to covariate shift, with coverage guarantees and methods for assessing prediction-error probabilities.

title: JAWS: Auditing Predictive Uncertainty Under Covariate Shift

abstract: Despite extensive studies, the underlying reason as to why overparameterizedneural networks can generalize remains elusive. Existing theory shows that common stochastic optimizers prefer flatter minimizers of the training loss, and thusa natural potential explanation is that flatness implies generalization. This workcritically examines this explanation. Through theoretical and empirical investigation, we identify the following three scenarios for two-layer ReLU networks: (1)flatness provably implies generalization; (2) there exist non-generalizing flattestmodels and sharpness minimization algorithms fail to generalize poorly, and (3)perhaps most strikingly, there exist non-generalizing flattest models, but sharpnessminimization algorithms still generalize. Our results suggest that the relationshipbetween sharpness and generalization subtly depends on the data distributionsand the model architectures and sharpness minimization algorithms do not onlyminimize sharpness to achieve better generalization. This calls for the search forother explanations for the generalization of over-parameterized neural networks

paragraphs: One proposed explanation for neural network generalization is that training favors flat regions of the loss landscape. In such regions, changing parameters has relatively little effect on training loss. This paper examines whether flatness adequately explains why sharpness-minimizing algorithms produce models that work beyond their training data.

Through theory and experiments on two-layer ReLU networks, the authors identify several relationships between flatness and generalization. They establish a setting where flatness provably implies generalization. They also find settings containing flattest models that do not generalize, showing that the quality of a flat solution depends on the surrounding problem rather than flatness alone.

The especially revealing case is one where non-generalizing flattest models exist, yet sharpness-minimization algorithms still generalize. Their success therefore cannot be fully explained by selecting the flattest available models. The results suggest that data distributions and model architecture affect the relationship, and that these algorithms have additional behavior relevant to generalization. Understanding that behavior requires explanations beyond the sharpness value of the final solution.
summary.tldr: Sharpness-minimizing algorithms can generalize even when the flattest models do not, indicating that flatness alone is an incomplete explanation.

title: Sharpness Minimization Algorithms Do Not Only Minimize Sharpness To Achieve Better Generalization

abstract: Computerized adaptive testing (CAT), as a tool that can efficiently measure student's ability, has been widely used in various standardized tests (e.g., GMAT and GRE). The adaptivity of CAT refers to the selection of the most informative questions for each student, reducing test length. Existing CAT methods do not explicitly target ability estimation accuracy since there is no student's true ability as ground truth; therefore, these methods cannot be guaranteed to make the estimate converge to the true with such limited responses. In this paper, we analyze the statistical properties of estimation and find a theoretical approximation of the true ability: the ability estimated by full responses to question bank. Based on this, a Bounded Ability Estimation framework for CAT (BECAT) is proposed in a data-summary manner, which selects a question subset that closely matches the gradient of the full responses. Thus, we develop an expected gradient difference approximation to design a simple greedy selection algorithm, and show the rigorous theoretical and error upper-bound guarantees of its ability estimate. Experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets, show that it can reach the same estimation accuracy using 15\% less questions on average, significantly reducing test length.

paragraphs: Adaptive tests aim to estimate a student's ability using a carefully chosen sequence of questions. The difficulty is deciding whether a short test produces an accurate estimate when true ability is not directly observable. This paper addresses that problem by analyzing the estimate that would be obtained from responses to the entire question bank as a theoretical approximation of true ability.

The proposed BECAT framework selects a smaller collection of questions whose estimation gradient closely matches that of the full responses. In plain terms, the selected questions should push the ability estimate in much the same direction as the complete bank would. An approximation to the expected gradient difference makes this idea usable through a simple greedy selection algorithm.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees, including an upper bound on estimation error. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets reach the same estimation accuracy with 15% fewer questions on average. This links shorter tests to an explicit accuracy objective, while retaining the distinction between true ability and its full-response approximation.
summary.tldr: BECAT selects questions to approximate full-bank ability estimation, achieving the same accuracy with 15% fewer questions on average in experiments.

title: A Bounded Ability Estimation for Computerized Adaptive Testing

abstract: The rise of datathons, also known as data or data science hackathons, has provided a platform to collaborate, learn, and innovate quickly. Despite their significant potential benefits, organizations often struggle to effectively work with data due to a lack of clear guidelines and best practices for potential issues that might arise. Drawing on our own experiences and insights from organizing +80 datathon challenges with +60 partnership organizations since 2016, we provide a guide that serves as a resource for organizers to navigate the data-related complexities of datathons. We apply our proposed framework to 10 case studies.

paragraphs: Datathons bring people together to collaborate, learn, and develop ideas quickly using data. Their potential depends partly on how well organizers handle the data involved. This paper addresses a practical obstacle: organizations often lack clear guidance and established practices for the data-related issues that can arise while arranging these events.

The authors develop an organizer-facing guide from their own experience running more than 80 datathon challenges with more than 60 partner organizations. That experience supplies the basis for a framework intended to help organizers navigate data-related complexity. The contribution is practical guidance grounded in organizing work, with the focus placed on supporting the conditions under which participants can work effectively.

The paper applies the proposed framework to 10 case studies. These applications show how the guidance can be brought to concrete datathon settings. Its value lies in turning accumulated organizing experience into a resource that others can use when handling data challenges, complementing the collaborative and rapid-development aims that make datathons attractive.
summary.tldr: The paper turns extensive datathon-organizing experience into a data-management guide and applies its framework to 10 case studies.

title: How to Data in Datathons

abstract: Constructing a directed cyclic graph (DCG) is challenged by both algorithmic difficulty and computational burden. Comparing multiple DCGs is even more difficult, compounded by the need to identify dynamic causalities across graphs. We propose to unify multiple DCGs with a single structural model and develop a limited-information-based method to simultaneously construct multiple networks and infer their disparities, which can be visualized by appropriate correspondence analysis. The algorithm provides DCGs with robust non-asymptotic theoretical properties. It is designed with two sequential stages, each of which involves parallel computation tasks that are scalable to the network complexity. Taking advantage of high-performance clusters, our method makes it possible to evaluate the statistical significance of DCGs using the bootstrap method. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our method by applying it to synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: A directed cyclic graph represents directed relationships that can form feedback loops. Constructing such a network is computationally and algorithmically challenging, and comparing several networks adds the problem of identifying how causal relationships differ. This paper addresses network construction and comparison through a shared structural model.

The proposed method uses limited information to construct multiple networks simultaneously and infer their disparities. Treating the networks within one model brings estimation and comparison into the same procedure. The resulting differences can be visualized using correspondence analysis, connecting the statistical comparison to a representation that helps expose relationships across networks.

The algorithm has two sequential stages, each containing tasks that can run in parallel as network complexity grows. With high-performance clusters, this organization makes bootstrap evaluation of statistical significance feasible. The authors also establish non-asymptotic theoretical properties, meaning their analysis is not restricted to an infinite-data limit. Applications to synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness for jointly learning and comparing these networks.
summary.tldr: A shared structural model enables joint estimation, statistical comparison, and visualization of multiple directed cyclic causal networks.

title: Analysis of Variance of Multiple Causal Networks

abstract: Training a single model on multiple input domains and/or output tasks allows for compressing information from multiple sources into a unified backbone hence improves model efficiency. It also enables potential positive knowledge transfer across tasks/domains, leading to improved accuracy and data-efficient training. However, optimizing such networks is a challenge, in particular due to discrepancies between the different tasks or domains: Despite several hypotheses and solutions proposed over the years, recent work has shown that uniform scalarization training, i.e., simply minimizing the average of the task losses, yields on-par performance with more costly SotA optimization methods. This raises the issue of how well we understand the training dynamics of multi-task and multi-domain networks. In this work, we first devise a large-scale unified analysis of multi-domain and multi-task learning to better understand the dynamics of scalarization across varied task/domain combinations and model sizes. Following these insights, we then propose to leverage population-based training to efficiently search for the optimal scalarization weights when dealing with a large number of tasks or domains.

It also enables potential positive knowledge transfer across tasks/domains, leading to improved accuracy and data-efficient training. However, optimizing such networks is a challenge, in particular due to discrepancies between the different tasks or domains: Despite several hypotheses and solutions proposed over the years, recent work has shown that uniform scalarization training, i.e., simply minimizing the average of the task losses, yields on-par performance with more costly SotA optimization methods. In this work, we first devise a large-scale unified analysis of multi-domain and multi-task learning to better understand the dynamics of scalarization across varied task/domain combinations and model sizes. Following these insights, we then propose to leverage population-based training to efficiently search for the optimal scalarization weights when dealing with a large number of tasks or domains.

paragraphs: A shared model can serve multiple tasks or domains, improving efficiency and potentially allowing knowledge transfer. Training becomes difficult when those tasks or domains impose different demands. This paper examines scalarization, which combines their losses into one objective, with particular attention to how the weighting of those losses affects training.

The motivation comes from earlier findings that simply averaging task losses can match more expensive state-of-the-art optimization methods. That observation raises questions about which aspects of joint training actually need more sophisticated treatment. The authors conduct a large-scale, unified analysis spanning both multi-task and multi-domain learning, varied task and domain combinations, and different model sizes.

Building on that analysis, they propose population-based training to search efficiently for scalarization weights when many tasks or domains are involved. The approach makes the relative importance of each loss a central optimization choice. The paper’s stated contribution is the broad analysis and resulting weight-search proposal; the abstract does not claim a universal advantage for a particular set of weights or a single training method.
summary.tldr: A large-scale study of joint training motivates population-based search for loss weights across many tasks or domains.

title: Scalarization for Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Learning at Scale

abstract: Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) play an essential role in summarising, synthesising and validating scientific evidence. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in using machine learning techniques to automate the identification of relevant studies for SLRs. However, the lack of standardised evaluation datasets makes comparing the performance of such automated literature screening systems difficult. In this paper, we analyse the citation screening evaluation datasets, revealing that many of the available datasets are either too small, suffer from data leakage or have limited applicability to systems treating automated literature screening as a classification task, as opposed to, for example, a retrieval or question-answering task. To address these challenges, we introduce CSMED, a meta-dataset consolidating nine publicly released collections, providing unified access to 325 SLRs from the fields of medicine and computer science. CSMED serves as a comprehensive resource for training and evaluating the performance of automated citation screening models. Additionally, we introduce CSMED-FT, a new dataset designed explicitly for evaluating the full text publication screening task. To demonstrate the utility of CSMED, we conduct experiments and establish baselines on new datasets.

Machine learning can help automate this screening, but evaluating competing systems requires suitable shared datasets. The paper examines existing evaluation resources and finds problems with small size, data leakage, and applicability across different ways of formulating the screening task.

title: CSMeD: Bridging the Dataset Gap in Automated Citation Screening for Systematic Literature Reviews

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an effective machine learning paradigm where multiple clients can train models based on heterogeneous data in a decentralized manner without accessing their private data. However, existing FL systems undergo performance deterioration due to feature-level test-time shifts, which are well investigated in centralized settings but rarely studied in FL. The common non-IID issue in FL usually refers to inter-client heterogeneity during training phase, while the test-time shift refers to the intra-client heterogeneity during test phase. Although the former is always deemed to be notorious for FL, there is still a wealth of useful information delivered by heterogeneous data sources, which may potentially help alleviate the latter issue. To explore the possibility of using inter-client heterogeneity in handling intra-client heterogeneity, we firstly propose a contrastive learning-based FL framework, namely FedICON, to capture invariant knowledge among heterogeneous clients and consistently tune the model to adapt to test data. In FedICON, each client performs sample-wise supervised contrastive learning during the local training phase, which enhances sample-wise invariance encoding ability. Through global aggregation, the invariance extraction ability can be mutually boosted among inter-client heterogeneity. During the test phase, our test-time adaptation procedure leverages unsupervised contrastive learning to guide the model to smoothly generalize to test data under intra-client heterogeneity. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed FedICON in taming heterogeneity to handle test-time shift problems.

paragraphs: Federated learning must contend with differences between clients' training data, but it also faces changes within a client's data at test time. This paper distinguishes those two problems and asks whether the first can help address the second. Diverse training clients may contain useful information for learning features that remain stable when test inputs change.

The proposed FedICON framework uses supervised contrastive learning during each client's local training. This encourages sample-level representations that capture invariant information. Global aggregation then combines learning across heterogeneous clients, aiming to strengthen that capability through their varied data. Client differences become a source of information for learning invariance.

At test time, an unsupervised contrastive-learning procedure adapts the model to incoming data. This connects the invariance learned during federated training to the distribution encountered by an individual client. The authors report extensive experiments supporting FedICON's effectiveness against feature-level test-time shifts. The evidence supports using inter-client diversity constructively within a framework that also performs explicit test-time adaptation.
summary.tldr: FedICON uses contrastive learning across heterogeneous clients and at test time to improve adaptation to feature-level distribution shifts.

title: Is Heterogeneity Notorious? Taming Heterogeneity to Handle Test-Time Shift in Federated Learning

abstract: Recently, growing interest has been aroused in extending the multimodal capability of large language models (LLMs), e.g., vision-language (VL) learning, which is regarded as the next milestone of artificial general intelligence. However, existing solutions are prohibitively expensive, which not only need to optimize excessive parameters, but also require another large-scale pre-training before VL instruction tuning. In this paper, we propose a novel and affordable solution for the effective VL adaption of LLMs, called Mixture-of-Modality Adaptation (MMA). Instead of using large neural networks to connect the image encoder and LLM, MMA adopts lightweight modules, i.e., adapters, to bridge the gap between LLMs and VL tasks, which also enables the joint optimization of the image and language models. Meanwhile, MMA is also equipped with a routing algorithm to help LLMs achieve an automatic shift between single- and multi-modal instructions without compromising their ability of natural language understanding. To validate MMA, we apply it to a recent LLM called LLaMA and term this formed large vision-language instructed model as LaVIN. To validate MMA and LaVIN, we conduct extensive experiments under two setups, namely multimodal science question answering and multimodal dialogue. The experimental results not only demonstrate the competitive performance and the superior training efficiency of LaVIN than existing multimodal LLMs, but also confirm its great potential as a general-purpose chatbot. More importantly, the actual expenditure of LaVIN is extremely cheap, e.g., only 1.4 training hours with 3.8M trainable parameters, greatly confirming the effectiveness of MMA. Our code is anonymously released at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LaVIN--1067.

paragraphs: Adding image understanding to a language model can require training many parameters and performing another large pre-training stage before instruction tuning. This paper proposes Mixture-of-Modality Adaptation, or MMA, as an affordable way to adapt language models to tasks involving both images and text.

MMA uses lightweight adapters to connect image and language processing, enabling joint optimization of the image and language models. It also includes a routing algorithm that switches between text-only and multimodal instructions while preserving natural-language understanding. Applied to LLaMA, this approach produces the vision-language instruction model LaVIN.

The authors evaluate LaVIN on multimodal science question answering and dialogue. They report competitive performance alongside better training efficiency than existing multimodal language models, with a reported training run taking 1.4 hours and updating 3.8 million parameters. The findings support lightweight adaptation as a practical route to multimodal instruction following, while the dialogue experiments indicate potential for a general-purpose chatbot. The efficiency result makes the adaptation mechanism a central contribution alongside the model’s task performance.
summary.tldr: MMA equips LLaMA with vision-language instruction following through lightweight adapters and modality routing, yielding competitive results with efficient training.

title: Cheap and Quick: Efficient Vision-Language Instruction Tuning for Large Language Models

abstract: We investigate replicable learning algorithms. Informally a learning algorithm is replicable if the algorithm outputs the same canonical hypothesis over multiple runs with high probability, even when different runs observe a different set of samples from the unknown data distribution. In general, such a strong notion of replicability is not achievable. Thus we consider two feasible notions of replicability called {\em list replicability} and {\em certificate replicability}. Intuitively, these notions capture the degree of (non) replicability. The goal is to design learning algorithms with optimal list and certificate complexities while minimizing the sample complexity. Our contributions are the following.1. We first study the learning task of estimating the biases of $d$ coins, up to an additive error of $\varepsilon$, by observing samples. For this task, we design a $(d+1)$-list replicable algorithm. To complement this result, we establish that the list complexity is optimal, i.e there are no learning algorithms with a list size smaller than $d+1$ for this task. We also design learning algorithms with certificate complexity $\tilde{O}(\log d)$. The sample complexity of both these algorithms is $\tilde{O}(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2})$ where $\varepsilon$ is the approximation error parameter (for a constant error probability). 2. In the PAC model, we show that any hypothesis class that is learnable with $d$-nonadaptive statistical queries can be learned via a $(d+1)$-list replicable algorithm and also via a $\tilde{O}(\log d)$-certificate replicable algorithm. The sample complexity of both these algorithms is $\tilde{O}(\frac{d^2}{\nu^2})$ where $\nu$ is the approximation error of the statistical query. We also show that for the concept class \dtep, the list complexity is exactly $d+1$ with respect to the uniform distribution. To establish our upper bound results we use rounding schemes induced by geometric partitions with certain properties. We use Sperner/KKM Lemma to establish the lower bound results.

paragraphs: Replicable learning asks whether repeated runs can produce the same canonical hypothesis despite receiving different samples from the same unknown distribution. Because this strong requirement is not generally achievable, the paper studies two relaxed notions: list replicability and certificate replicability. Their associated complexities quantify the degree of replicability while sample complexity measures the data needed.

For estimating the biases of d coins to additive error epsilon, the authors construct a list-replicable algorithm with list size d+1 and prove that no smaller list is possible. They also obtain certificate complexity of order log d, up to logarithmic factors. Both constructions use sample complexity of order d squared divided by epsilon squared, again up to logarithmic factors, for constant error probability.

The results extend to PAC learning for classes learnable with d nonadaptive statistical queries, with analogous list and certificate guarantees and dependence on query accuracy. The proofs use geometric partitions to construct rounding schemes and topological lemmas to establish lower bounds, linking achievable replicability to both algorithm design and impossibility results.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes achievable and optimal replicability complexities for coin-bias estimation and extends its constructions to statistical-query learning.

title: List and Certificate Complexities in Replicable Learning

abstract: In this paper, we propose an online convex optimization approach with two different levels of adaptivity. On a higher level, our approach is agnostic to the unknown types and curvatures of the online functions, while at a lower level, it can exploit the unknown niceness of the environments and attain problem-dependent guarantees. Specifically, we obtain $\mathcal{O}(\log V_T)$, $\mathcal{O}(d \log V_T)$ and $\hat{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{V_T})$ regret bounds for strongly convex, exp-concave and convex loss functions, respectively, where $d$ is the dimension, $V_T$ denotes problem-dependent gradient variations and the $\hat{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot)$-notation omits $\log V_T$ factors. Our result not only safeguards the worst-case guarantees but also directly implies the small-loss bounds in analysis. Moreover, when applied to adversarial/stochastic convex optimization and game theory problems, our result enhances the existing universal guarantees. Our approach is based on a multi-layer online ensemble framework incorporating novel ingredients, including a carefully designed optimism for unifying diverse function types and cascaded corrections for algorithmic stability. Notably, despite its multi-layer structure, our algorithm necessitates only one gradient query per round, making it favorable when the gradient evaluation is time-consuming. This is facilitated by a novel regret decomposition equipped with carefully designed surrogate losses.

paragraphs: Online optimization makes decisions as losses arrive, often without knowing their curvature or how predictable the environment will be. This paper develops a method that adapts to both uncertainties. It handles different convex function classes while using favorable gradient variation to obtain guarantees that depend on the problem's behavior.

The regret bounds scale logarithmically with gradient variation for strongly convex losses, with dimension times that logarithm for exp-concave losses, and with its square root up to logarithmic factors for general convex losses. Regret measures accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparator. The results preserve worst-case guarantees, imply small-loss bounds, and improve stated universal guarantees in optimization and game-theoretic applications.

The method uses a multi-layer online ensemble, with optimism to accommodate different function types and cascaded corrections to maintain stability. Despite this layered construction, it requires only one gradient query per round, supported by a new regret decomposition and surrogate losses. This matters when evaluating gradients is expensive: the ensemble's adaptivity does not require multiple gradient queries at each decision.
summary.tldr: A multi-layer online ensemble adapts to unknown loss curvature and gradient variation while requiring only one gradient query per round.

title: Universal Online Learning with Gradient Variations: A Multi-layer Online Ensemble Approach

abstract: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces (iBCIs) have shown promise for restoring rapid communication to people with neurological disorders such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, to maintain high performance over time, iBCIs typically need frequent recalibration to combat changes in the neural recordings that accrue over days. This requires iBCI users to stop using the iBCI and engage in supervised data collection, making the iBCI system hard to use. In this paper, we propose a method that enables self-recalibration of communication iBCIs without interrupting the user. Our method leverages large language models (LMs) to automatically correct errors in iBCI outputs. The self-recalibration process uses these corrected outputs ("pseudo-labels") to continually update the iBCI decoder online. Over a period of more than one year (403 days), we evaluated our Continual Online Recalibration with Pseudo-labels (CORP) framework with one clinical trial participant. CORP achieved a stable decoding accuracy of 93.84% in an online handwriting iBCI task, significantly outperforming other baseline methods. Notably, this is the longest-running iBCI stability demonstration involving a human participant. Our results provide the first evidence for long-term stabilization of a plug-and-play, high-performance communication iBCI, addressing a major barrier for the clinical translation of iBCIs.

This paper develops a way to update the decoder during use, addressing the practical burden of those repeated calibration sessions.

It maintains 93.84% decoding accuracy and significantly outperforms the compared baselines. The paper presents this as the longest-running human iBCI stability demonstration and initial evidence for long-term plug-and-play communication. The single-participant scope matters when interpreting the result: it establishes sustained performance in this demonstrated use case.
summary.tldr: CORP uses language-model-corrected outputs to recalibrate a brain-to-text interface during use, maintaining 93.84% accuracy over 403 days in one participant.

title: Plug-and-Play Stability for Intracortical Brain-Computer Interfaces: A One-Year Demonstration of Seamless Brain-to-Text Communication

abstract: Modern language models have the capacity to store and use immense amounts of knowledge about real-world entities, but it remains unclear how to update such knowledge stored in model parameters. While prior methods for updating knowledge in LMs successfully inject atomic facts, updated LMs fail to make inferences based on injected facts. In this work, we demonstrate that a context distillation-based approach can both impart knowledge about entities \emph{and} propagate that knowledge to enable broader inferences. Our approach consists of two stages: transfer set generation and distillation on the transfer set. We first generate a transfer set by prompting a language model to generate continuations from the entity definition. Then, we update the model parameters so that the distribution of the LM (the 'student') matches the distribution of the LM conditioned on the definition (the 'teacher') on the transfer set. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach is more effective at propagating knowledge updates than fine-tuning and other gradient-based knowledge-editing methods. Moreover, it does not compromise performance in other contexts, even when injecting the definitions of up to 150 entities at once.

paragraphs: Updating a language model with a fact is only part of making that knowledge useful. The model must also draw inferences that depend on the update. This paper addresses the gap between successfully inserting information about an entity and having that information influence the model’s broader responses.

The method has two stages. First, the authors prompt a language model with an entity definition and generate continuations to form a transfer set. Second, they update a student model so that its output distribution on that set matches a teacher distribution conditioned on the definition. This distills the behavior supported by the supplied definition into the model’s parameters.

Experiments find that the approach propagates updates more effectively than fine-tuning and other gradient-based knowledge-editing methods. The authors also report preserved performance in other contexts when injecting definitions for as many as 150 entities at once. The result supports using definition-conditioned behavior as a training signal for broader inference, extending the effect of an update beyond reproducing the inserted information.
summary.tldr: Context distillation helps language models use newly injected entity knowledge in broader inferences while preserving other-context performance in the reported experiments.

title: Propagating Knowledge Updates to LMs Through Distillation

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are crucial for machine learning applications with graph-structured data, but their success depends on sufficient labeled data. We present a novel active learning (AL) method for GNNs, extending the Expected Model Change Maximization (EMCM) principle to improve prediction performance on unlabeled data. By presenting a Bayesian interpretation for the node embeddings generated by GNNs under the semi-supervised setting, we efficiently compute the closed-form EMCM acquisition function as the selection criterion for AL without re-training. Our method establishes a direct connection with expected prediction error minimization, offering theoretical guarantees for AL performance. Experiments demonstrate our method's effectiveness compared to existing approaches, in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

We present a novel active learning (AL) method for GNNs, extending the Expected Model Change Maximization (EMCM) principle to improve prediction performance on unlabeled data. By presenting a Bayesian interpretation for the node embeddings generated by GNNs under the semi-supervised setting, we efficiently compute the closed-form EMCM acquisition function as the selection criterion for AL without re-training. Our method establishes a direct connection with expected prediction error minimization, offering theoretical guarantees for AL performance. paragraphs: Graph neural networks need enough labeled data to make useful predictions, but labeling every node can be impractical. This paper proposes an active learning method for choosing which nodes should be labeled next. Its selection principle is Expected Model Change Maximization: prioritize candidates according to how much they are expected to change the model.

The authors give a Bayesian interpretation of the node embeddings produced by a graph neural network in a semi-supervised setting. This interpretation allows the selection score, called an acquisition function, to be computed efficiently in closed form without retraining. That matters because evaluating possible label requests should not itself require repeatedly fitting the model.

The method also establishes a direct connection between expected model change and minimizing expected prediction error, supplying theoretical support for the selection strategy. Experiments show improvements over existing approaches in both accuracy and efficiency. The contribution therefore combines a principled reason for selecting informative labels with a computationally manageable way to score candidates on graph-structured data.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian interpretation of graph embeddings enables efficient active learning scores based on expected model change, with theoretical and empirical support.

title: No Change, No Gain: Empowering Graph Neural Networks with Expected Model Change Maximization for Active Learning

abstract: Backdoor attacks have emerged as a prominent threat to natural language processing (NLP) models, where the presence of specific triggers in the input can lead poisoned models to misclassify these inputs to predetermined target classes. Current detection mechanisms are limited by their inability to address more covert backdoor strategies, such as style-based attacks. In this work, we propose an innovative test-time poisoned sample detection framework that hinges on the interpretability of model predictions, grounded in the semantic meaning of inputs.We contend that triggers (e.g., infrequent words) are not supposed to fundamentally alter the underlying semantic meanings of poisoned samples as they want to stay stealthy. Based on this observation, we hypothesize that while the model's predictions for paraphrased clean samples should remain stable, predictions for poisoned samples should revert to their true labels upon the mutations applied to triggers during the paraphrasing process.We employ ChatGPT, a state-of-the-art large language model, as our paraphraser and formulate the trigger-removal task as a prompt engineering problem. We adopt fuzzing, a technique commonly used for unearthing software vulnerabilities, to discover optimal paraphrase prompts that can effectively eliminate triggers while concurrently maintaining input semantics.Experiments on 4 types of backdoor attacks, including the subtle style backdoors, and 4 distinct datasets demonstrate that our approach surpasses baseline methods, including STRIP, RAP, and ONION, in precision and recall.

paragraphs: Backdoored language models can assign an attacker-selected class when an input contains a trigger, including subtle stylistic cues. ParaFuzz detects potentially poisoned inputs at test time by examining prediction behavior under paraphrasing. Its premise is that a stealthy trigger should not fundamentally change the input's underlying meaning.

The authors hypothesize that meaning-preserving paraphrases should leave clean-input predictions stable, while changing a trigger can make a poisoned-input prediction return to its true label. They use ChatGPT to produce paraphrases and cast trigger removal as a prompt-search problem. Fuzzing guides that search toward prompts that alter triggers while retaining input semantics.

Experiments cover four attack types, including style-based backdoors, and four datasets. ParaFuzz exceeds STRIP, RAP, and ONION in precision and recall in the reported evaluation. The results support the proposed detection strategy across those tested attacks. Its interpretation still rests on the stated hypothesis connecting semantic stability, trigger mutation, and changes in model predictions.
summary.tldr: ParaFuzz searches for meaning-preserving paraphrases that expose backdoor-triggered predictions, outperforming compared detectors in the reported tests.

title: ParaFuzz: An Interpretability-Driven Technique for Detecting Poisoned Samples in NLP

abstract: We study distributionally robust offline reinforcement learning (RL), which seeks to find an optimal robust policy purely from an offline dataset that can perform well in perturbed environments. We propose a generic algorithm framework Doubly Pessimistic Model-based Policy Optimization ($\texttt{P}^2\texttt{MPO}$) for robust offline RL, which features a novel combination of a flexible model estimation subroutine and a doubly pessimistic policy optimization step. Here the double pessimism principle is crucial to overcome the distribution shift incurred by i) the mismatch between behavior policy and the family of target policies; and ii) the perturbation of the nominal model. Under certain accuracy assumptions on the model estimation subroutine, we show that $\texttt{P}^2\texttt{MPO}$ is provably sample-efficient with robust partial coverage data, which means that the offline dataset has good coverage of the distributions induced by the optimal robust policy and perturbed models around the nominal model. By tailoring specific model estimation subroutines for concrete examples including tabular Robust Markov Decision Process (RMDP), factored RMDP, and RMDP with kernel and neural function approximations, we show that $\texttt{P}^2\texttt{MPO}$ enjoys a $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-1/2})$ convergence rate, where $n$ is the number of trajectories in the offline dataset. Notably, these models, except for the tabular case, are first identified and proven tractable by this paper. To the best of our knowledge, we first propose a general learning principle --- double pessimism --- for robust offline RL and show that it is provably efficient in the context of general function approximations.

paragraphs: Robust offline reinforcement learning seeks policies that work under environmental perturbations using only previously collected data. This creates two distribution shifts: a learned policy may behave differently from the policy that collected the data, and the deployment environment may differ from the nominal model. The paper addresses both through a principle called double pessimism.

Its P²MPO framework combines flexible model estimation with policy optimization that accounts conservatively for both sources of shift. The authors prove sample efficiency under accuracy assumptions on model estimation and a condition called robust partial coverage. That coverage concerns distributions generated by the optimal robust policy and perturbed models around the nominal environment.

The framework is instantiated for tabular and factored robust decision processes, as well as kernel and neural function approximations. These cases achieve a convergence rate proportional to the inverse square root of the number of recorded trajectories, up to logarithmic factors. The results establish tractability for the stated settings and assumptions, extending the theoretical reach of robust offline learning beyond the tabular case.
summary.tldr: Double pessimism yields efficient robust offline reinforcement learning under model-estimation accuracy and robust partial-coverage assumptions.

title: Double Pessimism is Provably Efficient for Distributionally Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning: Generic Algorithm and Robust Partial Coverage

abstract: General physical scene understanding requires more than simply localizing and recognizing objects -- it requires knowledge that objects can have different latent properties (e.g., mass or elasticity), and that those properties affect the outcome of physical events. While there has been great progress in physical and video prediction models in recent years, benchmarks to test their performance typically do not require an understanding that objects have individual physical properties, or at best test only those properties that are directly observable (e.g., size or color). This work proposes a novel dataset and benchmark, termed Physion++, that rigorously evaluates visual physical prediction in artificial systems under circumstances where those predictions rely on accurate estimates of the latent physical properties of objects in the scene. Specifically, we test scenarios where accurate prediction relies on estimates of properties such as mass, friction, elasticity, and deformability, and where the values of those properties can only be inferred by observing how objects move and interact with other objects or fluids. We evaluate the performance of a number of state-of-the-art prediction models that span a variety of levels of learning vs. built-in knowledge, and compare that performance to a set of human predictions. We find that models that have been trained using standard regimes and datasets do not spontaneously learn to make inferences about latent properties, but also that models that encode objectness and physical states tend to make better predictions. However, there is still a huge gap between all models and human performance, and all models' predictions correlate poorly with those made by humans, suggesting that no state-of-the-art model is learning to make physical predictions in a human-like way. These results show that current deep learning models that succeed in some settings nevertheless fail to achieve human-level physical prediction in other cases, especially those where latent property inference is required. Project page: https://dingmyu.github.io/physion_v2/

paragraphs: Recognizing an object's appearance does not necessarily reveal how it will behave. Properties such as mass, friction, elasticity, and deformability may need to be inferred from motion and interaction. Physion++ is a dataset and benchmark designed to test physical predictions that depend specifically on these hidden properties.

Its scenarios require observing objects interacting with other objects or fluids before making accurate predictions. The authors compare several leading models that use different mixtures of learned behavior and built-in knowledge, and also collect human predictions. This setup examines whether models use the observed dynamics to infer properties that cannot simply be read from appearance.

Models trained with standard datasets and training regimes do not spontaneously acquire the required latent-property inference, according to the reported results. Models representing objects and physical states tend to do better, but all evaluated models remain far behind humans. Their predictions also correlate poorly with human responses, suggesting that success on other physical-prediction tasks does not establish human-like reasoning in these more demanding scenarios.
summary.tldr: Physion++ exposes large gaps between models and humans when physical prediction requires inferring hidden object properties from motion.

title: Physion++: Evaluating Physical Scene Understanding that Requires Online Inference of Different Physical Properties

abstract: Bayesian brain theory suggests that the brain employs generative models to understand the external world. The sampling-based perspective posits that the brain infers the posterior distribution through samples of stochastic neuronal responses. Additionally, the brain continually updates its generative model to approach the true distribution of the external world. In this study, we introduce the Hierarchical Exponential-family Energy-based (HEE) model, which captures the dynamics of inference and learning. In the HEE model, we decompose the partition function into individual layers and leverage a group of neurons with shorter time constants to sample the gradient of the decomposed normalization term. This allows our model to estimate the partition function and perform inference simultaneously, circumventing the negative phase encountered in conventional energy-based models (EBMs). As a result, the learning process is localized both in time and space, and the model is easy to converge. To match the brain's rapid computation, we demonstrate that neural adaptation can serve as a momentum term, significantly accelerating the inference process. On natural image datasets, our model exhibits representations akin to those observed in the biological visual system. Furthermore, for the machine learning community, our model can generate observations through joint or marginal generation. We show that marginal generation outperforms joint generation and achieves performance on par with other EBMs.

paragraphs: The paper develops a generative model inspired by the idea that stochastic neural responses represent samples from a posterior distribution. Its Hierarchical Exponential-family Energy-based model combines inference about observations with learning the distribution that generates them. This addresses both moment-to-moment interpretation and the ongoing adjustment of the model to its environment.

The method decomposes the partition function across layers and uses faster neurons to sample gradients of the resulting normalization terms.
