paragraphs: Reinforcement learning has strong theoretical tools for systems with linear dynamics, but practical agents often observe images or other high-dimensional features. Those observations need not evolve linearly. This paper studies a setting in which a hidden linear subspace within the observation features does have linear dynamics, making representation learning the link between rich inputs and simpler control structure.

The authors design learning objectives based on forward and inverse dynamics models. Their theoretical results show that these objectives can be optimized efficiently and that their local optimizers recover the hidden linear subspace. This is a structural recovery result: the learned representation captures the assumed space where linear dynamics hold.

Experiments on synthetic data verify the theoretical findings. The authors also generalize their approach to nonlinear settings and explore it on simple control tasks with rich observations. That exploration extends the practical investigation beyond the central theoretical setting, while the recovery guarantee itself relies on the specified hidden linear structure.
summary.tldr: Forward and inverse dynamics objectives provably recover a hidden linear subspace under the paper’s structural assumption about rich observations.

title: Extracting Latent State Representations with Linear Dynamics from Rich Observations

abstract: Self-play is a common method for constructing solutions in Markov games that can yield optimal policies in collaborative settings. However, these policies often adopt highly-specialized conventions that make playing with a novel partner difficult. To address this, recent approaches rely on encoding symmetry and convention-awareness into policy training, but these require strong environmental assumptions and can complicate policy training. To overcome this, we propose moving the learning of conventions to the belief space. Specifically, we propose a belief learning paradigm that can maintain beliefs over rollouts of policies not seen at training time, and can thus decode and adapt to novel conventions at test time. We show how to leverage this belief model for both search and training of a best response over a pool of policies to greatly improve zero-shot coordination. We also show how our paradigm promotes explainability and interpretability of nuanced agent conventions.

To overcome this, we propose moving the learning of conventions to the belief space. Specifically, we propose a belief learning paradigm that can maintain beliefs over rollouts of policies not seen at training time, and can thus decode and adapt to novel conventions at test time. We show how to leverage this belief model for both search and training of a best response over a pool of policies to greatly improve zero-shot coordination. We also show how our paradigm promotes explainability and interpretability of nuanced agent conventions.

paragraphs: Agents trained through self-play can become effective collaborators while relying on conventions unfamiliar to other partners. This creates a gap between coordinating with training partners and coordinating with someone new. The paper addresses that gap by changing how agents learn about conventions, placing this learning in their beliefs about behavior.

The proposed belief-learning approach can maintain beliefs over trajectories produced by policies that were not seen during training. This lets an agent interpret and adapt to unfamiliar conventions at test time. The authors use the belief model in two ways: to support search and to train a best response over a collection of policies.

The paper reports substantial improvements in zero-shot coordination, where cooperation must work with a novel partner without prior joint training. It also shows that the belief-based approach helps explain and interpret subtle agent conventions. The central contribution is a way to represent uncertainty about partners’ behavior that can generalize beyond the policies used to train the belief model.
summary.tldr: Learning beliefs that generalize to unseen policies helps cooperative agents interpret unfamiliar conventions and coordinate with new partners.

title: Generalized Beliefs for Cooperative AI

abstract: Causal discovery with latent confounders is an important but challenging task in many scientific areas. Despite the success of some overcomplete independent component analysis (OICA) based methods in certain domains, they are computationally expensive and can easily get stuck into local optima. We notice that interestingly, by making use of higher-order cumulants, there exists a closed-form solution to OICA in specific cases, e.g., when the mixing procedure follows the One-Latent-Component structure. In light of the power of the closed-form solution to OICA corresponding to the One-Latent-Component structure, we formulate a way to estimate the mixing matrix using the higher-order cumulants, and further propose the testable One-Latent-Component condition to identify the latent variables and determine causal orders. By iteratively removing the share identified latent components, we successfully extend the results on the One-Latent-Component structure to the Multi-Latent-Component structure and finally provide a practical and asymptotically correct algorithm to learn the causal structure with latent variables. Experimental results illustrate the asymptotic correctness and effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships becomes harder when unobserved variables influence several measured variables. Some existing approaches handle these hidden influences through overcomplete independent component analysis, but their optimization can be expensive and get trapped in local optima. This paper develops an alternative that uses higher-order cumulants, statistical quantities that describe distributional structure beyond ordinary covariance.

The starting point is a special mixing structure called One-Latent-Component. In this setting, the authors identify a closed-form solution and use cumulants to estimate the mixing matrix. They also introduce a testable condition for identifying latent variables and determining causal order. This turns a structural property of the data-generating process into a tool for causal discovery.

To handle multiple latent components, the method repeatedly removes shared components that it has already identified. The authors establish asymptotic correctness for the resulting algorithm and report experiments supporting its effectiveness. The result extends the special-case construction to a broader latent-variable structure; its correctness claim concerns the large-data limit within the analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: Higher-order cumulants enable a causal discovery algorithm that identifies and removes latent components, with asymptotic correctness in the analyzed setting.

title: Causal Discovery with Latent Confounders Based on Higher-Order Cumulants

abstract: Representation learning and exploration are among the key challenges for any deep reinforcement learning agent. In this work, we provide a singular value decomposition based method that can be used to obtain representations that preserve the underlying transition structure in the domain. Perhaps interestingly, we show that these representations also capture the relative frequency of state visitations, thereby providing an estimate for pseudo-counts for free. To scale this decomposition method to large-scale domains, we provide an algorithm that never requires building the transition matrix, can make use of deep networks, and also permits mini-batch training. Further, we draw inspiration from predictive state representations and extend our decomposition method to partially observable environments. With experiments on multi-task settings with partially observable domains, we show that the proposed method can not only learn useful representation on DM-Lab-30 environments (that have inputs involving language instructions, pixel images, rewards, among others) but it can also be effective at hard exploration tasks in DM-Hard-8 environments.

The method is also effective on difficult exploration tasks in DM-Hard-8. These findings support the central connection: a representation organized around environmental transitions can simultaneously provide useful learning features and information relevant to exploration.
summary.tldr: A scalable decomposition method learns transition-preserving representations that also provide visitation estimates useful for exploration.

title: Representations and Exploration for Deep Reinforcement Learning using Singular Value Decomposition

abstract: Many machine learning problems can be abstracted in solving game theory formulations and boil down to optimizing nested objectives, such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) and multi-agent reinforcement learning. Solving these games requires finding their stable fixed points or Nash equilibrium. However, existing algorithms for solving games suffer from empirical instability, hence demanding heavy ad-hoc tuning in practice. To tackle these challenges, we resort to the emerging scheme of Learning to Optimize (L2O), which discovers problem-specific efficient optimization algorithms through data-driven training. Our customized L2O framework for differentiable game theory problems, dubbed “Learning to Play Games" (L2PG), seeks a stable fixed point solution, by predicting the fast update direction from the past trajectory, with a novel gradient stability-aware, sign-based loss function. We further incorporate curriculum learning and self-learning to strengthen the empirical training stability and generalization of L2PG. On test problems including quadratic games and GANs, L2PG can substantially accelerate the convergence, and demonstrates a remarkably more stable trajectory. Codes are available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/L2PG.

paragraphs: Many learning problems involve interacting objectives, as in generative adversarial networks and multi-agent reinforcement learning. Solving these games requires seeking stable fixed points or equilibria, but existing algorithms can behave unstably and need substantial tuning. This paper approaches the problem by learning an optimization procedure from data.

The proposed Learning to Play Games framework, or L2PG, predicts an update direction from the previous optimization trajectory. Its training uses a sign-based loss that accounts for gradient stability, with the aim of reaching a stable fixed point quickly. Curriculum learning and self-learning are added to strengthen empirical training stability and generalization.

Tests on quadratic games and generative adversarial networks show that L2PG can substantially accelerate convergence and produce more stable trajectories. These are empirical findings on the evaluated problems. They support using the history of a game's optimization process to learn useful update behavior, especially when the interaction between objectives makes conventional optimization difficult to tune.
summary.tldr: L2PG learns update directions from optimization histories to accelerate and stabilize the solution of differentiable games in experiments.

title: Learning to Optimize Differentiable Games

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is typically evaluated using a single metric (linear probing on ImageNet), which neither provides insight into tradeoffs between models nor highlights how to improve them. To address this, we propose an SSL risk decomposition, which generalizes the classical approximation-estimation decomposition. Our decomposition consists of four error terms: approximation, representation usability, probe generalization, and encoder generalization. We provide efficient estimators for each term and use them to analyze the effect of 30 design choices on 169 SSL vision models evaluated on ImageNet. Our analysis gives valuable insights for designing and using SSL models. For example, it highlights the main source of errors and shows how to improve SSL in specific settings (full- vs few-shot) by trading off error components.

paragraphs: Self-supervised vision models are often compared through a single ImageNet linear-probing score. That score measures an outcome but offers limited insight into why a model succeeds or how to improve it. This paper develops an evaluation framework that separates prediction risk into several contributing sources of error.

The decomposition extends the classical distinction between approximation and estimation error. It contains four terms: approximation, representation usability, probe generalization, and encoder generalization. Separating these terms makes it possible to examine different aspects of the learned representation and the prediction procedure instead of attributing every score change to one undifferentiated measure of quality.

The authors provide efficient estimators for the terms and apply them to 169 self-supervised vision models, examining 30 design choices on ImageNet. Their analysis identifies major error sources and shows how improvements can involve trading one component against another. These tradeoffs differ between full-data and few-shot settings, making the framework useful for selecting or designing models around the amount of labeled data available.
summary.tldr: A four-part risk decomposition explains self-supervised model performance and reveals tradeoffs hidden by a single probing score.

title: Evaluating Self-Supervised Learning via Risk Decomposition

abstract: Estimating the effects of multi-dimensional treatments (i.e., joint treatment effects) is critical in many data-intensive domains, including genetics and drug evaluation. The main challenges for studying the joint treatment effects include the need for large sample sizes to explore different treatment combinations as well as potentially unsafe treatment interactions. In this paper, we develop machinery for estimating joint treatment effects by combining data from multiple experimental datasets. In particular, first, we develop new identification conditions for determining whether a joint treatment effect can be computed in terms of multiple interventional distributions under various scenarios. Further, we develop estimators with statistically appealing properties, including consistency and robustness to model misspecification and slow convergence. Finally, we perform simulation studies, which corroborate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Understanding several treatments used together requires estimating their joint effect. Directly studying many treatment combinations can demand large samples, and some combinations may involve unsafe interactions. This paper develops methods for using information spread across multiple experimental datasets to estimate these combined effects.

The first contribution concerns identification: determining whether the available experimental distributions contain enough information to compute the joint treatment effect. The authors derive new conditions for making that determination under several scenarios. This separates the question of whether an effect can be recovered from the question of how to estimate it using a finite collection of observations.

The second contribution is a set of estimators with properties including consistency and robustness to model misspecification and slow convergence. Simulation studies support the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The practical significance is a framework for combining experiments when its identification conditions apply, with statistical methods designed to tolerate specified estimation difficulties. The conditions remain central because combining datasets alone does not establish that a particular joint effect is recoverable.
summary.tldr: The paper gives identification conditions and robust estimators for recovering joint treatment effects from multiple experimental datasets.

title: Estimating Joint Treatment Effects by Combining Multiple Experiments

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a type of prompting where a transformer model operates on a sequence of (input, output) examples and performs inference on-the-fly. In this work, we formalize in-context learning as an algorithm learning problem where a transformer model implicitly constructs a hypothesis function at inference-time. We first explore the statistical aspects of this abstraction through the lens of multitask learning: We obtain generalization bounds for ICL when the input prompt is (1) a sequence of i.i.d. (input, label) pairs or (2) a trajectory arising from a dynamical system. The crux of our analysis is relating the excess risk to the stability of the algorithm implemented by the transformer. We characterize when transformer/attention architecture provably obeys the stability condition and also provide empirical verification. For generalization on unseen tasks, we identify an inductive bias phenomenon in which the transfer learning risk is governed by the task complexity and the number of MTL tasks in a highly predictable manner. Finally, we provide numerical evaluations that (1) demonstrate transformers can indeed implement near-optimal algorithms on classical regression problems with i.i.d. and dynamic data, (2) provide insights on stability, and (3) verify our theoretical predictions.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a transformer infer from examples supplied in its prompt. This paper formalizes that behavior as learning an algorithm: at inference time, the transformer implicitly constructs a hypothesis function from the examples. This perspective makes it possible to study the statistical behavior of the procedure implemented by the model.

Using a multitask-learning framework, the authors derive generalization bounds for prompts containing either independent input-label pairs or trajectories from a dynamical system. Their analysis connects excess risk to algorithmic stability, which concerns how the learned procedure responds to changes in its examples. They identify conditions under which transformer and attention architectures satisfy the required stability property and provide empirical verification.

For previously unseen tasks, the paper identifies a relationship between transfer risk, task complexity, and the number of training tasks. Numerical evaluations show that transformers can implement near-optimal algorithms on classical regression problems with independent and dynamic data. These results support both the algorithm-learning interpretation and the theory's predictions about stability and transfer.
summary.tldr: The paper treats in-context learning as algorithm learning and connects transformer generalization to stability, task complexity, and multitask training.

title: Transformers as Algorithms: Generalization and Stability in In-context Learning

abstract: In a vertical federated learning (VFL) system consisting of a central server and many distributed clients, the training data are vertically partitioned such that different features are privately stored on different clients. The problem of split VFL is to train a model split between the server and the clients. This paper aims to address two major challenges in split VFL: 1) performance degradation due to straggling clients during training; and 2) data and model privacy leakage from clients’ uploaded data embeddings. We propose FedVS to simultaneously address these two challenges. The key idea of FedVS is to design secret sharing schemes for the local data and models, such that information-theoretical privacy against colluding clients and curious server is guaranteed, and the aggregation of all clients’ embeddings is reconstructed losslessly, via decrypting computation shares from the non-straggling clients. Extensive experiments on various types of VFL datasets (including tabular, CV, and multi-view) demonstrate the universal advantages of FedVS in straggler mitigation and privacy protection over baseline protocols.

paragraphs: In vertical federated learning, different clients hold different features of the training data. A split model distributes its computation between those clients and a central server. This arrangement creates two problems addressed by the paper: slow clients can degrade training performance, and the embeddings clients upload can expose information about their private data or models.

FedVS introduces secret-sharing schemes for both local data and local models. The schemes allow the aggregate of all clients’ embeddings to be reconstructed losslessly from computation shares supplied by clients that are not straggling. This makes the reconstruction of the required aggregate central to both maintaining training progress and protecting the information held by participants.

The paper guarantees information-theoretic privacy against colluding clients and a curious server within its scheme. Experiments span tabular, computer-vision, and multi-view datasets, reporting advantages over baseline protocols in straggler mitigation and privacy protection. The contribution brings these two concerns into one design: privacy-preserving shared computation also supplies the mechanism for recovering the aggregate despite straggling clients.
summary.tldr: FedVS uses secret sharing to protect split-model federated learning while recovering exact embedding aggregates despite straggling clients.

title: FedVS: Straggler-Resilient and Privacy-Preserving Vertical Federated Learning for Split Models

abstract: Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects from observational data is a crucial task across many fields, helping policy and decision-makers take better actions. There has been recent progress on robust and efficient methods for estimating the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) function, but these methods often do not take into account the risk of hidden confounding, which could arbitrarily and unknowingly bias any causal estimate based on observational data. We propose a meta-learner called the B-Learner, which can efficiently learn sharp bounds on the CATE function under limits on the level of hidden confounding. We derive the B-Learner by adapting recent results for sharp and valid bounds of the average treatment effect (Dorn et al., 2021) into the framework given by Kallus & Oprescu (2023) for robust and model-agnostic learning of conditional distributional treatment effects. The B-Learner can use any function estimator such as random forests and deep neural networks, and we prove its estimates are valid, sharp, efficient, and have a quasi-oracle property with respect to the constituent estimators under more general conditions than existing methods. Semi-synthetic experimental comparisons validate the theoretical findings, and we use real-world data demonstrate how the method might be used in practice.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can differ across people, so decision-makers often want to estimate effects conditional on observed characteristics. Observational data complicates this task: unobserved factors may influence both treatment and outcomes, biasing causal estimates. The B-Learner addresses this uncertainty by learning bounds on the conditional average treatment effect under specified limits on hidden confounding.

The method combines results on sharp average treatment-effect bounds with a framework for robust learning of conditional treatment effects. It is a meta-learner, meaning its components can use different function estimators, including random forests and neural networks. This flexibility allows the bounding procedure to be paired with different predictive modeling tools.

The authors prove validity, sharpness, efficiency, and a quasi-oracle property relative to the component estimators under conditions more general than those of existing methods. These guarantees remain tied to the assumed limits on confounding. Semi-synthetic comparisons support the theory, while a real-data application illustrates practical use. The contribution is a way to represent causal uncertainty across different populations instead of relying solely on potentially biased point estimates.
summary.tldr: The B-Learner estimates sharp bounds on heterogeneous treatment effects under specified limits on hidden confounding.

title: B-Learner: Quasi-Oracle Bounds on Heterogeneous Causal Effects Under Hidden Confounding

abstract: State of the art reinforcement learning has enabled training agents on tasks of ever increasing complexity. However, the current paradigm tends to favor training agents from scratch on every new task or on collections of tasks with a view towards generalizing to novel task configurations. The former suffers from poor data efficiency while the latter is difficult when test tasks are out-of-distribution. Agents that can effectively transfer their knowledge about the world pose a potential solution to these issues. In this paper, we investigate transfer learning in the context of model-based agents. Specifically, we aim to understand where exactly environment models have an advantage and why. We find that a model-based approach outperforms controlled model-free baselines for transfer learning. Through ablations, we show that both the policy and dynamics model learnt through exploration matter for successful transfer. We demonstrate our results across three domains which vary in their requirements for transfer: in-distribution procedural (Crafter), in-distribution identical (RoboDesk), and out-of-distribution (Meta-World). Our results show that intrinsic exploration combined with environment models present a viable direction towards agents that are self-supervised and able to generalize to novel reward functions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents often learn each task from scratch, which uses substantial interaction data. Training on many tasks can help, but transferring to tasks outside that training distribution remains difficult. This paper investigates whether learning an environment model helps agents reuse knowledge and why such a benefit arises.

The authors compare model-based agents with controlled model-free baselines and find better transfer from the model-based approach. Ablation studies indicate that successful transfer depends on both the policy and the dynamics model learned through exploration. The result attributes value to the combination of learned behavior and knowledge about how the environment changes.

Across these settings, the findings support combining intrinsic exploration with environment models as a viable direction for self-supervised agents that adapt to new reward functions. The evidence concerns transfer across these tested domains and highlights which learned components contribute to it.
summary.tldr: Controlled experiments show that exploration-trained policies and dynamics models both contribute to stronger model-based transfer.

title: Investigating the Role of Model-Based Learning in Exploration and Transfer

abstract: Error correcting output codes (ECOCs) have been proposed to improve the robustness of deep neural networks (DNNs) against hardware defects of DNN hardware accelerators. Unfortunately, existing efforts suffer from drawbacks that would greatly impact their practicality: 1) robust accuracy (with defects) improvement at the cost of degraded clean accuracy (without defects); 2) no guarantee on better robust or clean accuracy using stronger ECOCs. In this paper, we first shed light on the connection between these drawbacks and error correlation, and then propose a novel comprehensive error decorrelation framework, namely COLA. Specifically, we propose to reduce inner layer feature error correlation by 1) adopting a separated architecture, where the last portions of the paths to all output nodes are separated, and 2) orthogonalizing weights in common DNN layers so that the intermediate features are orthogonal with each other. We also propose a regularization technique based on total correlation to mitigate overall error correlation at the outputs. The effectiveness of COLA is first analyzed theoretically, and then evaluated experimentally, e.g. up to 6.7% clean accuracy improvement compared with the original DNNs and up to 40% robust accuracy improvement compared to the state-of-the-art ECOC-enhanced DNNs.

paragraphs: Error-correcting output codes can help neural networks withstand defects in the hardware running them. Existing approaches, however, can improve accuracy under defects while reducing accuracy on functioning hardware. Stronger codes also do not necessarily improve either measure. This paper connects these problems to correlation among errors.

COLA aims to reduce that correlation at several levels. Its architecture separates the final portions of paths leading to output nodes. It also orthogonalizes weights in shared layers to encourage orthogonal intermediate features. A further regularization term, based on total correlation, addresses dependence among errors at the outputs. Together, these changes coordinate network learning with the error-correction mechanism.

The authors provide theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation. They report improvements of up to 6.7% in clean accuracy over the original networks and up to 40% in robust accuracy over state-of-the-art code-enhanced networks. These are reported maximum improvements with different comparison points. The results support error decorrelation as a useful design principle for neural inference exposed to hardware defects.
summary.tldr: COLA reduces correlated network errors to improve the effectiveness of error-correcting codes against hardware defects.

title: COLA: Orchestrating Error Coding and Learning for Robust Neural Network Inference Against Hardware Defects

abstract: Image inpainting refers to the task of generating a complete, natural image based on a partially revealed reference image. Recently, many research interests have been focused on addressing this problem using fixed diffusion models. These approaches typically directly replace the revealed region of the intermediate or final generated images with that of the reference image or its variants. However, since the unrevealed regions are not directly modified to match the context, it results in incoherence between revealed and unrevealed regions. To address the incoherence problem, a small number of methods introduce a rigorous Bayesian framework, but they tend to introduce mismatches between the generated and the reference images due to the approximation errors in computing the posterior distributions. In this paper, we propose CoPaint, which can coherently inpaint the whole image without introducing mismatches. CoPaint also uses the Bayesian framework to jointly modify both revealed and unrevealed regions but approximates the posterior distribution in a way that allows the errors to gradually drop to zero throughout the denoising steps, thus strongly penalizing any mismatches with the reference image. Our experiments verify that CoPaint can outperform the existing diffusion-based methods under both objective and subjective metrics.

Our experiments verify that CoPaint can outperform the existing diffusion-based methods under both objective and subjective metrics.

paragraphs: Image inpainting fills missing regions while keeping the result consistent with the visible parts of a reference image. Diffusion-based approaches often replace visible regions in generated images with reference pixels. The authors argue that this can leave the generated surroundings incoherent because the missing regions are not directly adjusted to fit that context.

CoPaint uses a Bayesian framework to modify visible and hidden regions jointly. Earlier Bayesian approaches can introduce mismatches through errors in approximating the posterior distribution. CoPaint instead uses an approximation whose errors are allowed to decrease to zero over the denoising steps, increasingly penalizing disagreement with the reference.

This connects two requirements of inpainting: the completed image should be coherent as a whole, and its revealed content should match the supplied image. Joint modification supports coherence, while the decreasing approximation error enforces reference agreement. Experiments show that CoPaint can outperform existing diffusion-based methods on both objective and subjective measures. The stated findings support controlling posterior approximation throughout denoising as a way to improve consistency in image completion.
summary.tldr: CoPaint jointly adjusts visible and missing image regions while reducing posterior approximation error to produce coherent, reference-consistent inpainting.

title: Towards Coherent Image Inpainting Using Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models

abstract: Recent works have identified that existing methods, which construct persistence diagrams in Topological Data Analysis (TDA), are not robust to noise and varied densities in a point cloud. We analyze the necessary properties of an approach that can address these two issues, and propose a new filter function for TDA based on a new data-dependent kernel which possesses these properties. Our empirical evaluation reveals that the proposed filter function provides a better means for t-SNE visualization and SVM classification than three existing methods of TDA.
originalAbstract: Recent works have identified that existing methods, which construct persistence diagrams in Topological Data Analysis (TDA), are not robust to noise and varied densities in a point cloud. We analyze the necessary properties of an approach that can address these two issues, and propose a new filter function for TDA based on a new data-dependent kernel which possesses these properties. Our empirical evaluation reveals that the proposed filter function provides a better means for t-SNE visualization and SVM classification than three existing methods of TDA.

paragraphs: Persistence diagrams are used in topological data analysis to describe structure in point clouds. The paper addresses two problems with existing construction methods: sensitivity to noise and to differences in how densely points are distributed. Both can make the resulting representation less useful when the observed point cloud is uneven or noisy.

The authors first analyze the properties an approach needs to address these two issues together. They then propose a filter function based on a new data-dependent kernel that has those properties. The contribution connects the construction of the representation to explicit requirements for handling noise and varied density, rather than treating the downstream task alone as the design objective.

The empirical evaluation compares the proposed filter with three existing topological data analysis methods. It yields better results for t-SNE visualization and SVM classification in those comparisons. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed construction for both visual exploration and predictive analysis. The evidence combines a property-based design argument with downstream tests of the resulting representation.
summary.tldr: A data-dependent kernel yields a topological filter designed for noise and varied density, improving the reported visualization and classification results.

title: Towards a Persistence Diagram that is Robust to Noise and Varied Densities

abstract: What is *agency,* and why does it matter? In this work, we draw from the political science and philosophy literature and give two competing visions of what it means to be an (ethical) agent. The first view, which we term *mechanistic*, is commonly— and implicitly—assumed in AI research, yet it is a fundamentally limited means to understand the ethical characteristics of AI. Under the second view, which we term volitional, AI can no longer be considered an ethical agent. We discuss the implications of each of these views for two critical questions: first, what the ideal system “ought” to look like, and second, how accountability may be achieved. In light of this discussion, we ultimately argue that, in the context of ethically-significant behavior, AI should be viewed not as an agent but as the outcome of political processes.

paragraphs: This position paper examines what it means to call AI an ethical agent. Drawing on political science and philosophy, the authors distinguish two competing conceptions of agency. The distinction matters because the meaning assigned to agency affects both judgments about desirable AI behavior and the way accountability is understood.

The authors call the first conception mechanistic and argue that AI research commonly assumes it without making that assumption explicit. They regard it as fundamentally limited for understanding AI’s ethical characteristics. Under the second conception, which they call volitional, AI does not qualify as an ethical agent. The argument therefore makes the choice of conceptual framework central to the ethical analysis.

The paper explores what each view implies for the kind of system that ought to be built and for achieving accountability. It ultimately argues that ethically significant AI behavior should be understood as an outcome of political processes. This shifts the proposed focus of analysis toward how AI comes to take its form and how that process bears on responsibility.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that AI ethics and accountability should examine AI as an outcome of political processes rather than assume ethical agency.

title: Position: Beyond Personhood: Agency, Accountability, and the Limits of Anthropomorphic Ethical Analysis

abstract: Rankings are ubiquitous across many applications, from search engines to hiring committees. In practice, many rankings are derived from the output of predictors. However, when predictors trained for classification tasks have intrinsic uncertainty, it is not obvious how this uncertainty should be represented in the derived rankings. Our work considers ranking functions: maps from individual predictions for a classification task to distributions over rankings. We focus on two aspects of ranking functions: stability to perturbations in predictions and fairness towards both individuals and subgroups. Not only is stability an important requirement for its own sake, but — as we show — it composes harmoniously with individual fairness in the sense of Dwork et al. (2012). While deterministic ranking functions cannot be stable aside from trivial scenarios, we show that the recently proposed uncertainty aware (UA) ranking functions of Singh et al. (2021) are stable. Our main result is that UA rankings also achieve group fairness through successful composition with multiaccurate or multicalibrated predictors. Our work demonstrates that UA rankings naturally interpolate between group and individual level fairness guarantees, while simultaneously satisfying stability guarantees important whenever machine-learned predictions are used.

paragraphs: When classification predictions are uncertain, converting them into a ranking raises questions about both stability and fairness. This paper studies ranking functions that map individual predictions to probability distributions over possible rankings. Stability concerns whether small changes in predictions lead to controlled changes in the resulting ranking distribution.

The authors show that deterministic ranking functions cannot provide the studied stability property except in trivial scenarios. Previously proposed uncertainty-aware ranking functions do satisfy it. They also establish that stability composes well with individual fairness, connecting the behavior of the ranking stage to fairness properties of the predictions it receives.

The main result extends this connection to groups: uncertainty-aware rankings achieve group-fairness guarantees when combined with multiaccurate or multicalibrated predictors. Those predictor conditions are part of the guarantee. Together, the findings show how uncertainty-aware ranking can connect individual and group fairness while preserving stability, providing a principled way to carry appropriate prediction-level properties into decisions expressed as rankings.
summary.tldr: Uncertainty-aware rankings are stable and can inherit individual and group fairness guarantees from predictors with the appropriate properties.

title: Stability and Multigroup Fairness in Ranking with Uncertain Predictions

abstract: To address the shortcomings of real-world datasets, robust learning algorithms have been designed to overcome arbitrary and indiscriminate data corruption. However, practical processes of gathering data may lead to patterns of data corruption that are localized to specific partitions of the training dataset. Motivated by critical applications where the learned model is deployed to make predictions about people from a rich collection of overlapping subpopulations, we initiate the study of multigroup robust algorithms whose robustness guarantees for each subpopulation only degrade with the amount of data corruption inside that subpopulation. When the data corruption is not distributed uniformly over subpopulations, our algorithms provide more meaningful robustness guarantees than standard guarantees that are oblivious to how the data corruption and the affected subpopulations are related. Our techniques establish a new connection between multigroup fairness and robustness.

paragraphs: Data corruption can be concentrated in particular parts of a training dataset rather than spread evenly throughout it. This matters when a model makes predictions about people belonging to many overlapping subpopulations. A robustness guarantee based only on overall corruption can miss how differently those groups are affected by the data-gathering process.

The paper introduces multigroup robustness, where each subpopulation receives a guarantee that degrades only with corruption inside that subpopulation. This changes what the analysis tracks: the relevant quantity is local corruption for each group, including groups that overlap, rather than a single corruption level applied indiscriminately to everyone.

The authors develop algorithms providing these guarantees and connect their techniques to multigroup fairness. When corruption is distributed unevenly, the resulting assurances are more meaningful than guarantees that ignore the relationship between corrupted data and affected groups. The contribution is a way of defining and achieving robustness that accounts for who is represented in the damaged portions of a dataset, rather than treating the dataset as homogeneous.
summary.tldr: Multigroup robustness gives each overlapping subpopulation guarantees that degrade only with the corruption within that group.

title: Multigroup Robustness

abstract: This paper proposes a step toward approximate Bayesian inference in on-policy actor-critic deep reinforcement learning. It is implemented through three changes to the Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) algorithm: (1) applying a ReLU function to advantage estimates, (2) spectral normalization of actor-critic weights, and (3) incorporating dropout as a Bayesian approximation. We prove under standard assumptions that restricting policy updates to positive advantages optimizes for value by maximizing a lower bound on the value function plus an additive term. We show that the additive term is bounded proportional to the Lipschitz constant of the value function, which offers theoretical grounding for spectral normalization of critic weights. Finally, our application of dropout corresponds to approximate Bayesian inference over both the actor and critic parameters, which enables adaptive state-aware exploration around the modes of the actor via Thompson sampling. We demonstrate significant improvements for median and interquartile mean metrics over A3C, PPO, SAC, and TD3 on the MuJoCo continuous control benchmark and improvement over PPO in the challenging ProcGen generalization benchmark.

paragraphs: This paper modifies A3C to move on-policy actor-critic learning toward approximate Bayesian inference. It makes three changes: passing advantage estimates through ReLU, applying spectral normalization to actor-critic weights, and using dropout as a Bayesian approximation. ReLU restricts policy updates to positive advantage estimates, focusing those updates on actions estimated to be better than the comparison value.

Under standard assumptions, the authors prove that positive-advantage updates maximize a lower bound on the value function plus an additive term. The additive term is bounded in proportion to the value function's Lipschitz constant, providing theoretical support for spectral normalization of critic weights. Dropout supplies approximate uncertainty over both actor and critic parameters, enabling state-aware exploration through Thompson sampling.

On MuJoCo continuous control, the combined method significantly improves median and interquartile-mean performance over A3C, PPO, SAC, and TD3. It also improves over PPO on the ProcGen generalization benchmark. These findings support the combined design empirically, while the positive-advantage justification remains conditional on the assumptions of the theoretical result.
summary.tldr: Positive-advantage updates, spectral normalization, and Bayesian-style dropout improve A3C, with conditional theoretical support and gains on control and generalization benchmarks.

title: ReLU to the Rescue: Improve Your On-Policy Actor-Critic with Positive Advantages

abstract: Spatio-temporal point processes (STPPs) are potent mathematical tools for modeling and predicting events with both temporal and spatial features. Despite their versatility, most existing methods for learning STPPs either assume a restricted form of the spatio-temporal distribution, or suffer from inaccurate approximations of the intractable integral in the likelihood training objective. These issues typically arise from the normalization term of the probability density function. Moreover, existing works only provide point prediction for events without quantifying their uncertainty, such as confidence intervals for the event’s arrival time and confidence regions for the event’s location, which is crucial given the considerable randomness of the data. To tackle these challenges, we introduce SMASH: a Score MAtching-based pSeudolikeliHood estimator for learning marked STPPs. Specifically, our framework adopts a normalization-free objective by estimating the pseudolikelihood of marked STPPs through score-matching and predicts confidence intervals/regions for event time and location by generating samples through a score-based sampling algorithm. The superior performance of our proposed framework is demonstrated through extensive experiments on both point and confidence interval/region prediction of events.

paragraphs: Predicting an event’s time and location involves more than selecting a single best guess. Spatio-temporal point processes model this kind of event data, but existing learning methods face a difficult normalization calculation. They often respond by restricting the distributions they can represent or approximating an integral inaccurately. The paper also identifies a second problem: point predictions alone do not communicate the randomness of future events.

The proposed method, SMASH, uses score matching to estimate a pseudolikelihood for marked spatio-temporal point processes. Its training objective avoids the normalization term responsible for the computational difficulty. This changes how the model is learned while also supporting predictions that describe a range of plausible outcomes.

SMASH generates samples through a score-based sampling algorithm and uses them to predict confidence intervals for arrival times and confidence regions for locations. The reported experiments show superior performance for both point predictions and these uncertainty predictions. The contribution therefore connects a normalization-free learning objective with a more informative account of where and when events may occur.
summary.tldr: SMASH learns spatio-temporal event models without a normalization term and uses sampling to predict event times, locations, and their uncertainty.

title: Beyond Point Prediction: Score Matching-based Pseudolikelihood Estimation of Neural Marked Spatio-Temporal Point Process

abstract: This paper introduces the Deep Functional Factor Model (DF2M), a Bayesian nonparametric model designed for analysis of high-dimensional functional time series. DF2M is built upon the Indian Buffet Process and the multi-task Gaussian Process, incorporating a deep kernel function that captures non-Markovian and nonlinear temporal dynamics. Unlike many black-box deep learning models, DF2M offers an explainable approach to utilizing neural networks by constructing a factor model and integrating deep neural networks within the kernel function. Additionally, we develop a computationally efficient variational inference algorithm to infer DF2M. Empirical results from four real-world datasets demonstrate that DF2M provides better explainability and superior predictive accuracy compared to conventional deep learning models for high-dimensional functional time series.

Unlike many black-box deep learning models, DF2M offers an explainable approach to utilizing neural networks by constructing a factor model and integrating deep neural networks within the kernel function. Additionally, we develop a computationally efficient variational inference algorithm to infer DF2M. paragraphs: High-dimensional functional time series involve many evolving functions, making forecasting a problem of both representing complex observations and modeling change over time. The Deep Functional Factor Model, or DF2M, addresses this through a Bayesian nonparametric factor model. Its structure is intended to make neural-network-based forecasting more explainable.

DF2M combines an Indian Buffet Process with a multi-task Gaussian Process and places a deep neural network inside the kernel function. This kernel captures nonlinear temporal relationships and non-Markovian dynamics, allowing the temporal description to extend beyond dependence on only the immediately preceding state. The factor model provides an explicit organizing structure around those learned relationships.

The authors also develop a computationally efficient variational inference algorithm for fitting the model. On four real-world datasets, they report better explainability and predictive accuracy than conventional deep learning approaches to high-dimensional functional time series. The findings support a design in which neural networks enrich a structured statistical model, combining flexible temporal modeling with a factor-based account of the data.
summary.tldr: DF2M combines Bayesian factor modeling and deep kernels to improve explainability and forecasting accuracy on four functional time-series datasets.

title: Deep Functional Factor Models: Forecasting High-Dimensional Functional Time Series via Bayesian Nonparametric Factorization

abstract: The combination of self-play and planning has achieved great successes in sequential games, for instance in Chess and Go. However, adapting algorithms such as AlphaZero to simultaneous games poses a new challenge. In these games, missing information about concurrent actions of other agents is a limiting factor as they may select different Nash equilibria or do not play optimally at all. Thus, it is vital to model the behavior of the other agents when interacting with them in simultaneous games. To this end, we propose Albatross: AlphaZero for Learning Bounded-rational Agents and Temperature-based Response Optimization using Simulated Self-play. Albatross learns to play the novel equilibrium concept of a Smooth Best Response Logit Equilibrium (SBRLE), which enables cooperation and competition with agents of any playing strength. We perform an extensive evaluation of Albatross on a set of cooperative and competitive simultaneous perfect-information games. In contrast to AlphaZero, Albatross is able to exploit weak agents in the competitive game of Battlesnake. Additionally, it yields an improvement of 37.6% compared to previous state of the art in the cooperative Overcooked benchmark.

paragraphs: In simultaneous games, players choose actions without seeing what others are choosing at that moment. This complicates the transfer of planning and self-play methods successful in sequential games. Even when the game state is visible, other players may select different equilibria or act imperfectly, making their behavior an essential part of the decision problem.

Albatross addresses this by learning responses to agents with different levels of playing strength. It introduces a Smooth Best Response Logit Equilibrium and uses simulated self-play with temperature-based response optimization. The equilibrium concept is designed to support both cooperation and competition with players across levels of ability.

The evaluation covers cooperative and competitive simultaneous games with perfect information. In Battlesnake, Albatross exploits weak opponents in a way the evaluated AlphaZero approach does not. In Overcooked, it improves on the previous state of the art by 37.6%. These findings support explicitly accounting for bounded rationality when learning to interact with others, instead of relying only on expectations of optimal play.
summary.tldr: Albatross models differing player strengths to improve cooperation and competition in simultaneous games.

title: Mastering Zero-Shot Interactions in Cooperative and Competitive Simultaneous Games

abstract: Actor-critic (AC) is a powerful method for learning an optimal policy in reinforcement learning, where the critic uses algorithms, e.g., temporal difference (TD) learning with function approximation, to evaluate the current policy and the actor updates the policy along an approximate gradient direction using information from the critic. This paper provides the tightest non-asymptotic convergence bounds for both the AC and natural AC (NAC) algorithms. Specifically, existing studies show that AC converges to an $\epsilon+\varepsilon_{\text{critic}}$ neighborhood of stationary points with the best known sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ (up to a log factor), and NAC converges to an $\epsilon+\varepsilon_{\text{critic}}+\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\text{actor}}}$ neighborhood of the global optimum with the best known sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$, where $\varepsilon_{\text{critic}}$ is the approximation error of the critic and $\varepsilon_{\text{actor}}$ is the approximation error induced by the insufficient expressive power of the parameterized policy class. This paper analyzes the convergence of both AC and NAC algorithms with compatible function approximation. Our analysis eliminates the term $\varepsilon_{\text{critic}}$ from the error bounds while still achieving the best known sample complexities. Moreover, we focus on the challenging single-loop setting with a single Markovian sample trajectory. Our major technical novelty lies in analyzing the stochastic bias due to policy-dependent and time-varying compatible function approximation in the critic, and handling the non-ergodicity of the MDP due to the single Markovian sample trajectory. Numerical results are also provided in the appendix.

paragraphs: Actor-critic methods alternate between evaluating a policy with a critic and improving it with an actor. Earlier finite-sample guarantees include an error term caused by approximating the critic. This paper analyzes actor-critic and natural actor-critic with compatible function approximation and removes that critic approximation term from their error bounds.

The analysis preserves the best previously known sample complexities: an order of epsilon to the minus two, up to a logarithmic factor, for actor-critic, and epsilon to the minus three for natural actor-critic. The targets remain different. Actor-critic approaches stationarity, while natural actor-critic approaches the global optimum with a remaining contribution from limited policy-class expressiveness.

The results cover a single-loop procedure using one Markovian sample trajectory. The technical work handles stochastic bias from a critic approximation that changes with the policy, as well as non-ergodicity in this setting. Numerical results accompany the theory. The improvement sharpens finite-sample accuracy guarantees without requiring a worse sample-complexity order.
summary.tldr: Compatible function approximation removes the critic approximation term from single-loop actor-critic guarantees while preserving the best known sample-complexity orders.

title: Non-Asymptotic Analysis for Single-Loop (Natural) Actor-Critic with Compatible Function Approximation

abstract: Irregular Multivariate Time Series (IMTS) forecasting is challenging due to the unaligned nature of multi-channel signals and the prevalence of extensive missing data. Existing methods struggle to capture reliable temporal patterns from such data due to significant missing values. While pre-trained foundation models show potential for addressing these challenges, they are typically designed for Regularly Sampled Time Series (RTS). Motivated by the visual Mask AutoEncoder’s (MAE) powerful capability for modeling sparse multi-channel information and its success in RTS forecasting, we propose VIMTS, a framework adapting Visual MAE for IMTS forecasting. To mitigate the effect of missing values, VIMTS first processes IMTS along the timeline into feature patches at equal intervals. These patches are then complemented using learned cross-channel dependencies. Then it leverages visual MAE’s capability in handling sparse multichannel data for patch reconstruction, followed by a coarse-to-fine technique to generate precise predictions from focused contexts. In addition, we integrate self-supervised learning for improved IMTS modeling by adapting the visual MAE to IMTS data. Extensive experiments demonstrate VIMTS’s superior performance and few-shot capability, advancing the application of visual foundation models in more general time series tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/WHU-HZY/VIMTS.

paragraphs: Forecasting irregular multivariate time series is difficult because channels are not aligned in time and many observations are missing. Those gaps make reliable temporal patterns harder to learn. VIMTS adapts a visual masked autoencoder to this setting, drawing on its ability to reconstruct sparse information across multiple channels.

The framework first groups the irregular observations into feature patches at equal time intervals. It supplements those patches using learned relationships between channels, reducing the effect of missing values. The visual autoencoder then reconstructs patches, and a coarse-to-fine procedure turns focused contextual information into more precise predictions. Self-supervised learning further adapts the visual model to irregular time-series data.

Experiments report superior forecasting performance and strong few-shot capability. The approach matters because it provides a structured route for using a visual foundation model on data that does not arrive as a regularly sampled sequence. Its patch construction, cross-channel completion, and reconstruction stages work together to address the sparse, misaligned observations that motivate the method.
summary.tldr: VIMTS adapts visual masked autoencoders to irregular time series through temporal patches, cross-channel completion, and coarse-to-fine forecasting.

title: IMTS is Worth Time $\times$ Channel Patches: Visual Masked Autoencoders for Irregular Multivariate Time Series Prediction

abstract: Tokenization is a fundamental component of large language models (LLMs), yet its influence on model scaling and performance is not fully explored. In this paper, we introduce Over-Tokenized Transformers, a novel framework that decouples input and output vocabularies to improve language modeling performance. Specifically, our approach scales up input vocabularies to leverage multi-gram tokens. Through extensive experiments, we uncover a log-linear relationship between input vocabulary size and training loss, demonstrating that larger input vocabularies consistently enhance model performance, regardless of model size. Using a large input vocabulary, we achieve performance comparable to double-sized baselines with no additional cost. Our findings highlight the importance of tokenization in scaling laws and provide practical insight for tokenizer design, paving the way for more efficient and powerful LLMs.

paragraphs: Language-model scaling usually invites questions about model size and training data, but the vocabulary also shapes what the model receives. This paper investigates scaling the input vocabulary as a route to improved language modeling. Its Over-Tokenized Transformer framework separates the vocabularies used for input and output, allowing the input side to grow independently.

The expanded input vocabulary includes multi-gram tokens, representing groups of tokens as input units. Across extensive experiments, the authors find a log-linear relationship between input vocabulary size and training loss. Larger input vocabularies consistently improve performance across the model sizes studied, making vocabulary size an additional dimension to consider in scaling.

With a large input vocabulary, the method achieves performance comparable to baselines twice its size, with no additional cost as reported in the abstract. These findings suggest that input representation can materially affect the performance available from a model. They also motivate tokenizer design that considers the benefits of input-vocabulary expansion separately from decisions about the output vocabulary.
summary.tldr: Separating input and output vocabularies lets transformers benefit from larger multi-gram input vocabularies, improving performance across the tested model sizes.

title: Over-Tokenized Transformer: Vocabulary is Generally Worth Scaling

abstract: Recent studies on the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) have revealed that existing approaches often operate superficially, leaving models vulnerable to various adversarial attacks. Despite their significance, these studies generally fail to offer actionable solutions beyond data augmentation for achieving more robust safety mechanisms. This paper identifies a fundamental cause of this superficiality: existing alignment approaches often presume that models can implicitly learn a safety-related reasoning task during the alignment process, enabling them to refuse harmful requests. However, the learned safety signals are often diluted by other competing objectives, leading models to struggle with drawing a firm safety-conscious decision boundary when confronted with adversarial attacks. Based on this observation, by explicitly introducing a safety-related binary classification task and integrating its signals with our attention and decoding strategies, we eliminate this ambiguity and allow models to respond more responsibly to malicious queries. We emphasize that, with less than 0.2x overhead cost, our approach enables LLMs to assess the safety of both the query and the previously generated tokens at each necessary generating step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves the resilience of LLMs against various adversarial attacks, offering a promising pathway toward more robust generative AI systems.

paragraphs: This paper examines why safety alignment can remain vulnerable to adversarial requests. The authors identify a problem with expecting a model to learn safety-related reasoning implicitly during alignment: competing objectives can dilute the safety signal. As a result, the model may struggle to maintain a clear safety decision boundary under attack.

The proposed approach introduces an explicit binary safety-classification task and integrates its signals into attention and decoding. Safety assessment can then consider both the incoming query and tokens already generated at each necessary generation step. This makes the safety judgment an explicit part of the response-generation process rather than leaving it entirely implicit in alignment training.

The authors report an overhead cost below 0.2 times the original cost and significant improvements in resilience against various adversarial attacks. These findings support explicit safety signals as a practical way to strengthen the evaluated models’ responses to malicious queries. The reported improvement concerns resistance across tested attacks, while the mechanism addresses how safety information influences ongoing generation.
summary.tldr: Explicit safety classification integrated with attention and decoding improves reported attack resilience with less than 0.2 times additional overhead.

title: Safety Alignment Can Be Not Superficial With Explicit Safety Signals

abstract: We extend anytime constraints to the Markov game setting and the corresponding solution concept of anytime-constrained equilibrium (ACE). Then, we present a comprehensive theory of anytime-constrained equilibria that includes (1) a computational characterization of feasible policies, (2) a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for computing ACE, and (3) a polynomial-time algorithm for approximately computing ACE. Since computing a feasible policy is NP-hard even for two-player zero-sum games, our approximation guarantees are the best possible so long as $P \neq NP$. We also develop the first theory of efficient computation for action-constrained Markov games, which may be of independent interest.

The authors introduce an associated solution concept, an anytime-constrained equilibrium, to describe strategic behavior under these requirements.

Their theory addresses both whether a policy is feasible and how an equilibrium can be computed. It includes a computational characterization of feasible policies, a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for computing these equilibria, and a polynomial-time algorithm for approximate computation. These results provide different routes to computation, depending on whether one uses the parameterized formulation or accepts approximation.

The difficulty is substantial: even finding a feasible policy is NP-hard for two-player zero-sum games. The authors show that their approximation guarantees are the best possible under the assumption that P differs from NP. They also develop a theory of efficient computation for action-constrained Markov games. Together, the results clarify both the algorithms available for constrained strategic decision-making and the complexity barriers that shape their guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper defines anytime-constrained equilibria and gives computation and approximation algorithms with guarantees that are optimal assuming P differs from NP.

title: Anytime-Constrained Equilibria in Polynomial Time

abstract: This paper explores image modeling from the frequency space and introduces DCTdiff, an end-to-end diffusion generative paradigm that efficiently models images in the discrete cosine transform (DCT) space. We investigate the design space of DCTdiff and reveal the key design factors. Experiments on different frameworks (UViT, DiT), generation tasks, and various diffusion samplers demonstrate that DCTdiff outperforms pixel-based diffusion models regarding generative quality and training efficiency. Remarkably, DCTdiff can seamlessly scale up to 512$\times$512 resolution without using the latent diffusion paradigm and beats latent diffusion (using SD-VAE) with only 1/4 training cost. Finally, we illustrate several intriguing properties of DCT image modeling. For example, we provide a theoretical proof of why ‘image diffusion can be seen as spectral autoregression’, bridging the gap between diffusion and autoregressive models. The effectiveness of DCTdiff and the introduced properties suggest a promising direction for image modeling in the frequency space. The code is at https://github.com/forever208/DCTdiff.

Across these evaluations, the authors report better image quality and training efficiency than pixel-based diffusion models. summary.tldr: DCTdiff generates images in frequency space, improving reported quality and training efficiency while connecting diffusion to spectral autoregression.

title: DCTdiff: Intriguing Properties of Image Generative Modeling in the DCT Space

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) has demonstrated remarkable success in large language models (LLMs) due to its adaptability and parameter-free nature. However, it also introduces a critical vulnerability to backdoor attacks, where adversaries can manipulate LLM behaviors by simply poisoning a few ICL demonstrations. In this paper, we propose, for the first time, the dual-learning hypothesis, which posits that LLMs simultaneously learn both the task-relevant latent concepts and backdoor latent concepts within poisoned demonstrations, jointly influencing the probability of model outputs. Through theoretical analysis, we derive an upper bound for ICL backdoor effects, revealing that the vulnerability is dominated by the concept preference ratio between the task and the backdoor. Motivated by these findings, we propose ICLShield, a defense mechanism that dynamically adjusts the concept preference ratio. Our method encourages LLMs to select clean demonstrations during the ICL phase by leveraging confidence and similarity scores, effectively mitigating susceptibility to backdoor attacks. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and tasks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art defense effectiveness, significantly outperforming existing approaches (+26.02% on average). Furthermore, our method exhibits exceptional adaptability and defensive performance even for closed-source models (e.g., GPT-4).

This paper proposes a dual-learning hypothesis: a model can infer both the intended task concept and a malicious backdoor concept from the same demonstrations. title: ICLShield: Exploring and Mitigating In-Context Learning Backdoor Attacks

abstract: In this paper, we present a benchmark to pressure-test today’s frontier models’ multimodal decision-making capabilities in the very long-context regime (up to one million tokens) and investigate whether these models can learn from large numbers of expert demonstrations in their context. We evaluate the performance of Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash Experimental, GPT-4o, o1-mini, o1-preview, and o1 as policies across a battery of simple interactive decision-making tasks: playing tic-tac-toe, chess, and Atari, navigating grid worlds, solving crosswords, and controlling a simulated cheetah. We study increasing amounts of expert demonstrations in the context — from no demonstrations to 512 full episodes. Across our tasks, models rarely manage to fully reach expert performance, and often, presenting more demonstrations has little effect. Some models steadily improve with more demonstrations on a few tasks. We investigate the effect of encoding observations as text or images and the impact of chain-of-thought prompting. To help quantify the impact of other approaches and future innovations, we open source our benchmark that covers the zero-, few-, and many-shot regimes in a unified evaluation.

paragraphs: LMAct tests whether language models can learn to act from expert demonstrations placed directly in their context. It focuses on very long contexts, reaching one million tokens, and varies the demonstration count from none to 512 complete episodes. This makes it possible to examine whether supplying more examples translates into better interactive decision-making.

The benchmark evaluates frontier models across tic-tac-toe, chess, Atari, grid navigation, crosswords, and simulated cheetah control. Models serve as policies that choose actions in these tasks. The study also examines whether observations are represented as text or images and investigates the effect of chain-of-thought prompting.

Across the tasks, models rarely reach full expert performance, and adding demonstrations often has little effect. Some models improve steadily on a few tasks, so the results do not indicate uniformly absent learning. Instead, they expose an uneven ability to use long demonstration contexts. The open-source benchmark provides a unified way to compare zero-, few-, and many-demonstration performance as methods develop.
summary.tldr: LMAct finds that very long contexts of expert demonstrations often bring limited gains in tested models’ interactive decision-making.

title: LMAct: A Benchmark for In-Context Imitation Learning with Long Multimodal Demonstrations

abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) predominantly rely on decode-only transformer architectures, which exhibit exceptional in-context learning (ICL) capabilities. It is widely acknowledged that the cornerstone of their ICL ability lies in the induction heads mechanism, which necessitates at least two layers of attention. To more effectively harness the model’s induction capabilities, we revisit the induction heads mechanism and provide theoretical proof that KV shifting attention reduces the model’s dependency on the depth and width of the induction heads mechanism. Our experimental results confirm that KV shifting attention enhances the learning of induction heads and improves language modeling performance. This leads to superior performance or accelerated convergence, spanning from toy models to pre-trained models with over 10 billion parameters.

paragraphs: This paper investigates an attention mechanism associated with language models’ ability to learn from examples in their context. Its starting point is induction heads, which the abstract describes as a cornerstone of this ability and as requiring at least two attention layers. The authors ask whether this mechanism can be supported more efficiently.

They propose KV shifting attention and provide a theoretical proof that it reduces the induction-head mechanism’s dependence on model depth and width. The contribution therefore concerns how much architectural capacity is needed to support induction. It connects a change in attention to an analysis of the mechanism that the change is intended to improve.

Experiments report improved learning of induction heads together with better language modeling. The reported benefits take the form of superior performance or faster convergence, across settings ranging from toy models to pretrained models exceeding ten billion parameters. These results connect the theoretical motivation to observed training and modeling benefits across substantially different model scales.
summary.tldr: KV shifting attention reduces architectural demands on induction mechanisms and improves language modeling performance or convergence in experiments.

title: KV Shifting Attention Enhances Language Modeling

abstract: We propose a framework to combine strong non-linear expressiveness with strict SO(3)-equivariance in prediction of the electronic-structure Hamiltonian, by exploring the mathematical relationships between SO(3)-invariant and SO(3)-equivariant quantities and their representations. The proposed framework, called TraceGrad, first constructs theoretical SO(3)-invariant trace quantities derived from the Hamiltonian targets, and use these invariant quantities as supervisory labels to guide the learning of high-quality SO(3)-invariant features. Given that SO(3)-invariance is preserved under non-linear operations, the learning of invariant features can extensively utilize non-linear mappings, thereby fully capturing the non-linear patterns inherent in physical systems. Building on this, we propose a gradient-based mechanism to induce SO(3)-equivariant encodings of various degrees from the learned SO(3)-invariant features. This mechanism can incorporate powerful non-linear expressive capabilities into SO(3)-equivariant features with correspondence of physical dimensions to the regression targets, while theoretically preserving equivariant properties, establishing a strong foundation for predicting electronic-structure Hamiltonian. Experimental results on eight challenging benchmark databases demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in Hamiltonian prediction.

paragraphs: Predicting an electronic-structure Hamiltonian requires respecting how physical quantities change when a system rotates. TraceGrad aims to combine strict three-dimensional rotation equivariance with expressive nonlinear learning. Equivariance means that rotating the input produces the corresponding transformation in the output, preserving the relationship required by the physical prediction task.

The framework first derives rotation-invariant trace quantities from the target Hamiltonians and uses them as supervision. These quantities remain unchanged under rotation. Because nonlinear operations preserve invariance, the model can use rich nonlinear mappings while learning invariant features, capturing complex patterns without breaking that symmetry property.

A gradient-based mechanism then converts the learned invariant features into equivariant encodings of different degrees. The construction theoretically preserves equivariance while connecting the expressive learned features to representations appropriate for the regression targets. Experiments on eight benchmark databases report state-of-the-art Hamiltonian prediction performance. The contribution is a route from nonlinear invariant learning to symmetry-respecting outputs, supported by both the construction's theoretical properties and the reported prediction results.
summary.tldr: TraceGrad learns nonlinear rotation-invariant features and converts them through gradients into equivariant representations for accurate Hamiltonian prediction.

title: TraceGrad: a Framework Learning Expressive SO(3)-equivariant Non-linear Representations for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction

abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to learn semantically structured representations for discovering novel categories in unlabeled data using supervision from known classes. Most existing methods rely on self-supervised contrastive learning (CL) with consistency and uniformity objectives. We identify an inherent optimization conflict between these objectives: while uniformity enforces global feature dispersion, it can hinder the formation of class-discriminative and semantically coherent structures. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage framework that decouples representation learning from self-contrastive regularization. The first stage learns category-anchored representations aligned with known class prototypes, while the second stage extends the representation space to novel categories via a consistency objective enhanced with unified semantic regularization. We further introduce a Semantic Exploration Energy mechanism to capture shared semantics across categories and mitigate information loss caused by prototype orthogonalization. The resulting framework, termed Consistency-under-Unified Semantic Regularization(CURE), achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks and substantially reduces the performance gap between known and novel categories.
