paragraphs: Generalized category discovery uses labeled examples of known classes to help identify previously unseen categories in unlabeled data. The paper identifies a conflict in common contrastive-learning objectives: spreading features uniformly can interfere with organizing them into coherent, distinguishable classes. This creates tension between global dispersion and useful semantic structure.

CURE separates learning into two stages. The first builds representations anchored to prototypes of known classes. The second extends that representation space toward novel categories using consistency together with unified semantic regularization. This staged design separates representation learning from self-contrastive regularization, addressing the optimization conflict identified by the authors.

The framework also introduces Semantic Exploration Energy to capture meaning shared across categories and reduce information loss associated with making prototypes orthogonal. Across multiple benchmarks, CURE reports state-of-the-art performance and a substantially smaller performance gap between known and novel categories. The findings support organizing the representation space around semantic relationships while adapting it to categories that lack direct supervision.
summary.tldr: CURE separates representation learning into stages to preserve semantic structure and improve discovery of previously unseen categories.

title: CURE: Consistency-under-Unified Semantic Regularization for Generalized Category Discovery

abstract: Subgraph counting is a fundamental problem in graph analysis. Motivated by practical scenarios where graph analytics are performed on subgraphs induced by selected vertices – rather than on the entire graph – and by growing privacy concerns, we initiate the study of differentially private range subgraph counting (DPRSC). The goal is to privately count occurrences of a fixed pattern graph within induced subgraphs defined by multi-dimensional attribute ranges. Unlike classical point counting, subgraph counting is inherently nonlinear and exhibits high sensitivity: a single edge modification can affect many subgraph occurrences. We present the first efficient algorithms for DPRSC with small additive error. Our approach introduces a subgraph projection that reduces DPRSC to weighted orthogonal range counting, enabling the use of range trees and local sensitivity estimation to achieve accurate private query answering. We complement our algorithms with matching lower bounds, obtained by reducing reconstruction attacks to DPRSC and leveraging discrepancy theory. In particular, we show that any differentially private algorithm for DPRSC must incur additive error exponential in the dimension. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our algorithms significantly outperform baseline methods in accuracy and runtime while maintaining strong privacy guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to privately count graph patterns within portions of a graph selected by attribute ranges. A query first selects vertices whose attributes fall within specified ranges, then counts a fixed pattern in the graph induced by those vertices. Privacy is difficult because changing one edge can alter many pattern occurrences at once.

The authors introduce a subgraph projection that transforms this nonlinear counting problem into weighted orthogonal range counting. That transformation makes it possible to use range trees together with local sensitivity estimates to answer queries accurately while preserving differential privacy. The contribution is an efficient algorithmic route to a problem where directly protecting individual pattern counts is challenging.

In particular, it shows that private algorithms must incur additive error exponential in the number of attribute dimensions. This identifies an inherent cost of high-dimensional queries. Empirical evaluations report better accuracy and runtime than baseline methods while retaining strong privacy guarantees.
summary.tldr: A projection enables efficient private graph-pattern counting over attribute ranges, with lower bounds revealing an exponential cost in dimension.

title: Differentially Private Range Subgraph Counting

abstract: Recent approaches to real-time long video generation typically employ streaming tuning strategies, attempting to train a long-context student using a short-context (memoryless) teacher. In these frameworks, the student performs long rollouts but receives supervision from a teacher limited to short 5-second windows. This structural discrepancy creates a critical student-teacher mismatch: the teacher’s inability to access long-term history prevents it from guiding the student on global temporal dependencies, effectively capping the student’s context length. To resolve this, we propose Context Forcing, a novel framework that trains a long-context student via a long-context teacher. By ensuring the teacher is aware of the full generation history, we eliminate the supervision mismatch, enabling the robust training of models capable of long-term consistency. To make this computationally feasible for extreme durations (e.g., 2 minute), we introduce a context management system that transforms the linearly growing context into a Slow-Fast Memory architecture, significantly reducing visual redundancy. Extensive results demonstrate that our method enables effective context lengths exceeding 20 seconds—$6\text{–}10\times$ longer than state-of-the-art methods like LongLive and Infinite-RoPE. By leveraging this extended context, Context Forcing preserves superior consistency across long durations, surpassing state-of-the-art baselines on various long video evaluation metrics.

paragraphs: A video generator needs access to earlier events to maintain consistency over long sequences. The paper identifies a mismatch in streaming training methods: a student produces long rollouts, but its teacher supervises only short, five-second windows. A teacher without the longer history cannot guide dependencies that extend beyond those windows, limiting the student’s effective use of context.

Context Forcing trains the student with a teacher that also has long context and is aware of the full generation history. The key finding connects supervision and memory: longer history becomes useful when the teacher can supervise its consequences and the system can manage that history computationally.
summary.tldr: Context Forcing combines a long-context teacher with compressed memory to improve consistency in long autoregressive video generation.

title: Context Forcing: Consistent Autoregressive Video Generation with Long Context

abstract: Graph neural networks often degrade on heterophilous graphs because repeated neighbor aggregation can reinforce self-aligned low-frequency components while suppressing phase-inconsistent signals. We propose GESC, a complex-valued graph network that augments attention-based message passing with gauge-consistent U(1) transport and projection-based self-interference cancellation. For each transported neighbor message, GESC removes the component parallel to the target representation before computing attention and applies a sign-aware gate based on gauge-invariant complex alignment. We prove gauge equivariance of the hidden update and derive coefficient-frozen stability bounds showing that SIC contracts self-parallel message components. On nine benchmarks, GESC ranks first on seven datasets and remains within the top three on the other two. These results suggest that explicit self-parallel cancellation is an effective mechanism for improving message passing under heterophily. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChoiYoonHyuk/GESC.

paragraphs: Graph networks can struggle under heterophily, where connected nodes need not have similar properties. The paper identifies a mechanism in repeated neighbor aggregation: components aligned with a node's own representation can become reinforced while signals with inconsistent phases are suppressed. GESC changes how neighbor messages are processed to reduce this self-reinforcement.

GESC uses complex-valued representations and transports messages consistently under U(1) phase transformations. For each transported neighbor message, it removes the component parallel to the target node's representation before computing attention. A sign-aware gate then uses complex alignment that is invariant to these transformations. This design combines consistent handling of phase with explicit cancellation of self-parallel message content.

The authors prove that the hidden update is gauge-equivariant and derive stability bounds with coefficients held fixed, showing contraction of self-parallel message components. On nine benchmarks, GESC ranks first on seven and in the top three on the remaining two. These results suggest that cancelling this specific component can improve message passing under heterophily, alongside the stated symmetry and conditional stability results.
summary.tldr: GESC improves evaluated heterophilous graph learning by cancelling self-parallel neighbor-message components within a gauge-equivariant complex-valued network.

title: Gauge-Equivariant Graph Networks via Self-Interference Cancellation

abstract: Outlier detection (OD) is widely used in practice; but its effective deployment on new tasks is hindered by lack of labeled outliers, which makes algorithm and hyperparameter selection notoriously hard. Foundation models (FMs) have transformed ML, and OD is no exception: Shen et al. (2025) introduced FOMO-0D, the first FM for OD, achieving remarkable performance against numerous baselines. This work introduces OUTFORMER, which advances FOMO-0D with (1) a mixture of synthetic priors and (2) self-evolving curriculum training. OUTFORMER is pretrained solely on synthetic labeled datasets and infers test labels of a new task by using its training data as in-context input. Inference is fast and zero-shot, requiring merely forward pass and no labeled outliers. Thanks to in-context learning, it requires zero additional work—no OD model training or bespoke model selection—enabling truly plug-and-play deployment. OUTFORMER achieves state-of-the-art performance on the prominent ADBench, as well as two new large-scale OD benchmarks that we introduce, comprising over 1,500 datasets, while maintaining speedy inference.

OUTFORMER achieves state-of-the-art performance on the prominent ADBench, as well as two new large-scale OD benchmarks that we introduce, comprising over 1,500 datasets, while maintaining speedy inference.

paragraphs: Outlier detection is difficult to configure for a new dataset when labeled anomalies are unavailable. Without those labels, selecting an algorithm and its settings becomes challenging. OUTFORMER addresses this deployment problem with a foundation model pretrained to perform tabular outlier detection using examples supplied directly in its input context.

The method advances FOMO-0D through a mixture of synthetic priors and a self-evolving training curriculum. Pretraining uses only synthetic labeled datasets. For a new task, the model takes that task's training data as context and predicts labels for test examples through a forward pass. This requires no labeled outliers, additional outlier-model training, or bespoke model selection at deployment.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on ADBench and on two newly introduced large-scale outlier-detection benchmarks comprising more than 1,500 datasets, while retaining fast inference. These findings support synthetic pretraining and in-context learning as a practical combination for transferring outlier detection to new tasks. Here, zero-shot deployment still uses the new task's data as context.
summary.tldr: OUTFORMER uses synthetic pretraining and in-context learning for fast tabular outlier detection without task-specific training or labeled outliers.

title: From Zero to Hero: Advancing Zero-Shot Foundation Models for Tabular Outlier Detection

abstract: Cross-subject generalization in biomedical time-series aims to learn representations that generalize to unseen subjects while suppressing subject-specific variability. Most existing methods implicitly suppress the variability through model building or subject adversarial learning, but rarely model it explicitly. We introduce spectral drift as a new perspective to characterize subject specific variability. Specifically, BTS signals under the same label often share consistent oscillatory structure, yet exhibit subject-dependent magnitude or phase shifts in specific frequency components, which we interpret as subject-specific variability. Building on this insight, we propose BioFormer. At its core is a Frequency-Band Alignment Module (FBAM) that generates band-wise modulation factors from the spectral distribution and adaptively adjusts amplitude and phase to align spectral structure, thereby mitigating variability. We further pair FBAM with Sample Conditional Layer Normalization, which infers normalization parameters from intrinsic signal statistics rather than subject identity, stabilizing cross-subject representations. Extensive experiments on six datasets demonstrate that BioFormer outperforms 12 baselines, yielding absolute F1-score improvements of 6%.

BioFormer also derives normalization parameters from each signal’s own statistics instead of subject identity. This complements frequency alignment by stabilizing representations across people. Across six datasets, the paper reports performance above 12 baselines, with absolute F1-score improvements of 6%. These results support explicitly modeling spectral variation as a useful route to cross-subject generalization.
summary.tldr: BioFormer improves cross-subject biomedical prediction by aligning frequency structure and normalizing signals using their intrinsic statistics.

title: BioFormer: Rethinking Cross-Subject Generalization via Spectral Structural Alignment in Biomedical Time-Series

abstract: Instance-wise feature selection is a valuable tool for interpreting labeled data and the predictions of black-box models. In contrast to global feature selection techniques, instance-wise methods dynamically identify important features for each instance. A growing number of methods learn a selector, which identifies important features, and a predictor, which uses these to make predictions. However, these pioneering methods face challenges including information leakage and lack of differentiability, which can slow training. In this paper, we present Hide&Seek, an end-to-end differentiable model for instance-wise feature selection. We jointly learn feature selection and prediction under a single objective without information leakage. Hide&Seek outperforms existing state-of-the-art models across a range of experiments and is fast to train. We achieve this by reformulating feature removal as a differentiable operation where instead of discretely removing features, we replace a proportion of each feature. Training is further stabilized via a parsimony-weight annealing framework.

paragraphs: Instance-wise feature selection identifies which inputs matter for each individual example. This can help explain labeled data or the predictions of a black-box model. A common approach trains a selector to choose features and a predictor to use them, but existing methods can suffer from information leakage and operations that are difficult to differentiate.

Hide&Seek jointly learns selection and prediction under a single objective. Its main change is to make feature removal continuous: it replaces a proportion of each feature instead of making an entirely discrete removal decision. That reformulation permits end-to-end differentiation, allowing the selector and predictor to be optimized together within the same training process.

The authors also gradually adjust the weight encouraging parsimonious feature use to stabilize training. They report that the resulting model avoids information leakage, trains quickly, and outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches across their experiments. The contribution connects an explanation mechanism to a practical optimization strategy: learning which features to retain becomes part of the differentiable prediction process.
summary.tldr: Hide&Seek learns per-example feature explanations through differentiable partial feature replacement, jointly training selection and prediction without information leakage.

title: Hide&Seek: Learning to Explain in an End-to-End Differentiable Network

abstract: Time series forecasting fundamentally involves learning probability distributions over future observations. However, existing loss functions rely on point-wise Euclidean metrics, neglecting the intrinsic geometric structure of probability distributions. This leads to suboptimal alignment between predicted and true distributions, particularly for uncertainty quantification. We propose InfoGeo Loss, a principled loss function grounded in information geometry that measures distributional discrepancies on statistical manifolds. Our approach comprises three key components: (1) a distribution parameterization module that models predictions with learnable sufficient statistics, (2) a Fisher information metric that quantifies intrinsic distributional distance, and (3) a Bregman divergence component that captures asymmetric prediction errors. We further introduce a natural gradient weighting strategy for efficient optimization on statistical manifolds. Theoretically, we prove statistical consistency and establish convergence guarantees. Extensive experiments on seven datasets with five architectures show that InfoGeo Loss consistently outperforms existing losses, achieving average improvements of 6.8% in MSE and 5.3% in MAE.

paragraphs: InfoGeo Loss treats forecasting as learning distributions over future observations. The paper argues that pointwise Euclidean errors overlook the geometry of those distributions, making predicted and true distributions harder to align, especially for uncertainty quantification. Its proposed loss therefore evaluates discrepancies using the structure of the statistical space in which the distributions live.

A Fisher information metric measures intrinsic distributional distance, while a Bregman divergence accounts for asymmetric prediction errors. Experiments spanning seven datasets and five architectures report consistent improvements over existing losses, averaging 6.8% in MSE and 5.3% in MAE. These results indicate that a distribution-oriented training objective can also improve the conventional pointwise forecasting metrics used in the evaluation.
summary.tldr: InfoGeo Loss uses probability-distribution geometry to train forecasters, improving average MSE and MAE across the reported evaluations.

title: Information Geometry Loss for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Transformers have revolutionized deep learning across various domains but understanding the precise token dynamics remains a theoretical challenge. Existing theories of deep Transformers with layer normalization typically predict that tokens cluster to a single point; however, these results rely on deterministic weight assumptions, which fail to capture the standard initialization scheme in Transformers. In this work, we show that accounting for the intrinsic stochasticity of random initialization alters this picture. More precisely, we analyze deep Transformers where noise arises from the random initialization of value matrices. Under diffusion scaling and token-wise RMS normalization, we prove that, as the number of Transformer layers goes to infinity, the discrete token dynamics converge to an interacting-particle system on the sphere where tokens are driven by a common matrix-valued Brownian noise. In this limit, we show that initialization noise prevents the collapse to a single cluster predicted by deterministic models. For two tokens, we prove a phase transition governed by the interaction strength and the token dimension: unlike deterministic attention flows, antipodal configurations become attracting with positive probability. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted transition, reveal that antipodal formations persist for more than two tokens, and demonstrate that suppressing the intrinsic noise degrades accuracy.

paragraphs: Some mathematical accounts of deep Transformers predict that token representations eventually collapse into a single cluster. This paper revisits that prediction by including randomness from the initialization of value matrices. The authors argue that deterministic weight assumptions miss a source of stochastic behavior present in standard Transformer initialization.

Their analysis considers token-wise RMS normalization and a particular diffusion scaling as the number of layers tends to infinity. Under those conditions, discrete token updates converge to an interacting-particle system on a sphere. All tokens experience a shared matrix-valued Brownian noise. Within this limiting system, initialization noise prevents the single-cluster collapse predicted by deterministic models.

For two tokens, the authors prove a phase transition controlled by interaction strength and representation dimension. The result makes initialization randomness part of the explanation of token organization, rather than an incidental detail.
summary.tldr: Under an infinite-depth stochastic model, random initialization prevents token collapse and can make opposite-point token configurations attracting.

title: Clustering in Deep Stochastic Transformers

abstract: Model soups are strange and strangely effective combinations of parameters. They take a model (the stock), fine-tune it into multiple models (the ingredients), and then mix their parameters back into one model (the soup) to improve predictions. While all known soups require supervised learning, and optimize the same loss on labeled data, our recipes for Self-Soupervision generalize soups to self-supervised learning (SSL). Our Self-Souping lets us flavor ingredients on new data sources, e.g. from unlabeled data from a task for transfer or from a shift for robustness. We show that Self-Souping on corrupted test data, then fine-tuning back on uncorrupted train data, boosts robustness by +3.5% (ImageNet-C) and +7% (LAION-C). Self-Soupervision also unlocks countless SSL algorithms to cook the diverse ingredients needed for more robust soups. We show for the first time that ingredients can differ in their SSL hyperparameters—and more surprisingly, in their SSL algorithms. We cook soups of MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, and LeJEPA ingredients that are more accurate than any single SSL ingredient.

paragraphs: A model soup combines the parameters of several models adapted from a common starting model into one model. Existing recipes have relied on supervised learning with a shared loss on labeled data. Self-Soupervision extends the approach to self-supervised learning, allowing unlabeled data to shape the models being combined.

Self-Souping can adapt ingredients to a new task’s unlabeled data or to data reflecting a distribution shift. In one reported procedure, the models use corrupted test data before being fine-tuned back on uncorrupted training data. This improves robustness by 3.5% on ImageNet-C and 7% on LAION-C, connecting unlabeled adaptation with resilience to corruption.

The paper also demonstrates that ingredients can differ in their self-supervised hyperparameters and even their learning algorithms. Soups combining MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, and LeJEPA ingredients are more accurate than any individual ingredient in the reported experiments. This expands the sources of useful diversity available for parameter averaging, beyond models trained with the same supervised objective.
summary.tldr: Self-Soupervision extends parameter-averaged model soups to unlabeled adaptation and mixtures of different self-supervised learning algorithms.

title: Self-Soupervision: Cooking Model Soups without Labels

abstract: Weak-to-strong generalization provides a promising paradigm for scaling large language models (LLMs) by training stronger models on samples from aligned weaker ones, without requiring human feedback or explicit reward modeling. However, its robustness and generalization are hindered by the noise and biases in weak-model outputs, which limit its applicability in practice. To address this challenge, we leverage implicit rewards, which approximate explicit rewards through log-likelihood ratios, and reveal their structural equivalence with Contrastive Decoding (CD), a decoding strategy shown to reduce noise in LLM generation. Building on this connection, we propose Contrastive Weak-to-Strong Generalization (ConG), a framework that employs contrastive decoding between pre- and post-alignment weak models to generate higher-quality samples. This approach enables more reliable capability transfer, denoising, and improved robustness, substantially mitigating the limitations of traditional weak-to-strong methods. Empirical results across different model families confirm consistent improvements, demonstrating the generality and effectiveness of ConG. Taken together, our findings highlight the potential of ConG to advance weak-to-strong generalization and provide a promising pathway toward AGI. Our code is available at: https://github.com/jianghoucheng/ConG

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization trains a more capable language model using examples produced by a weaker aligned model. This offers a way to transfer alignment without human feedback or a separately trained reward model. However, the weaker model's samples can carry noise and bias, making the quality of those training examples a central obstacle to reliable transfer.

The paper connects two ideas: implicit rewards expressed through log-likelihood ratios, and contrastive decoding, which compares model predictions during generation. It identifies a structural equivalence between them and builds ConG around that connection. ConG generates examples by contrasting a weak model before and after alignment, using the difference between those versions to obtain higher-quality samples for the stronger model.

Across different model families, the authors report consistent improvements in weak-to-strong generalization, including better denoising and robustness. The contribution is a method for improving the supervision supplied by a weak model through the generation process itself. These experiments support its applicability across the tested families, while the broader promise for more capable AI remains prospective.
summary.tldr: ConG contrasts weak models before and after alignment to generate cleaner training examples for stronger models.

title: Contrastive Weak-to-Strong Generalization

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) offers a privacy-preserving pathway for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs); however, existing frameworks typically enforce a monolithic reward model, inevitably averaging out inherently conflicting user preferences (e.g., helpfulness vs. harmlessness). While Variational Preference Learning (VPL) offers a pathway to personalization, adapting it to decentralized settings presents a fundamental challenge: posterior collapse driven by severe local data scarcity and heterogeneity. In this paper, we propose Federated Variational Preference Alignment with Gumbel-Softmax Prior (FedVPA-GP), a framework designed to disentangle diverse preferences without compromising privacy. To stabilize variational inference, we introduce a Federated Mixture Prior that enables clients to leverage the aggregate population distribution as a dynamic prior. Furthermore, we incorporate an Orthogonal Loss that explicitly enforces the separation of preference prototypes in the latent space. Experiments on the HH-RLHF dataset demonstrate that FedVPA-GP significantly outperforms monolithic baselines, successfully disentangling conflicting user intents and enabling dynamic preference switching.

paragraphs: A shared reward model can average together preferences that different users want kept distinct. This paper studies personalized language-model alignment in federated learning, where preferences are learned across decentralized clients. Its central challenge is that small, heterogeneous local datasets can cause posterior collapse, undermining a variational model’s ability to represent different preferences.

FedVPA-GP addresses this with a Federated Mixture Prior. Each client can draw on an aggregate population distribution as a changing prior, helping stabilize local variational inference. The framework also adds an Orthogonal Loss that explicitly separates preference prototypes in the latent representation. These mechanisms aim to preserve distinct user preferences while supporting personalization in the federated setting.

Experiments on the HH-RLHF dataset show significant improvements over monolithic baselines. The authors report that the method separates conflicting user intents and supports dynamic switching between preferences. The result matters because personalization requires more than fitting an average judgment: the model must retain distinguishable alternatives that can guide different behavior. The reported evidence supports that capability on the evaluated dataset.
summary.tldr: FedVPA-GP uses a shared population prior and separated preference prototypes to improve personalized federated alignment and support preference switching.

title: Federated Variational Preference Alignment with Gumbel-Softmax Prior for Personalized User Preferences

abstract: Hazard and survival functions are natural, interpretable targets in time-to-event prediction tasks such as patient survival and disease progression modeling, but their inherent non-additivity fundamentally limits standard additive explanation methods. We introduce Survival Functional Decomposition (SurvFD), a principled approach for analyzing feature interactions in machine learning survival models. By decomposing higher-order effects into time-dependent and time-independent components, SurvFD offers a previously unrecognized perspective on survival explanations, explicitly characterizing when and why additive explanations fail. Building on this theoretical decomposition, we propose SurvSHAP-IQ, which extends Shapley interactions to time-indexed functions, providing a practical estimator for higher-order, time-dependent interactions. We validate the framework on simulated data and demonstrate its utility through cancer survival applications, including multi-modal breast cancer prognosis combining histopathology with clinical features. Together, SurvFD and SurvSHAP-IQ establish an interaction- and time-aware interpretability approach for survival modeling, with broad applicability across medicine, healthcare and other time-to-event prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Survival models predict how events unfold over time, with hazard and survival functions serving as natural explanation targets. These functions are inherently non-additive, which limits explanations that assign separate contributions to features and simply add them together. The paper investigates how interactions between features contribute to this difficulty.

Survival Functional Decomposition, or SurvFD, separates higher-order effects into components that depend on time and components that do not. This provides a way to characterize when and why additive explanations fail. Building on that decomposition, SurvSHAP-IQ extends Shapley interaction analysis to functions indexed by time, giving a practical estimator of interactions among multiple features as predictions evolve.

The authors validate the framework on simulated data and demonstrate applications to cancer survival, including breast cancer prognosis using both histopathology and clinical features. These applications show how the framework can examine joint feature effects in multimodal survival models. Its central contribution is an explanation approach that treats feature interactions and their time dependence as explicit parts of the prediction.
summary.tldr: SurvFD and SurvSHAP-IQ explain survival predictions by separating and estimating feature interactions that may change over time.

title: Functional Decomposition and Shapley Interactions for Interpreting Survival Models

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have inherent limitations of faithfulness and factuality, commonly referred to as hallucinations. Several benchmarks have been developed that provide a test bed for factuality evaluation within the context of English-centric datasets, while relying on supplementary informative context like web links or text passages but ignoring the available structured factual resources. To this end, Knowledge Graphs (KGs) have been identified as a useful aid for hallucination mitigation, as they provide a structured way to represent the facts about entities and their relations with minimal linguistic overhead. We bridge the lack of KG paths and multilinguality for factual language modeling within the existing hallucination evaluation benchmarks and propose a KG-based multilingual, multihop benchmark called MultiHal framed for generative text evaluation. As part of our data collection pipeline, we mined 140k KG-paths from open-domain KGs, from which we pruned noisy KG-paths, curating a high-quality subset of 25.9k. Our baseline evaluation shows an absolute scale improvement by approximately 0.12 to 0.36 points for the semantic similarity score, 0.16 to 0.36 for NLI entailment and 0.29 to 0.42 for hallucination detection in KG-RAG over vanilla QA across multiple languages and multiple models, demonstrating the potential of KG integration. We anticipate MultiHal will foster future research towards several graph-based hallucination mitigation and fact-checking tasks.

paragraphs: Many hallucination benchmarks concentrate on English and ground factual evaluation in text passages or web links. MultiHal adds multilingual evaluation based on knowledge graphs, which represent entities and their relationships in a structured form. Its multihop design uses paths through these relationships to support evaluation of generated text.

The collection pipeline begins with 140,000 paths mined from open-domain knowledge graphs. After removing noisy paths, the authors retain a curated subset of 25,900. This gives the benchmark a factual structure that can connect several relationships while supporting evaluation across languages, addressing two gaps identified in existing benchmark coverage.

Reported absolute score improvements range from approximately 0.12–0.36 for semantic similarity, 0.16–0.36 for entailment, and 0.29–0.42 for hallucination detection. summary.tldr: MultiHal evaluates multilingual factual generation using curated knowledge-graph paths and finds benefits from graph-grounded retrieval.

title: MultiHal: Multilingual Dataset for Knowledge-Graph Grounded Evaluation of LLM Hallucinations

abstract: The rise of auto-bidding in online advertising has created new challenges for ensuring advertiser incentive compatibility, particularly when advertisers delegate bidding to agents with high-level constraints. One challenge is the multiplicity of equilibria with reported constraints. Alimohammadi et al. (2023) proposed a notion of Auto-bidding Incentive Compatibility (AIC) which serves to highlight that standard auctions may not incentivize truthful reporting of these constraints. However, their definition of AIC is very stringent as it requires that the worst-case outcome of an advertiser’s truthful report is at least as good as the best-case outcome of any of the advertiser’s possible deviations. In this paper, we introduce two refined and relaxed concepts: Risk-Averse Auto-bidding Incentive Compatibility (RAIC) and Optimistic Auto-bidding Incentive Compatibility (OAIC). RAIC (OAIC) stipulates that truthful reporting is preferred if its least (most) favorable equilibrium outcome is no worse than the least (most) favorable equilibrium outcome from any misreport. We demonstrate that SPA satisfies both RAIC and OAIC. These findings clarify SPA’s incentive properties under auto-bidding, specifically regarding advertiser perspectives on equilibrium selection.

paragraphs: When advertisers delegate bidding to automated agents, they report high-level constraints that influence auction outcomes. A complication is that the same reports can support multiple equilibria. Whether truthful reporting is attractive therefore depends partly on how an advertiser evaluates the range of possible equilibrium outcomes.

An existing incentive-compatibility definition requires the worst truthful outcome to be at least as good as the best outcome obtainable through any misreport. The paper introduces two weaker comparisons. Risk-Averse Auto-bidding Incentive Compatibility compares the worst truthful outcome with the worst outcome under each misreport. Optimistic Auto-bidding Incentive Compatibility instead compares the best truthful outcome with the best outcome under each misreport.

The authors show that the second-price auction satisfies both refined notions. This clarifies its incentive properties for advertisers who assess equilibrium possibilities pessimistically or optimistically. The result preserves the distinction between those perspectives and the stronger earlier requirement: it establishes truthfulness under the two specified comparisons, rather than resolving equilibrium selection through a single universal criterion.
summary.tldr: Second-price auctions satisfy two relaxed truthfulness criteria that compare equilibrium outcomes from risk-averse or optimistic advertiser perspectives.

title: Risk-Averse and Optimistic Advertiser Incentive Compatibility in Auto-bidding

abstract: Existing Cross-Tokenizer Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) methods can fail to outperform simple supervised fine-tuning when vocabulary overlap is low due to severe alignment noise. We identify this phenomenon as the “Low-Overlap negative transfer regime”. To overcome this, we propose Entropy-aware Span-Constrained Optimal Transport (E-SCOT), a robust framework that treats distillation as a sparse transport problem built upon a vocabulary-agnostic ground metric. Unlike prior OT approaches that incur quadratic costs via dense sequence-level optimization, E-SCOT employs span-anchored lexical alignment to construct a deterministic, locality-preserving support set in linear time with respect to sequence length. Furthermore, we introduce Rényi-entropy adaptive reweighting to dynamically concentrate the distillation budget on informative positions exhibiting significant uncertainty-profile gaps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that E-SCOT achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse model families, effectively eliminating negative transfer even in challenging low-overlap scenarios.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers information between models, but different tokenizers can make their predictions difficult to align. When their vocabularies overlap little, noisy correspondences can make distillation perform worse than ordinary supervised fine-tuning. The paper identifies this as a low-overlap negative-transfer regime and develops E-SCOT to address it.

E-SCOT treats alignment as a sparse transport problem using a comparison measure that does not depend on shared vocabulary. It anchors lexical matches to text spans, restricting which correspondences are considered and preserving locality. An entropy-based weighting mechanism then directs more distillation effort toward informative positions with substantial differences in uncertainty profiles.

Across experiments involving diverse model families, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and elimination of negative transfer in the tested low-overlap settings. The findings show why both correspondence quality and selective allocation of the learning signal matter when transferring knowledge across incompatible tokenizations.
summary.tldr: E-SCOT combines sparse span alignment with uncertainty-based weighting to improve distillation between models with different tokenizers.

title: Entropy-aware Span-Constrained Optimal Transport for Robust Cross-Tokenizer Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) excel in semantic recognition but exhibit systematic failures in spatial reasoning tasks such as mental rotation. While often attributed to data scale, this work argues that the limitation arises from the intrinsic circuit complexity of the architecture. By formalizing spatial understanding as a Group Homomorphism Problem—where latent embeddings preserve the algebraic structure of physical transformations acting on images—we identify a fundamental computational bottleneck. Specifically, for non-solvable groups (e.g., $\mathrm{SO}(3)$), maintaining such structure-preserving embeddings is lower-bounded by the Word Problem, which is $\mathsf{NC^1}$-complete. In contrast, constant-depth ViTs with polynomial precision are strictly bounded by the complexity class $\mathsf{TC^0}$. Under the standard conjecture $\mathsf{TC^0} \subsetneq \mathsf{NC^1}$, a complexity boundary emerges: constant-depth architectures lack the logical depth required to capture non-solvable spatial structures in a single forward pass. To empirically validate this theoretical gap, we propose the Latent Space Algebra (LSA) benchmark, which reveals a significant degradation in ViT representations as the compositional depth of non-solvable tasks increases.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can recognize image content while struggling with spatial operations such as mental rotation. This paper investigates an architectural explanation for that gap. It formalizes spatial understanding as preserving the algebra of physical transformations inside image embeddings: composing transformations should have a corresponding structure in the representation.

For non-solvable transformation groups, including three-dimensional rotations, the authors connect this requirement to an NC¹-complete Word Problem. Constant-depth Vision Transformers with polynomial precision are instead bounded by TC⁰. Under the conjecture that TC⁰ is strictly weaker than NC¹, this creates a computational boundary: those architectures do not have enough logical depth to preserve the relevant spatial structure in one forward pass.

The authors introduce the Latent Space Algebra benchmark to examine the predicted gap empirically. Representations degrade substantially as the compositional depth of non-solvable tasks increases. The conclusion is specifically tied to the stated architecture, precision, and complexity conjecture. It suggests that increasing data alone may not resolve this form of spatial reasoning when the model's computational depth remains constrained.
summary.tldr: Under a standard complexity conjecture, constant-depth Vision Transformers face a structural limit in representing certain composed spatial transformations.

title: On the Intrinsic Limits of Transformer Image Embeddings in Non-Solvable Spatial Reasoning

abstract: Abstract reasoning ability reflects the intelligence and generalization capacity of LLMs to extract and apply abstract rules. However, accurately measuring this ability remains challenging: existing benchmarks either rely on expensive manual annotation, limiting their scale, or risk measuring memorization rather than genuine reasoning. To address this, we introduce an automated pipeline named A$^2$RBench, encompassing generation, expansion, evaluation, and analysis. Specifically, in the generation stage, LLMs create diverse tasks demanding genuine reasoning; in the expansion stage, LLMs reuse validated rules and expand new input spaces to generate task variations, achieving scaling. However, such a process may cause hallucinations. To eliminate it, we further establish a theoretical framework and prove that programmatic verification—testing whether the inverse operation perfectly reverses the forward operation (cycle consistency)—guarantees a unique solution. Through extensive evaluations on mainstream LLMs, we find: (1) Current LLMs exhibit fundamental deficiencies in abstract reasoning, with top models significantly underperforming humans on a representative subset (39.8% vs. 68.5%). (2) Current LLMs fall far short of 2D and 1D in the complexity of generated 3D tasks, revealing their lack of understanding of high-dimensional tasks. (3) Counterintuitively, inputs with higher information complexity can simplify the reasoning process. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/MAC-AutoML/A2Rbench.

paragraphs: A²RBench tackles a measurement problem: how to test whether language models can discover and apply abstract rules without relying on costly manual task creation or inadvertently testing memorization. Its automated pipeline covers task generation, expansion, evaluation, and analysis, making benchmark construction part of the research contribution.

Language models first generate reasoning tasks, then expand them by applying validated rules to new input spaces. Because generated examples can contain errors, the authors introduce programmatic verification. Within their theoretical framework, they prove that cycle consistency—an inverse operation perfectly undoing a forward operation—guarantees a unique solution. This gives the expansion process a formal check on answer uniqueness.

Evaluations reveal substantial weaknesses in the tested models. On a representative subset, top models score 39.8%, compared with 68.5% for humans. Models also struggle to generate comparably complex three-dimensional tasks relative to one- and two-dimensional tasks. Another finding complicates intuitive difficulty estimates: inputs containing more information can sometimes make the underlying rule easier to infer.
summary.tldr: A²RBench automatically generates and verifies abstract reasoning tasks, exposing substantial gaps between tested language models and human performance.

title: A$^2$RBench: An Automatic Paradigm for Formally Verifiable Abstract Reasoning Benchmark Generation

abstract: Instruction fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) often involves selecting a subset of instruction training data from a large candidate pool, using a small query set from the target task. Despite growing interest, the literature on targeted instruction selection remains fragmented and opaque: methods vary widely in selection budgets, often omit zero-shot baselines, and frequently entangle the contributions of key components. As a result, practitioners lack actionable guidance on selecting instructions for their target tasks. In this work, we aim to bring clarity to this landscape by disentangling and systematically analyzing the two core ingredients: data representation and selection algorithms. Our framework enables controlled comparisons across models, tasks, and budgets. We find that only gradient-based data representations choose subsets whose similarity to the query consistently predicts performance across datasets,models, and candidate pools. While no single method dominates, gradient-based representations paired with greedy round-robin selection often perform best on average at low budgets, but these gains diminish at larger budgets. Finally, we unify several existing selection algorithms as forms of approximate distance minimization between the selected subset and the query set, and support this view with new generalization bounds. More broadly, our findings provide critical insights and a foundation for more principled data selection in LLM fine-tuning. The code is available at https://github.com/dcml-lab/targeted-instruction-selection.

paragraphs: Targeted instruction selection uses a few examples of a desired task to choose training instructions from a larger pool. Comparing selection methods has been difficult because studies use different budgets, sometimes omit zero-shot comparisons, and combine several design choices. This paper introduces a framework that separates how examples are represented from how a subset is selected, enabling controlled comparisons across models, tasks, and budgets.

In these comparisons, only gradient-based representations consistently make similarity between the selected subset and the query set predictive of performance. These representations describe examples through their relationship to model updates. Pairing them with greedy round-robin selection often gives the strongest average results when selection budgets are small. However, no method wins everywhere, and the advantages shrink at larger budgets.

The authors also connect several existing selection algorithms through a shared interpretation: approximately minimizing distance between the selected data and the query examples. New generalization bounds support this interpretation. Together, the results clarify when matching a training subset to a target task is informative and why the available selection budget matters.
summary.tldr: Controlled comparisons clarify when gradient-based representations help targeted instruction selection, with advantages strongest at small selection budgets.

title: A Critical Look at Targeted Instruction Selection: Disentangling What Matters (and What Doesn’t)

abstract: Tensor Product Representations provide the structural fidelity required for symbolic reasoning in models but suffer from exponential dimensionality growth when encoding deep recursive structures. Conversely, Vector Symbolic Architectures maintain constant dimensionality but sacrifice capacity and fidelity due to noisy compression via superposition. In this work, we propose Orthogonal Subspace Carving (OSC), a memory architecture that binds fillers to roles by projecting onto the null space of the role basis before aggregating into a fixed order-$p$ tensor. OSC uses projections to enforce geometric orthogonality between bound structures within a static memory trace. We show that this mechanism decouples the tensor order from the structural depth, enabling deep recursive binding within a constant memory footprint. This construction allows for component vectors that are orders of magnitude smaller than the memory tensor, giving excellent memory efficiency in settings involving high superposition. We also show that TPR is a special case of binding in Clifford algebra, and give a Clifford formulation of OSC.

paragraphs: Representing nested symbolic structures creates a memory trade-off. Tensor Product Representations preserve structure but grow exponentially with recursive depth. Vector Symbolic Architectures keep a fixed dimensionality, but compression through superposition introduces noise that reduces capacity and fidelity. This paper proposes a different geometric way to organize recursive bindings.

These projections enforce orthogonality between bound structures within a static memory trace. The construction separates tensor order from structural depth, allowing deeper recursive binding without increasing the memory footprint.

The authors also show that component vectors can be orders of magnitude smaller than the memory tensor, yielding strong memory efficiency when many structures are superposed. A further mathematical contribution expresses Tensor Product Representations as a special case of binding in Clifford algebra and formulates OSC in that language. The work connects compact recursive memory to explicit geometric organization of its contents.
summary.tldr: Orthogonal Subspace Carving uses geometric projections to encode deep recursive bindings in a fixed-order tensor with constant memory footprint.

title: Recursive Binding on a Budget: Subspace Carving in Order-$p$ Tensor Memories

abstract: The choice of training objective is central to diffusion-based generative modeling in terms of both sample quality and distribution coverage. While standard maximum likelihood training provides a principled objective with strong theoretical grounding, empirical studies indicate that previous training objectives in diffusion models often face an inverse correlation between likelihood optimization and perceptual evaluations. We propose the Rényi diffusion model, a unified generative framework that formulates training objectives using Rényi divergence. This yields a generalized score matching objective providing explicit control over the trade-off between sample quality and distribution coverage. Experiments demonstrate improved balance between density estimation and sample generation performances across multiple datasets without modifying model architectures or sampling procedures.

We propose the Rényi diffusion model, a unified generative framework that formulates training objectives using Rényi divergence. This yields a generalized score matching objective providing explicit control over the trade-off between sample quality and distribution coverage. paragraphs: Training a generative model involves both representing the data distribution and producing samples that look good. These goals can pull in different directions: the abstract notes empirical evidence that likelihood improvement in diffusion models can accompany worse perceptual evaluations. This paper addresses that tension by changing the objective used during training.

Rényi diffusion models formulate their objectives through Rényi divergence, yielding a generalized score-matching objective. The framework provides explicit control over the balance between sample quality and distribution coverage. Coverage concerns how broadly the model represents the data distribution, while sample quality concerns the properties of the individual outputs it generates.

Across multiple datasets, experiments show a better balance between density estimation and sample generation performance. These gains are obtained without changing model architectures or sampling procedures, locating the contribution in how learning is directed. The result supports treating the quality–coverage balance as an adjustable part of training, rather than assuming that optimizing a single conventional objective will automatically improve both aspects together.
summary.tldr: Rényi diffusion models provide a training objective that explicitly controls the balance between sample quality and distribution coverage.

title: Rényi Diffusion Models

abstract: Auto-Regressive (AR) models with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) are a dominant paradigm for achieving “System 2” reasoning. However, this approach suffers from significant latency due to the serial, token-by-token generation mechanism of AR models. In contrast, Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) offer inherent speed advantages via parallel sequence generation, yet they often struggle with accuracy in complex reasoning due to a lack of rigorous search, evaluation, and revision capabilities. Directly applying MCTS to diffusion models faces architectural barriers, since the denoising generation process lacks the discrete decision steps that naturally accommodate tree search. To retain efficiency while improving the reasoning ability, we propose DiffuReason, a Monte Carlo tree search reasoning algorithm for diffusion models. By modeling the generation process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), DiffuReason discretizes the continuous diffusion flow into searchable thought blocks. During the reverse generation process, DiffuReason recursively performs four MCTS-style stages: select the best node (block), expand to obtain candidate nodes, simulate to evaluate node values, and revise the unsatisfactory nodes. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DiffuReason significantly improves the reasoning ability of diffusion models, and achieves superior balance of accuracy and efficiency even compared with auto-regressive models.

paragraphs: DiffuReason aims to give diffusion language models more deliberate reasoning while retaining the efficiency of parallel generation. Autoregressive models can combine token-by-token generation with tree search, but the resulting serial process adds latency. Diffusion models generate differently and lack the natural discrete decision points that such search procedures expect.

The method represents diffusion generation as a Markov decision process and divides its continuous progression into searchable thought blocks. These blocks supply the units needed to organize alternative reasoning paths into a tree. During reverse generation, the algorithm repeatedly selects a promising block, expands candidate continuations, simulates to evaluate their values, and revises unsatisfactory nodes.

This construction supplies explicit search, evaluation, and revision within diffusion generation. Its contribution is therefore both a reasoning procedure and a way to reconcile tree search with a different generation architecture. Mathematical reasoning experiments show significant improvements in diffusion-model reasoning, along with a better accuracy–efficiency balance even against autoregressive models in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: DiffuReason turns diffusion generation into searchable thought blocks, improving mathematical reasoning and the reported balance between accuracy and efficiency.

title: DiffuReason: Enhancing Reasoning Ability for Diffusion Language Models via Monte Carlo Tree Search

abstract: Safe deployment of Large Language Model (LLM) agents in autonomous settings requires reliable oversight mechanisms. A central challenge is detecting scheming, where agents covertly pursue misaligned goals. One approach to mitigating such risks is LLM-based monitoring: using language models to examine agent behaviors for suspicious actions. We study constitutional black-box monitors: prompted classifiers that detect scheming using only externally observable inputs and outputs, optimized on synthetic data generated from natural-language behavior specifications. We introduce two pipelines for generating synthetic agent trajectories, STRIDE (iterative refinement) and Gloom (agent-environment simulation), from which we generate 1,000 samples each. We optimize monitors on these datasets via prompt sweeps, human refinement, and automated prompt optimization, and evaluate performance on 7,500 held-out trajectories from Control Arena, a suite of grounded environments where agents operate in more realistic contexts. Our results demonstrate that monitors selected purely on synthetic data can generalize to more realistic environments, capturing a meaningful scheming signal. However, we find that performance saturates quickly in our setting, with simple prompt sweeps matching the results of more extensive optimization. Pushing beyond this limit yields no further improvements and instead leads to overfitting.

paragraphs: This paper studies monitors that try to detect agents covertly pursuing misaligned goals. The monitors are language-model classifiers that inspect externally visible inputs and outputs, without relying on access to internal reasoning. Natural-language behavior specifications guide the creation of synthetic examples used to develop and select the monitoring prompts.

Two pipelines generate those examples: STRIDE iteratively refines agent trajectories, while Gloom uses agent-environment simulation. Each produces 1,000 samples. The researchers compare prompt sweeps, human refinement, and automated prompt optimization, then evaluate the resulting monitors on 7,500 held-out trajectories from Control Arena, where agents act in more realistic, grounded environments.

Monitors selected entirely using synthetic data capture a meaningful scheming signal on the more realistic evaluation. The study therefore supports synthetic data as a useful source of monitoring supervision while identifying a concrete limit to additional prompt optimization.
summary.tldr: Monitors selected on synthetic agent behavior can detect scheming in more realistic environments, but further prompt optimization quickly saturates and can overfit.

title: Constitutional Black-Box Monitoring for Scheming in LLM Agents

abstract: With the current surge in spatial reasoning, researchers have made significant progress in understanding indoor scenes, but still struggle with more diverse applications. This paper aims to advance all-scale spatial reasoning by tackling two key challenges: 1) the heavy reliance on indoor 3D scans and labor-intensive annotations for dataset curation; 2) the absence of all-scale modeling, which often leads to overfitting to single scenes. In this paper, we introduce a holistic solution that integrates a structured spatial reasoning knowledge system, scale-aware modeling, and a progressive training paradigm, as the first attempt to broaden the scope of all-scale spatial intelligence. Using a task-specific, specialist-driven automated pipeline, we curate over 38K video scenes across 5 spatial scales to create SpaceVista-1M, a dataset comprising 1M spatial QAs spanning 19 diverse tasks. While specialist models offer valuable domain knowledge, they are often unreliable evaluators. Therefore, we build an all-scale benchmark with precise annotations by manually recording and retrieving videos. Nevertheless, naive training with SpaceVista-1M often yields suboptimal results due to the potential knowledge conflict. Accordingly, we introduce SpaceVista-7B, a spatial reasoning model that accepts inputs beyond semantics and uses scale as an anchor for scale-aware experts and progressive rewards. Finally, extensive evaluations across 5 benchmarks, including our SpaceVista-Bench, demonstrate competitive performance, showcasing generalization across all scales and scenarios. All materials will be released at https://mm2km.github.io/.

paragraphs: Visual spatial reasoning has advanced in indoor scenes, but extending it across different physical scales requires broader data and modeling. SpaceVista addresses reliance on indoor scans and costly annotations, alongside models’ tendency to specialize in single-scene settings. It combines a structured spatial knowledge system, scale-aware modeling, and progressive training.

An automated pipeline driven by task-specific specialist models collects more than 38,000 video scenes across five spatial scales. The resulting SpaceVista-1M dataset contains one million spatial questions and answers across 19 tasks. SpaceVista-7B therefore uses scale to organize specialized experts and progressive rewards, with inputs extending beyond semantics. The contribution joins broader coverage with a model designed to account for differences between scales.
summary.tldr: SpaceVista combines a million-question dataset with scale-aware training to extend visual spatial reasoning across five physical scales.

title: SpaceVista: All-Scale Visual Spatial Reasoning from mm to km

abstract: Affine Maximizer Auctions (AMAs), a generalized mechanism family from VCG, are widely used in automated mechanism design due to their inherent dominant-strategy incentive compatibility (DSIC) and individual rationality (IR). However, as the payment form is fixed, AMA’s expressiveness is restricted, especially in distributions where bidders’ valuations are correlated. In this paper, we propose Correlation-Aware AMA (CA-AMA), a novel framework that augments AMA with a new correlation-aware payment. We show that any CA-AMA preserves the DSIC property and formalize finding optimal CA-AMA as a constraint optimization problem subject to the IR constraint. Then, we theoretically characterize scenarios where classic AMAs can perform arbitrarily poorly compared to the optimal revenue, while the CA-AMA can reach the optimal revenue. For optimizing CA-AMA, we design a practical two-stage training algorithm. We derive that the target function’s continuity and the generalization bound on the degree of deviation from strict IR. Finally, extensive experiments showcase that our algorithm can find an approximate optimal CA-AMA in various distributions with improved revenue and a low degree of violation of IR.

paragraphs: Affine Maximizer Auctions are useful in automated auction design because they support truthful bidding and individual rationality. Their fixed payment structure, however, can limit revenue when bidders’ valuations are correlated. This paper expands the payment mechanism so that the auction can make use of those relationships.

The proposed Correlation-Aware AMA preserves dominant-strategy incentive compatibility: truthful bidding remains a dominant strategy. Choosing the best mechanism becomes a constrained optimization problem with individual rationality as a requirement. The authors characterize scenarios where conventional AMAs can earn arbitrarily little relative to optimal revenue, whereas the expanded family can attain that optimum.

A practical two-stage training procedure searches for these mechanisms. The analysis establishes continuity of the target function and a generalization bound concerning deviations from strict individual rationality. Experiments find approximately optimal mechanisms across various distributions, with improved revenue and small individual-rationality violations. This distinction matters: the theoretical truthfulness property is preserved, while the trained mechanisms are evaluated for how closely they satisfy the separate participation constraint.
summary.tldr: Correlation-aware payments expand affine maximizer auctions’ revenue potential while preserving dominant-strategy truthfulness.

title: Enhancing Affine Maximizer Auctions with Correlation-Aware Payment

abstract: Vision-language foundation models such as CLIP and SigLIP provide widely used representations for multimodal learning systems. While these models are typically compared through downstream performance, such evaluations often do not explain how their representations differ structurally. In this work, we study this problem through the task of Contrastive Embedding Clustering: identifying sample subsets that are weakly clustered under one representation but strongly clustered under another. We propose Kernel Optimization for Discrepancy Analysis (KODA), a kernel-based framework for contrastive representation comparison and alignment. KODA constructs unified multimodal kernels through modality-wise kernel composition and formulates discrepancy discovery as a constrained optimization problem that searches for coherent structures in one representation while suppressing coherence in a reference representation. This yields interpretable discrepancy directions associated with specific sample subsets and modality interactions. To scale KODA to large vision-language datasets, we develop randomized low-dimensional approximations of joint kernels using random projections, including Random Fourier Features for shift-invariant kernels. Empirically, KODA identifies consistent and interpretable discrepancy structures across vision-language representations and provides sample subsets for representation alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/yokiwuuu/KODA.

paragraphs: Vision-language models are commonly compared by their performance on downstream tasks, but those scores reveal little about how the models organize information internally. KODA studies structural differences by searching for groups of examples that cluster tightly in one representation but weakly in another. These groups make disagreement between representations more concrete.

The framework builds multimodal similarity kernels by composing kernels for individual modalities. It then solves a constrained optimization problem that favors coherent structure in one representation while suppressing coherence in a reference representation. The resulting discrepancy directions connect differences to particular sample subsets and interactions between modalities, making the comparison interpretable.

To handle large datasets, the authors approximate joint kernels in lower-dimensional spaces using randomized projections, including Random Fourier Features for suitable kernels. Empirically, KODA finds consistent, interpretable discrepancies across vision-language representations and supplies sample subsets for alignment. Its contribution is therefore both diagnostic and constructive: it identifies where representations organize data differently and produces examples that can be used when aligning them.
summary.tldr: KODA finds interpretable groups of examples that vision-language models organize differently and provides subsets for representation alignment.

title: KODA: Contrastive Representation Comparison and Alignment for Vision-Language Foundation Models

abstract: Training data plays a central role in large language models (LLMs) optimization, motivating extensive research on data scheduling strategies. Most existing approaches concentrate on adjusting the overall data distribution but neglect the underlying interactions between samples during training. However, we argue that such interactions cannot be overlooked, as real-world data samples frequently exhibit directional influences on each other, making the training order crucial. Intuitively, we can prioritize train-units with greater influence to improves learning efficiency. In this work, we propose $D^3$, a Dynamic, Directional graph-constrained Data scheduling framework. $D^3$ formulates the complex interactions among train-units as a dynamic influence graph, where edges represent loss-based dependencies. It then solves a constrained optimization problem over this graph to derive the training order, which ensures that the data sequence respects the evolving information flow throughout training. Our approach is theoretically motivated and yields consistent improvements over existing data scheduling methods across both pre-training and post-training phases. Furthermore, for scalability, $D^3$ also employs an efficient approximation algorithm that keeps the additional computational overhead within a manageable range. For future research, the code is available at https://github.com/xuyj233/D3.

paragraphs: Choosing training data involves more than deciding how much to sample from each source. This paper argues that training examples can influence one another directionally, making their order consequential. Learning from an influential training unit earlier may change how effectively the model learns from other units later.

D³ represents these relationships as a changing directed graph. Its edges describe dependencies measured through loss, and a constrained optimization procedure uses the graph to determine training order. Because the graph evolves during learning, the schedule can reflect changes in the relationships between training units instead of following one fixed ordering throughout.

The authors provide theoretical motivation and report consistent improvements over existing scheduling approaches during both pre-training and post-training. They also introduce an approximation algorithm to keep the additional computation manageable. The contribution is therefore a way to make interactions among training units operational: those interactions guide sequencing, while the approximation addresses the cost of applying that idea at scale.
summary.tldr: D³ schedules language-model training using a dynamic directed graph of loss-based dependencies between training units.

title: D$^3$: Dynamic Directional Graph-Constrained Data Scheduling for LLM Training

abstract: Current linear State-Space Models (SSMs) for 3D point clouds typically rely on 1D serialization schemes (e.g., Hilbert curves) for global modeling. In dense scenes, such imposed order can disrupt spatial continuity and induce what we call serialization bias. We propose AnIsoNet, a framework that decouples anisotropic geometry from isotropic semantics via two dedicated modules: Local Anisotropy Geometric Modeling (LAGM) and Global Isotropy Semantic Aggregation (GISA). LAGM uses ellipsoidal encoding to capture local directionality without relying on global order. GISA is configured according to dataset-level geometric density: dense-scene datasets use Identity Mode to avoid additional geometry-driven re-serialization, whereas sparse-object datasets use Morton serialization to provide a lightweight spatial prior. This avoids redundant multi-view scanning while preserving O(N) complexity. On S3DIS, reducing artificial serialization in dense scenes yields 82.62% mIoU, surpassing PCM by 3.0%. On ScanObjectNN, Morton serialization for sparse objects reaches 94.21% OA (+1.6%). On ScanNetV2, our model achieves 78.52% mIoU, surpassing PTv3 (77.5%) without pre-training, with only 12.2M parameters and 37G FLOPs.

paragraphs: Turning a 3D point cloud into a one-dimensional sequence can impose an order that disrupts spatial continuity, especially in dense scenes. This paper calls that effect serialization bias. AnIsoNet addresses it by separating local directional geometry from global semantic aggregation, allowing each component to handle a different aspect of the data.

The local module uses ellipsoidal encoding to capture directionality without depending on a global ordering. The global module is configured according to dataset-level geometric density: dense scenes use Identity Mode to avoid further geometry-driven reordering, while sparse objects use Morton serialization as a lightweight spatial prior. On ScanNetV2, the model reaches 78.52% mIoU without pretraining, compared with 77.5% for PTv3, using 12.2 million parameters and 37G FLOPs. These findings support tailoring serialization to the dataset's geometric density rather than imposing the same ordering strategy across dense scenes and sparse objects.
summary.tldr: AnIsoNet separates local geometry from global semantics and adjusts serialization to dataset density while retaining linear complexity.

title: Rethinking Serialization in Linear 3D Vision: Decoupling Anisotropic Geometry from Isotropic Semantics

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) exhibit remarkable general capabilities but struggle significantly with spatial reasoning tasks. In this paper, we uncover a critical representation-output misalignment via linear probing: LVLMs correctly encode spatial features internally, but generate incorrect results in the final text. To address this, we pioneer the Inference-time Geometric Manifold Adaptation paradigm and propose GRASP (Geometric Rectification for Active Spatial Perception), a training-free framework to awaken these latent capabilities. GRASP employs Manifold Differential Search to identify optimal geometric counterfactuals, which then drive a dual-level rectification mechanism: Implicit Trajectory Correction to rectify attenuated intrinsic geometric features in intermediate decoder layers, and Explicit Distribution Alignment to break the dominance of language priors at the output layer. Extensive experiments spanning diverse architectures (LLaVA, Qwen 2.5/3-VL) and positional encoding paradigms (1D APE, 2D/3D RoPE) across image and video benchmarks (WhatsUp, VSR, VSI-Bench) demonstrate that GRASP significantly mitigates spatial hallucinations without parameter updates, achieving accuracy gains of up to 26.1% on image benchmarks and 9.7% on video reasoning tasks, consistently outperforming baseline methods.

paragraphs: GRASP investigates why vision-language models can give incorrect spatial answers even when relevant spatial information is present internally. Using linear probes, the authors identify a mismatch between encoded spatial features and final text outputs. Their approach therefore focuses on bringing existing geometric information into the model's answer during inference.

The framework searches for geometric counterfactuals and uses them to guide two forms of correction. Inside the decoder, it strengthens geometric features that have become attenuated along the computation. At the output, it adjusts the distribution to counter the dominance of language priors. These interventions require no parameter updates, making the method a training-free adaptation of inference.

Experiments span multiple model architectures, positional encoding schemes, and image and video benchmarks. The authors report reduced spatial hallucinations and accuracy gains of up to 26.1% on image benchmarks and 9.7% on video reasoning tasks, consistently exceeding the tested baselines. These findings support the idea that some spatial errors arise from how available representations influence outputs, and can be mitigated by correcting that pathway.
summary.tldr: GRASP corrects the pathway from internal spatial features to text outputs at inference time, improving spatial reasoning without parameter updates.

title: GRASP: Awakening Latent Spatial Reasoning in LVLMs via Training-free Geometric Rectification

abstract: Humans abstract experiences into structured representations to facilitate pattern inference and knowledge transfer. While the hippocampal-entorhinal (HPC-MEC) circuit is known to represent both spatial and conceptual spaces, the mechanisms for concurrently extracting abstract structures from continuous, high-dimensional dynamics remain poorly understood. We propose a brain-inspired hierarchical model that simultaneously infers latent transitions and constructs a predictive visual world model. Our architecture employs an inverse model for structural extraction alongside an HPC-MEC coupling model that dissociates relational structures (MEC) from integrated episodic scenes (HPC). Using rotation dynamics as a benchmark, we demonstrate the model’s capacity for structural abstraction. By leveraging velocity-driven path integration, the framework enables robust prediction and structural reuse across diverse contexts, thereby achieving structural generalization. This work provides a novel computational framework for understanding how brain-inspired, self-supervised learning of world models facilitates the acquisition of reusable abstract knowledge.
