paragraphs: This paper studies how a visual world model can extract reusable structure from continuous, high-dimensional experience. Its inspiration is the hippocampal-entorhinal circuit, which represents spatial and conceptual relationships. The authors propose a hierarchical computational model that learns latent transitions while also constructing a model for predicting visual experience.

An inverse model extracts structure, while a coupling model separates relational representations associated with the medial entorhinal cortex from integrated episodic scenes associated with the hippocampus. This separation gives relational knowledge a distinct role within the architecture. The framework also uses velocity-driven path integration to support predictions as the modeled dynamics evolve.

Using rotation dynamics as a benchmark, the authors demonstrate structural abstraction, robust prediction, and reuse of structure across diverse contexts. These findings support structural generalization within the studied setting: learned relationships can contribute to predictions beyond a single context. The work offers a computational account of how brain-inspired, self-supervised world modeling can acquire reusable abstract knowledge, connecting its architectural separation of structure and scenes to the reported generalization behavior.
summary.tldr: A hippocampal-entorhinal-inspired world model separates relational structure from episodic scenes and demonstrates structural reuse on rotation dynamics.

title: Structure Abstraction and Generalization in a Hippocampal-Entorhinal Inspired World Model

abstract: Autonomous code agents built on large language models are reshaping software and AI development through tool use, long-horizon reasoning, and self-directed interaction. However, this autonomy introduces a previously unrecognized security risk: agentic interaction fundamentally expands the LLM attack surface, enabling systematic probing and recovery of hidden system prompts that guide model behavior. We identify system prompt extraction as an emergent vulnerability intrinsic to code agents and present JustAsk, a self-evolving framework that autonomously discovers effective extraction strategies through interaction alone. Unlike prior prompt-engineering or dataset-based attacks, JustAsk requires no handcrafted prompts, labeled supervision, or privileged access beyond standard user interaction. It formulates extraction as an online exploration problem, using Upper Confidence Bound-based strategy selection and a hierarchical skill space spanning atomic probes and high-level orchestration. These skills exploit imperfect system-instruction generalization and inherent tensions between helpfulness and safety. Evaluated on 41 black-box commercial models across multiple providers, JustAsk consistently achieves full or near-complete system prompt recovery, revealing recurring design- and architecture-level vulnerabilities. Our results expose system prompts as a critical yet largely unprotected attack surface in modern agent systems.

paragraphs: Autonomous coding agents can use tools and pursue extended interactions, expanding the ways they interact with language models. This paper examines a security consequence: those capabilities can support systematic recovery of hidden system prompts. The authors present prompt extraction as an emergent vulnerability of agentic interaction and investigate it across commercial models.

Their framework, JustAsk, learns extraction strategies through interaction without handcrafted attack prompts, labeled supervision, or privileged access beyond ordinary user interaction. The results highlight the security importance of evaluating sustained, adaptive agent interactions when assessing protection of hidden instructions.
summary.tldr: JustAsk autonomously discovers prompt-extraction strategies and reports full or near-complete system prompt recovery across 41 commercial models.

abstract: Markov decision processes are an effective tool in modeling decision-making in uncertain dynamic environments. Since the parameters of these models are typically estimated from data, learned from experience, or designed by hand, it is not surprising that the actual performance of a chosen strategy often significantly differs from the designer’s initial expectations due to unavoidable model uncertainty. In this paper, we present a percentile criterion that captures the trade-off between optimistic and pessimistic points of view on MDP with parameter uncertainty. We describe tractable methods that take parameter uncertainty into account in the process of decision making. Finally, we propose a costeffective exploration strategy when it is possible to invest (money, time or computation efforts) in actions that will reduce the uncertainty in the parameters.

Since the parameters of these models are typically estimated from data, learned from experience, or designed by hand, it is not surprising that the actual performance of a chosen strategy often significantly differs from the designer’s initial expectations due to unavoidable model uncertainty. In this paper, we present a percentile criterion that captures the trade-off between optimistic and pessimistic points of view on MDP with parameter uncertainty. paragraphs: A Markov decision process can describe decisions in an uncertain, changing environment, but its own parameters may also be uncertain. Parameters estimated from data, learned through experience, or specified by hand can differ from the true system. Consequently, a strategy’s actual performance may depart substantially from what its designer expected.

The paper proposes a percentile-based criterion for choosing strategies under this parameter uncertainty. The criterion expresses a trade-off between optimistic and pessimistic assessments of possible performance. The authors also describe tractable methods that incorporate uncertainty into decision making, making uncertainty part of strategy selection itself.

The approach extends to exploration when resources can be spent on actions that reduce uncertainty about model parameters. Those resources may be money, time, or computation. The authors propose a cost-effective exploration strategy for this setting. The connection is that learning about the model can itself be a decision with a cost: exploration is useful insofar as reducing uncertainty helps subsequent choices justify that investment.
summary.tldr: A percentile criterion balances optimism and pessimism in uncertain MDPs and supports resource-aware exploration to reduce parameter uncertainty.

title: Percentile optimization in uncertain Markov decision processes with application to efficient exploration

abstract: We extend the well-known BFGS quasi-Newton method and its limited-memory variant (LBFGS) to the optimization of nonsmooth convex objectives. This is done in a rigorous fashion by generalizing three components of BFGS to subdifferentials: The local quadratic model, the identification of a descent direction, and the Wolfe line search conditions. We apply the resulting sub(L)BFGS algorithm to L 2 -regularized risk minimization with binary hinge loss, and its direction-finding component to L 1 -regularized risk minimization with logistic loss. In both settings our generic algorithms perform comparable to or better than their counterparts in specialized state-of-the-art solvers.

We apply the resulting sub(L)BFGS algorithm to L 2 -regularized risk minimization with binary hinge loss, and its direction-finding component to L 1 -regularized risk minimization with logistic loss. paragraphs: This paper adapts BFGS and its limited-memory version, LBFGS, to convex optimization problems whose objectives are not smooth. These problems can contain corners where an ordinary gradient is insufficient to describe how the objective changes. The goal is to retain the usefulness of these established optimization methods while giving their treatment of nonsmooth objectives a rigorous foundation.

The authors generalize three connected ingredients using subdifferentials, which describe possible slopes at nonsmooth points. These ingredients are the local quadratic approximation, the procedure for finding a direction that decreases the objective, and the Wolfe conditions used to choose a step along that direction. Addressing all three makes the extension a coordinated optimization method.

They apply the resulting sub(L)BFGS algorithm to L2-regularized learning with binary hinge loss. They also apply its direction-finding component to L1-regularized learning with logistic loss. In both settings, the generic methods perform comparably to or better than corresponding components of specialized leading solvers. The results support the practical value of a broadly applicable nonsmooth optimization approach.
summary.tldr: The paper extends BFGS to nonsmooth convex objectives and reports competitive performance against specialized solvers in two learning settings.

title: A quasi-Newton approach to non-smooth convex optimization

abstract: Almost all tree kernels proposed in the literature match substructures without taking into account their relative positioning with respect to one another. In this paper, we propose a novel family of kernels which explicitly focus on this type of information. Specifically, after defining a family of tree kernels based on routes between nodes, we present an efficient implementation for a member of this family. Experimental results on four different datasets show that our method is able to reach state of the art performances, obtaining in some cases performances better than computationally more demanding tree kernels.
originalAbstract: Almost all tree kernels proposed in the literature match substructures without taking into account their relative positioning with respect to one another. In this paper, we propose a novel family of kernels which explicitly focus on this type of information. Specifically, after defining a family of tree kernels based on routes between nodes, we present an efficient implementation for a member of this family. Experimental results on four different datasets show that our method is able to reach state of the art performances, obtaining in some cases performances better than computationally more demanding tree kernels.

paragraphs: Tree kernels compare tree-structured objects through their constituent structures. The paper identifies a gap in almost all earlier tree kernels: they match substructures without accounting for how those pieces are positioned relative to one another. This can leave relational information outside the comparison, even when the pieces themselves are recognized.

The authors propose a family of kernels based on routes between tree nodes. Routes make relative positioning an explicit part of the representation used to compare trees. They also provide an efficient implementation of one member of the family, connecting the proposed similarity measure to a computationally usable method.

Experiments on four datasets show that the method reaches state-of-the-art performance. In some cases it performs better than tree kernels that require more computation. These findings support including the arrangement of substructures when comparing trees, while also showing that the implemented route kernel can be computationally competitive. The empirical advantage is reported for some comparisons, rather than as uniform superiority over all tree kernels.
summary.tldr: Route-based tree kernels capture relative positioning and achieve competitive results with an efficient implementation.

title: Route kernels for trees

abstract: Graph based semi-supervised learning (SSL) methods play an increasingly important role in practical machine learning systems. A crucial step in graph based SSL methods is the conversion of data into a weighted graph. However, most of the SSL literature focuses on developing label inference algorithms without extensively studying the graph building method and its effect on performance. This article provides an empirical study of leading semi-supervised methods under a wide range of graph construction algorithms. These SSL inference algorithms include the Local and Global Consistency (LGC) method, the Gaussian Random Field (GRF) method, the Graph Transduction via Alternating Minimization (GTAM) method as well as other techniques. Several approaches for graph construction, sparsification and weighting are explored including the popular k-nearest neighbors method (kNN) and the b-matching method. As opposed to the greedily constructed kNN graph, the b-matched graph ensures each node in the graph has the same number of edges and produces a balanced or regular graph. Experimental results on both artificial data and real benchmark datasets indicate that b-matching produces more robust graphs and therefore provides significantly better prediction accuracy without any significant change in computation time.

As opposed to the greedily constructed kNN graph, the b-matched graph ensures each node in the graph has the same number of edges and produces a balanced or regular graph. paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning first turns data into a weighted network and then uses that network to infer labels. This paper examines the first stage, arguing that graph construction deserves attention alongside the label-inference algorithm. Different choices of connections and weights can change the structure on which inference depends.

The authors empirically compare graph construction, sparsification, and weighting methods across several inference algorithms, including Local and Global Consistency, Gaussian Random Fields, and Graph Transduction via Alternating Minimization. A central comparison is between nearest-neighbor graphs and b-matching. Whereas nearest-neighbor construction is greedy, b-matching ensures every node has the same number of edges, producing a balanced graph.

Experiments on artificial data and real benchmark datasets indicate that b-matching produces more robust graphs and significantly better prediction accuracy without a significant change in computation time. These results highlight graph construction as a consequential modeling choice. The reported gains come from improving the network supplied to inference, demonstrating that progress need not depend solely on changing the label-inference procedure.
summary.tldr: Balanced graphs built with b-matching improve reported semi-supervised prediction accuracy without significantly changing computation time.

title: Graph construction and b-matching for semi-supervised learning

abstract: For centuries, scholars have explored the deep links among human languages. In this paper, we present a class of probabilistic models that use these links as a form of naturally occurring supervision. These models allow us to substantially improve performance for core text processing tasks, such as morphological segmentation, part-of-speech tagging, and syntactic parsing. Besides these traditional NLP tasks, we also present a multilingual model for the computational decipherment of lost languages.

These models allow us to substantially improve performance for core text processing tasks, such as morphological segmentation, part-of-speech tagging, and syntactic parsing. Besides these traditional NLP tasks, we also present a multilingual model for the computational decipherment of lost languages.

paragraphs: The paper uses relationships among human languages as a source of information for learning. Its central idea is that these relationships can provide naturally occurring supervision: structure shared or linked across languages can help guide a model. The authors develop a class of probabilistic models around this multilingual learning approach.

They report substantial performance improvements on several core language-processing tasks. These include morphological segmentation, which concerns the meaningful pieces within words; part-of-speech tagging, which assigns grammatical categories; and syntactic parsing, which identifies sentence structure. The range of tasks matters because the contribution is presented as a broader modeling approach rather than a method for only one linguistic prediction.

The paper also presents a multilingual model for computational decipherment of lost languages. This extends the use of cross-language relationships beyond the traditional tasks considered in the study. Taken together, the contributions show how probabilistic models can make linguistic connections useful as learning signals, with reported gains on established tasks and a further application to decipherment.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic multilingual models use relationships among languages as natural supervision, improving core language tasks and supporting a model for deciphering lost languages.

title: Climbing the Tower of Babel: Unsupervised Multilingual Learning

abstract: We propose a new fast algorithm for approximate MAP inference on factor graphs, which combines augmented Lagrangian optimization with the dual decomposition method. Each slave subproblem is given a quadratic penalty, which pushes toward faster consensus than in previous subgradient approaches. Our algorithm is provably convergent, parallelizable, and suitable for fine decompositions of the graph. We show how it can efficiently handle problems with (possibly global) structural constraints via simple sort operations. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that our approach compares favorably with the state-of-the-art.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that our approach compares favorably with the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: The paper addresses approximate maximum a posteriori inference on factor graphs: finding a high-scoring joint assignment while respecting the relationships and constraints represented by the graph. Its proposed algorithm combines dual decomposition, which divides the inference problem into smaller subproblems, with augmented Lagrangian optimization to coordinate their solutions.

Each subproblem receives a quadratic penalty that encourages agreement with the others. This matters because solving the pieces independently is insufficient when they make conflicting choices about shared variables. The penalty is intended to drive consensus faster than earlier approaches based on subgradients. The algorithm is parallelizable and supports fine decompositions, allowing the graph to be divided into many small pieces.

The authors establish convergence and describe how simple sorting operations can efficiently accommodate structural constraints, including constraints that may span the whole problem. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data compare favorably with competing methods. The convergence result concerns the proposed approximate inference algorithm; the abstract does not equate convergence with exact MAP recovery.
summary.tldr: Quadratic agreement penalties make decomposed approximate MAP inference convergent, parallelizable, and able to handle structural constraints efficiently.

title: An Augmented Lagrangian Approach to Constrained MAP Inference

abstract: We present a new anytime algorithm that achieves near-optimal regret for any instance of finite stochastic partial monitoring. In particular, the new algorithm achieves the minimax regret, within logarithmic factors, for both “easy” and “hard” problems. For easy problems, it additionally achieves logarithmic individual regret. Most importantly, the algorithm is adaptive in the sense that if the opponent strategy is in an “easy region” of the strategy space then the regret grows as if the problem was easy. As an implication, we show that under some reasonable additional assumptions, the algorithm enjoys an O(√ T ) regret in Dynamic Pricing, proven to be hard by Bartok et al. (2011).

paragraphs: The paper studies finite stochastic partial monitoring, where a learner must make decisions using incomplete feedback. It introduces an anytime algorithm with near-optimal regret across problem instances. Regret measures the cumulative cost of learning compared with a reference decision strategy, so controlling its growth captures how quickly the learner makes effective use of feedback.

The algorithm achieves minimax regret up to logarithmic factors for both easy and hard problem classes. For easy problems, it also obtains logarithmic instance-specific regret. Its distinctive feature is adaptation within a problem: when the opponent’s strategy lies in an easy region of the strategy space, regret grows at the rate associated with an easy problem.

This distinction matters because a problem’s worst-case classification need not describe the difficulty of the strategy actually encountered. As an application, the authors establish square-root-in-time regret for dynamic pricing under additional assumptions, even though that problem is classified as hard. The pricing guarantee is conditional on those assumptions, while illustrating the benefit of adapting to favorable regions.
summary.tldr: An adaptive partial-monitoring algorithm achieves near-optimal regret and can exploit easy regions even within generally hard problems.

title: An adaptive algorithm for finite stochastic partial monitoring
